title: National Populations
description:
The 'Population, total' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is based on the de facto definition of population, which counts all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship. The values shown are midyear estimates. Population estimates are usually based on national population censuses. Estimates for the years before and after the census are interpolations or extrapolations based on demographic models. Errors and undercounting occur even in high-income countries. The spatial coverage of this data set is global and on the national level, and the temporal coverage runs from 1960 through present day. In developing countries errors may be substantial because of limits in the transport, communications, and other resources required to conduct and analyze a full census. The quality and reliability of official demographic data are also affected by public trust in the government, government commitment to full and accurate enumeration, confidentiality and protection against misuse of census data, and census agencies' independence from political influence. Moreover, comparability of population indicators is limited by differences in the concepts, definitions, collection procedures, and estimation methods used by national statistical agencies and other organizations that collect the data. The currentness of a census and the availability of complementary data from surveys or registration systems are objective ways to judge demographic data quality. Some European countries' registration systems offer complete information on population in the absence of a census. The United Nations Statistics Division monitors the completeness of vital registration systems. Some developing countries have made progress over the last 60 years, but others still have deficiencies in civil registration systems. International migration is the only other factor besides birth and death rates that directly determines a country's population growth. Estimating migration is difficult. At any time many people are located outside their home country as tourists, workers, or refugees or for other reasons. Standards for the duration and purpose of international moves that qualify as migration vary, and estimates require information on flows into and out of countries that is difficult to collect. Population projections, starting from a base year are projected forward using assumptions of mortality, fertility, and migration by age and sex through 2050, based on the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects database medium variant.

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](64c948a6-5e34-4ef2-bb69-6a6535967bd5) as a replacement.**_
  
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS.  The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot /fire pixels. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Historical Gridded Population
description:
### Overview  
  
The History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE version 3.2), is a combination of gridded historical population and land use estimates. The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time; then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator).
  
  

HYDE is the first spatially explicit estimate of population and land use going back to 10,000 BC. Population is represented by maps of total, urban, and rural population, population density and built-up area. This dataset on Resource Watch describes the population data of HYDE, and the land use data can be viewed [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088c-HYDE-Anthromes).
   
  

The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2017 AD at a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km). HYDE was developed by the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency, and is used by the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project ([CMIP6](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/wgcm-cmip/wgcm-cmip6)).   
  
### Methodology  
  
The authors estimated population totals at the state or province level by using a variety of historical sources and then used algorithms to spatially distribute the state level population to 5 arc minute pixels. 
   
  

The basis for the state level population data is the United Nations World Populations Prospects (2008 Revision) for the 1950–2017 period. The pre-1950 historical estimates were largely taken from McEvedy and Jones (1978), Livi-Bacci (2007), and Maddison (2001). The authors supplemented these sources with the sub-national population numbers of Populstat (Lahmeyer, personal communication, 2004) and many other country specific sources. The country specific sources of population estimates are outlined in the supplementary information of their [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/). The authors then used interpolation techniques to fill in gaps between population sources. 
   
  

For the present population spatial distribution, the authors used the spatial patterns from the Gridded Population of the World (GPW v3) and LandScan (2014) for the year 2012 to allocate the total population for each administrative unit to the 5 arc minute pixel level. LandScan is a global population database with information on population totals at 1 km resolution from the Department of Energy’s Oak Ridge National Laboratory. In order to distribute the state level population to the pixel resolution (5 arc minutes), the 2012 population patterns from LandScan are gradually replaced with weighting maps based on various proxies such as soil suitability, slope, distance to water and case studies from several disciplines (e.g. history, archaeology).
   
  

For simplicity, current administrative level boundaries (town, county, etc.) were kept constant over time, and every historical source was adjusted to match the current subnational boundaries (e.g. by taking fractions of former larger empires). Country and regional totals were then checked against other historical estimates. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows data from the HYDE dataset with land use data categorized under [Anthropogenic Biomes](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088c-HYDE-Anthromes).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The HYDE dataset has additional population data including population count, rural population count, urban population count, and urban built-up area. HYDE also provides data on land use including pasture areas, irrigated crops and rainfed crops. The HYDE dataset covers 10,000 BC to 2017 at the following time intervals: every 1000 years from 10,000 BC to 0 AD, every 100 years from 0 AD to 1700 AD, every 10 years from 1700 AD to 2000, and every year from 2000 to 2017. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: City Expansion Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The city expansion index dataset shows outward and upward urban growth in 377 cities globally that have a population of over 1 million residents. Outward growth is the horizontal expansion of buildings and upward growth is the vertical expansion of buildings. The final dataset was normalized into comparable values called the Upward Growth Index and Outward Growth Index. A higher expansion index value means more growth is occurring. The dataset uses remote sensing data collected between 2000 and 2014.

  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the World Resources Report (WRR) Towards a More Equal City. It is intended to highlight regional trends in urban expansion and differences in urban structure within and between cities. Ultimately, it can be used to help governments understand how urban expansion can be managed in a way that achieves more equitable access to core services for the under-served while bringing wider economic and environmental benefits to cities. For the dataset to paint a complete picture it should ideally be used in conjunction with a matching dataset on the socioeconomic information of the city.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created using a combination of remote sensing data to determine upward and outward expansion in cities with a metropolitan population greater than 1 million. Remote sensing data was collected from mean summer backscatter power ratio (PR) from NASA's SeaWinds microwave scatterometer (Ku-band, 13.4 GHz) and built-up area from the multitemporal Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL). The data showed the outward growth of urban built-up areas between 2000 and 2014 measured from the Global Human Settlement Layer (GHSL) and upward growth between 2001 and 2009 measured using the power ratio (PR) from NASA’s SeaWinds microwave scatterometer. Each dataset was reprocessed to have the same spatial resolution of 0.05 degrees (about 5.6 km at the equator). To determine which cities had a metropolitan population greater than 1 million, Landscan data created by the Oak Ridge National Laboratory was combined with the Oxford Economics database to create a combined dataset of 377 cities. 
  
  
 Researchers overlayed an 11x11 pixel grid (121 total pixels) over each city using the dataset Populated Places from Natural Earth to create a unified boundary to measure the cities growth. The 11x11 grids were extracted and all grid cells with a built up value less than 20 percent were masked in GHSL. Total upward and outward growth were then calculated using the remaining pixels for each city by using a cluster analysis to group each pixel into similar urban growth patterns and structures. Finally, the values were converted into the upward urban growth index and outward urban growth index to allow for comparison of the values across cities. 
  
  
The final dataset was presented in raster format at a spatial resolution of 0.28 degrees (20.98 square kilometers at the equator). For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Availability of Ruminant Based Foods
description:
As nations urbanize and citizens become wealthier, people generally increase the share of resource-intensive foods—such as meats and dairy—in their diets. Ruminant meats (beef, lamb, goat), are particularly resource-intensive. Although some of this shift reflects health and welfare gains for many people, shifts to high-meat diets will make it harder for the world to achieve several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including those on hunger, healthy lives, water management, climate change, and terrestrial ecosystems.  
  
The availability of ruminant meat data represent retail-level availability of ruminant meats (beef, lamb, goat) per capita per day across the world, from 1961-2013, with a "business as usual" projection, RCP 8.5, out to 2050.  Data for 1961-2013 are from FAO's Food Balance Sheets. Data for 2050 are from FAO's projection of food demand and production.  
  
Because FAO projects that sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia in 2050 will still have insufficient calories to feed everyone adequately, WRI adjusted food amounts upward in those two regions to ensure 3,000 calories are available per person per day in all regions. Data for 2014-2050 are linear interpolations between observed (2013) and projected (2050) data.

title: Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual maximum extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for select years between 1980-2020. Antarctic sea ice typically reaches its maximum extent in September. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during September for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual maximum Antarctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent),natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent.

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081).

  
  
Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors:
- GSFC data:
  - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987
  - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991
  - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995
  - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007
  - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present
- NRTSI data:
  - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present

  
  
The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. 

  
  
Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. 

  
  
GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).

title: U.S. Ozone Above Regulatory Standards
description:
The Tracking Network uses Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) air quality monitor data to calculate Number of Days with Maximum 8-Hour Average Ozone Concentration Over the National Ambient Air Quality Standard. For each county with complete monitoring data, the data include: the year, state, county FIPS code, total county population, population with monitors, population without monitors, number of days above benchmark (default NAAQS), person-days above benchmark (default federal NAAQS). To calculate the annual number of days over the daily NAAQS, number of days with ozone levels over the daily 8-hr NAAQS for the entire year are summed. To calculate Person-days with ozone levels over the daily 8-hr NAAQS, the number of days over the daily NAAQS by the total population of the county are multiplied.

EPA Air Quality Standard monitoring data, which are used in the calculation of measures, are not present for all counties and days. Since ozone levels decrease significantly in the colder parts of the year in many areas, ozone is required to be monitored only during the "ozone season." Ozone seasons are designated on a State by State basis. When creating measures, we only consider monitors with 75% completeness during the ozone season. Additionally, the data for this indicator represent only counties that have air monitors; thus the data tend to reflect urban air quality (where most people live). Although populations in areas without monitors also may be exposed to ozone that exceeds the standard, they are not counted.

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Gross Domestic Product Per Capita
description:
### Overview  
  
Gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided per person. The gridded GDP per capita dataset used national GDP, gridded population data, and other factors to estimate GDP per capita at a 5 arc-minute resolution for each year from 1990 to 2015. This gridded GDP per capita dataset is important because it can be used for research at the sub-national level.   
  
GDP per capita measurements are in purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 U.S. dollars. The data was created at Aalto University. The authors also created the [gridded GDP](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc073-Gridded-GDP) data set.  
  
### Methodology  
  
To create a high resolution, complete picture of GDP per capita, the author calculated it using the World Bank Development Indicators database. For missing countries, they used data from the Central Intelligence Agency World Factbook. The temporal coverage of both the national and sub-national data varied considerably. To fill in the missing values, temporal interpolation and extrapolation approaches were used.  
  
To be consistent between the sub-national and national datasets, and to ensure the data set would represent official national statistics, the authors did not use the sub-national GDP per capita directly, but instead used the sub-national data to scale national GDP per capita. This was done for each year by first calculating population-weighted national GDP per capita from sub-national GDP per capita data and the HYDE 3.2 population data set. This output was then used in each sub-national unit to calculate the ratio between population-weighted national GDP and reported sub-national GDP. The final sub-national GDP per capita (in PPP) was calculated by multiplying the ratio with the reported national GDP per capita. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: India Projected Change in Average Temperature
description:
This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in average temperature over the Indian subcontinent. 

These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp).

Projected change in average temperature is computed using daily mean near-surface air temperature in degrees Celsius for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average.

The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.

title: Drivers of Deforestation
description:
This data set on deforestation drivers was adapted from Hosonuma et al. (2012) and illustrates the contribution of various industries ("drivers") to deforestation in Africa, the Americas and Asia (including Oceania). The driver data are summarized and analyzed for each of the 3 continents. Agriculture is the main driver of deforestation, but with geographic differences in the importance of commercial versus subsistence agriculture. The data include continental-level estimations for the relative area proportion and absolute net forest area change in km2 yr−1 (FAO 2010) for the period 2000–2010, deforestation drivers, and the relative disturbed forest area fraction of degradation drivers. The estimates are based on data from 46 tropical and subtropical countries and were obtained by the authors from REDD+ reports as well as Center for International Forestry Research country profiles (which include driver and activity information for deforestation and forest degradation), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change National Communications, and other reports. In total, driver data were available for 46 of the 100 (sub)tropical non-Annex I countries. These 46 countries account for 78% of the total forest area (in 2010) and 81% of forest loss (in 2000–2010) of the 100 countries under consideration, according to 2010 data from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization Forest Resources Assessment (FAO 2010), and cover a range of forest transition (FT) phases on each continent.

title: Chlorophyll Concentration
description:
### Overview  
  
The Chlorophyll Concentration dataset shows global near-real-time concentrations of chlorophyll-a in the ocean. Concentrations are presented in milligrams per cubic meter (mg/m3). Chlorophylls are pigments found in photosynthetic plants that transform sunlight into energy. Chlorophyll-a is a certain type of chlorophyll found in green plants and is responsible for their green hues. Chlorophyll-a concentration in the ocean is used as a way of measuring phytoplankton. High concentrations of chlorophyll-a indicate a large amount, or bloom, of phytoplankton. Phytoplankton are small floating plants that form at the surface of the ocean. Chlorophyll-a concentrations were derived from data measured by a remote sensor aboard the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Aqua satellite. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km) and averaged at the end of each month. 

  
  
Chlorophyll concentration maps provide valuable information about the health of the oceans and Earth's climate system. They can be used to measure changes in oceanic productivity and model the Earth’s carbon and nitrogen cycles. The near real-time data is particularly useful for tracing oceanographic currents, jets and plumes. Most phytoplankton blooms are a sign of good ocean health, such as the large blooms that occur in the North Atlantic Ocean every spring. As they grow, phytoplankton take in carbon dioxide and produce oxygen, which could have a positive impact on climate change. However, some phytoplankton blooms can grow out of control into harmful algal blooms. As phytoplankton rapidly die and decay, they can rob the ocean of oxygen and create dead zones where fish and other marine organisms cannot survive. 

  
  
The Chlorophyll Concentration dataset is a combination of work from several organizations within [NASA](https://www.nasa.gov/). The [Aqua satellite](https://aqua.nasa.gov/) and [Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS)](https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/) instrument are managed by [NASA’s Earth Observing System (EOS) Project Science Office](https://eospso.nasa.gov/). Satellite data is processed by [NASA’s Ocean Biology Processing Group (OBPG)](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/) and satellite imagery is generated by [NASA Earth Observations (NEO)](https://neo.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov/). Collectively, these groups work towards improving the understanding of the Earth as a system by providing a picture of climate and environmental changes as they occur.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Chlorophyll Concentration (mg/m3) was derived from ocean color data measured by the MODIS remote-sensing instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite. Launched in 2002, the Aqua satellite views the entire surface of the Earth every two days and continuously measures data in 36 spectral bands. The primary product derived from MODIS measurements is [remote sensing reflectances (Rrs)](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/atbd/rrs/). Rrs is the spectral distribution of reflected visible solar radiation upwelling from below the ocean surface and passing through the boundary between the ocean and the atmosphere . Chlorophyll Concentration was calculated by two algorithms: the standard band ratio algorithm (OC3M) merged with the color index (CI) of [Hu et al. (2012)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/resolve/doi?DOI=10.1029/2011JC007395). Both algorithms use the empirical relationship derived from in-situ measurements of chlorophyll near the ocean’s surface and MODIS-measured Rrs in the blue-to-green region of the visible color spectrum. The CI algorithm was used for chlorophyll retrievals below 0.15 mg/m3 and the OC3M algorithm was used for chlorophyll retrievals above 0.2 mg/m3. For chlorophyll retrievals between those values, the CI and OC3M algorithm were blended using a weighted approach. Additional information about the chlorophyll-a algorithm can be found [here](https://oceancolor.gsfc.nasa.gov/atbd/chlor_a/). 

  
  
Satellite data was measured daily at a 1 km spatial resolution. The final Chlorophyll Concentration dataset was produced by averaging the processed data each month and remapping cloud-free ocean bins.

title: Biomes Outlines
description:
Ecoregions displayed by biome, created by RESOLVE, show the 14 terrestrial biomes of the world. Seven are forested and seven are not forested. Plant communities in the same biome can appear quite similar in structure but contain very different sets of species. Ecoregions represent geographically distinct assemblages of biodiversity whose boundaries encompass the space required to sustain key ecological processes. Biomes represent major ecological communities of organisms that are adapted to a particular climatic or environmental condition on a large geographic area in which they occur. The temporal coverage of this map is 2017 and the spatial coverage is global. An analysis was conducted across the biomes identifying the ecoregions within them that are protected, and to what extent. 

This RESOLVE Ecoregions map is an updated version of the Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World from Olson et. al (2001). The map is based upon more than 100 years of biogeographic scholarship, including extensive field investigations. For this reason, ecoregions reflect the on-the-ground distribution of regional biotas differently than do biogeographic units derived from parametric approaches. Please see publication for more detail on the methodology and datasets used for the making of this map.

title: Global Surface Heat Flow
description:
The Global Map of Solid Earth Surface Heat Flow was created by J. Huw Davies of the School of Earth and Ocean Sciences at Cardiff University (CU SEOS) using a raw heat-flow data set provided by Gabi Laske and Guy Masters of Reference Earth Model at the University of California San Diego (REM UCSD).   
  
The data behind the Global map of Earth Surface Heat Flow uses ocean heat flux estimates in mW m-2  in regions with oceanic crust younger than 67.7 million years. The data and geology correlation components use the median as opposed to the mean in deriving the estimates in the merged polygons. The map was presented on an equal 2°x 2° area grid.  
  
 The result was calculated assuming the median of the data measurements and the median of the geology correlation in the merged polygons; and then also the median of the heat flow value in the union polygons in a grid cell. The resulting data was used to create a map on GIS.

title: [Archived] PRODES deforestation
description:
The PRODES deforestation dataset was developed by Global Forest Watch (GFW) at the World Resources Institute (WRI) using data from the PRODES project, which is operated by the National Institute of Space Research (INPE) in collaboration with the Minister of the Environment (MMA) and the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA). The dataset shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon between 2000 and 2015.   
  
 Since 2002, all PRODES data is publicly available online. Input images for each of the 220 Landsat footprints that cover the Brazilian Amazon are selected based on their lack of cloud cover and their capture date. The PRODES system uses the seasonal year, starting on August 1st, to calculate annual deforestation, so images are selected as near to this date as possible (generally from July, August, and September). From 2003 to 2005, analysts used image transformation to determine the components of vegetation, soil, and shadow using the program SPRING. These components were segmented and classified into the classes of forest, non-forest, deforestation in the target year, previous deforestation, clouds, and water, which are then manually corrected by experts.   
  
Starting in 2005, a new methodology was implemented which makes use of the open source TerraAmazon platform. The platform allows the PRODES analysis to be more uniform and can incorporate imagery from a variety of satellites. As before, images are selected to be as cloud free as possible. The images are then masked to exclude non-forest, previous deforestation, and water using the previous year’s analysis. Analysts then delineate deforested polygons in the intact forest of the previous year.

title: Human Impacts on Oceans
description:
The Human Impacts on Oceans data set identifies the areas of the oceans that are most- and least- impacted by human stressors. This 5 km resolution global map was created by Stanford University (Stanford), Imperial College London (Imperial), and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB). This study considered 20 ocean ecosystem types and 19 stressors. The 19 stressors considered were artisanal fishing, 5 types of commercial fishing (pelagic vs. demersal, high vs. lowbycatch, destructive of habitat vs. nondestructive), commercial shipping, inorganic pollution, organic pollution, nutrient pollution, ocean-based pollution, light pollution, invasive species, 4 climate-change stressors (warming, acidification, sea-level rise, UV changes), direct human use, and oil rigs. Stressor inputs into the model come from data sets for years ranging from 1981 to 2013. The sensitivity of each ecosystem type to each stressor was determined by surveying 135 experts from 19 countries, and these sensitivities were used to weight the impacts of the stressors in different areas of the ocean.    
  
Modeling the vulnerability of ecosystems is challenging for many reasons. Ecosystem response to different stressors is often simplified for model development and the combined effects of multiple stressors on an ecosystem are not always well-understood. Additionally, relevant data may be missing or contain errors. Ignoring this uncertainty can lead to poor ocean management decisions.  This map identifies regions of the oceans with high and low human impacts that were robust to these uncertainties, meaning that these areas were identified as being highly or minimally impacted by humans in simulations run over a range of plausible ecological conditions.    
  
Seven different factors of uncertainty were tested in 3000 simulations, each of which produced a map of the human impact on different parts of the ocean. Within each map, the 25% of ocean areas with the highest and lowest human impacts, respectively, were identified.  The number of times each grid cell was categorized as a high-impact area or a low-impact area was counted. This map shows grid cells that were identified in each category in 75-90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Likely) and in over 90% of the simulation runs (High/Low Impact Very Likely). title: Land Use Harmonization Projected Land Use under RCP 2.6 SSP1 (from IMAGE)
description: As part of the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6), the international community is developing the next generation of advanced Earth System Models (ESM) able to estimate the combined effects of human activities (e.g. land use and fossil fuel emissions) on the carbon-climate system. In addition, a set of historical data based on HYDE, and multiple alternative scenarios of the future (2015-2100) developed by Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) teams, are being developed as input for these models. The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. Please see publications for more detail on the development of the Land-Use Harmonization model. In this data set Resource Watch displays the land-use patterns of the projected section of data (2015 – 2100) under RCP 2.6 SSP1 (from IMAGE), and classified pixels as the land use category that had the maximum fractional cover.  RCP2.6 (also referred to as RCP3PD) represented a very low emission scenario and explores the feasibility of limiting climate change to less than 2°C by limiting radiative forcing to a peak of 3 Wm^−2 in mid-century, declining to 2.6 W/m^2 in 2100.

title: Maximum Arctic Sea Ice
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maximum Arctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual maximum extent of sea ice in the Arctic for select years between 1980-2020. Arctic sea ice typically reaches its maximum extent in March. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during March for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual maximum Arctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. 

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Maximum Arctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081).

  
  
Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors:
- GSFC data:
  - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987
  - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991
  - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995
  - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007
  - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present
- NRTSI data:
  - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present

  
  
The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. 

  
  
Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. 

  
  
GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: India Projected Change in Precipitation
description:
This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in precipitation over the Indian subcontinent. 

These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp).

Projected change in precipitation is computed using daily precipitation in kilograms per square meter per second for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average.

The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.

The Index proves an understandable way for evaluating and comparing the situation of households, social groups, and societies among all regions of the developing world. title: [Archived] Boat Detection
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows boats detected using satellite data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument. VIIRS only detects the activity of lit boats. The data shows patterns of vessel activity and can provide indications of fishing activity within marine protected areas (MPAs) and across exclusive economic zone (EEZ) boundaries. Generally, EEZs are defined as the area within 200 nautical miles of a country’s coastline.   
  
The dataset is published by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA) and the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI). The dataset has global spatial coverage, gives point location (latitude and longitude) of boat detections. The data collection began in 2017 and is updated daily.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Lit fishing boat features detected by the VIIRS day/night band (DNB) data show up as spikes of light. A set of algorithms has been developed for automatic detection of spikes and characterization of the sharpness of spike features.   
  
A spike detection algorithm generates a list of candidate boat detections. A second algorithm measures the height of the spikes for the discard of ionospheric energetic particle detections and to rate boat detections as either strong or weak. A sharpness index is used to label boat detections that appear blurry due to the scattering of light by clouds. The candidate spikes are then compared with a separate VIIRS gas flares data set to identify detections that were also found to be gas flares.   
  
Based on the sharpness index, scan properties, and the gas flare indication, each candidate spike is assigned a quality flag that separates the detections into boats, blurry detections, and gas flares. Based on the location of the boat detections, they are also assigned information such as whether it is in an exclusive economic zone (EEZ) or a marine protected area (MPA). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/7/3/3020).

description:
Crude Rate of Emergency Department Visits for Asthma per 10,000 Population data set contains case counts of asthma emergency department (ED) visits using admission date among residents of the United States. It includes emergency department visits during a calendar year with asthma as the primary diagnosis (including records for emergency department visits resulting in a hospitalization.) These data are stratified by year of admission, county (only for Asthma), state, and gender. Annual Crude rates are calculated using Midyear and postcensal resident population, by age and sex, for state and county. Age-adjusted rates are calculated by method to Year 2000 US Standard Population. ED visits data were submitted by 25 states and 1 city: California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, New York City, Oregon, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Utah, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin. CDC Tracking Network suppresses data for counties with non-zero counts less than 6 and population less than 100,000 to protect confidentiality.

These measures can be used to assess the burden of Asthma, monitor trends over time, identify high-risk groups, and enhance prevention, education, and evaluation efforts.

title: Tree Cover Loss
description:
This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss.  
  

In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced.  
  

This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. title: Fires
description:
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS.  The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot /fire pixels. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: U.S. Monthly Maximum Temperature Normals
description: The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.

title: [Archived] Cooling Degree Days (Decadal)
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc) as a replacement.**_
  
A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This Cooling Degree Days data set shows CDDs for decades between 1971-2090 under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. 

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). 

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on Resource Watch. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm. 

Resource Watch shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Learn More link. For access to the processed data set, please contact the PREPdata team at https://www.prepdata.org/.

title: Availability of Animal Based Foods
description:
As nations urbanize and citizens become wealthier, people generally increase the share of resource-intensive foods—such as meats and dairy—in their diets. Although some of this shift reflects health and welfare gains for many people, shifts to high-meat diets will make it harder for the world to achieve several of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, including those on hunger, healthy lives, water management, climate change, and terrestrial ecosystems.  
  
The availability of animal based foods data here represent retail-level availability of animal-based foods (meat, dairy, fish, eggs) per capita per day across the world, from 1961-2013, with a "business as usual" projection, RCP 8.5, out to 2050.  Data for 1961-2013 are from FAO's Food Balance Sheets. Data for 2050 are from FAO's projection of food demand and production.  
  
Because FAO projects that sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia in 2050 will still have insufficient calories to feed everyone adequately, WRI adjusted food amounts upward in those two regions to ensure 3,000 calories are available per person per day in all regions. Data for 2014-2050 are linear interpolations between observed (2013) and projected (2050) data.

title: Biomes
description:
Ecoregions displayed by biome, created by RESOLVE, show the 14 terrestrial biomes of the world. Seven are forested and seven are not forested. Plant communities in the same biome can appear quite similar in structure but contain very different sets of species. Ecoregions represent geographically distinct assemblages of biodiversity whose boundaries encompass the space required to sustain key ecological processes. Biomes represent major ecological communities of organisms that are adapted to a particular climatic or environmental condition on a large geographic area in which they occur. The temporal coverage of this map is 2017 and the spatial coverage is global. An analysis was conducted across the biomes identifying the ecoregions within them that are protected, and to what extent.   
  
This RESOLVE Ecoregions map is an updated version of the Terrestrial Ecoregions of the World from Olson et. al (2001). The map is based upon more than 100 years of biogeographic scholarship, including extensive field investigations. For this reason, ecoregions reflect the on-the-ground distribution of regional biotas differently than do biogeographic units derived from parametric approaches. Please see publication for more detail on the methodology and datasets used for the making of this map. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Historical Anthropogenic Biomes
description:
### Overview  
  
The History Database of the Global Environment (HYDE version 3.2), is a combination of gridded historical population and land use estimates. The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time; then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator).
  
  

HYDE is the first spatially explicit estimate of population and land use going back to 10,000 BC. This dataset on Resource Watch describes the land use data of HYDE and the population data can be viewed [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2).
  
  

Land use is represented in HYDE in two formats. The first representation shows each land use category as fractional coverage per pixel, or how much of the land in that pixel is devoted to each land use category. The second representation has pixels classified as [Anthropogenic Biomes](http://ecotope.org/anthromes/v1/guide/) or “Anthromes” from [Ellis and Ramankutty (2008)](https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1890/070062). 
  
  

Anthropogenic Biomes are globally significant ecological patterns created by sustained interactions between humans and ecosystems.  In a similar way that classic biomes are formed by global patterns of climate, anthromes are formed by global patterns in human populations and their use of land over the long-term. Anthropogenic Biome categories are grouped as urban, dense settlements, villages, croplands, rangelands, semi-natural woodlands, semi-natural areas, and wild. These categories are further subdivided into specific land uses to give greater detail.
  
  

The dataset has global coverage from 10,000 BC to 2017 AD at  a resolution of 5 arc minutes (about 10 km). HYDE was developed by the PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency, and is used by the World Climate Research Program Coupled Model Intercomparison Project ([CMIP6](https://www.wcrp-climate.org/wgcm-cmip/wgcm-cmip6)).   
  
### Methodology  
  
The authors used historical records to model population at the province level and land use areas at the national level through time and then used algorithms to spatially distribute the total population and land use areas to 5 arc minute pixels (about 10 kilometers at the equator).
  
  

For recent country totals of cropland and pasture, the authors used data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO 2015), who present country totals for cropland and pasture for the post-1960 period. 
  
  

For country totals of cropland and pasture in the pre-1960 period, the authors first estimated land use per capita for each country. This represents how much cropland and pasture area is needed per person. For 1960 onwards the per capita cropland and grazing land was derived from FAO data and then modelled back in time. Modeling was done assuming agricultural land use  was not constant, but instead followed a curved trajectory that is country dependent and based on limited historical references. The historical country totals of cropland and pasture were then calculated by multiplying the estimated per capita rate by the total population from their [population](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2) dataset.
  
  

Further specific input statistics on cropland and pastureland at a subnational level were used for some of the larger countries in the world, such as the USA (USDA, 2006), Canada (Urquhart and Buckley, 1965), Mexico (World Atlas of Agriculture, 1969), Argentina (Vazquez-Presedo, 1988), Brazil (N. Ramankutty, personal communication, 2001), India (Flint and Richards, 1991; Indiastat, 2009), China (China National Bureau of Statistics, 2008; Ge et al., 2008; He et al., 2012, 2013) and Australia (Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2001). Furthermore, other country-specific sources were used when available for specific information per country. These sources are outlined in the supplementary information of their [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/). 
  
  

Once the country totals were determined for cropland and pasture, the authors used allocation algorithms to spatialize the country totals. 
For present day, the authors allocated country totals using the European Space Agency’s Land Cover 2010 consortium map (ESA, 2016; Hollman et al., 2013). The authors used country specific allocation algorithms to distribute country totals from FAO to the most likely ESA land cover categories. 
The authors determined historical distributions of cropland and pasture using population, soil suitability, climate suitability accessibility, and other factors to allocate the country level totals to the pixel level.
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/9/927/2017/).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows data from the HYDE dataset showing [population density](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc088a-HYDE-Historical-Population-2).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The HYDE dataset has additional data on population count, rural population count, urban population count, and urban built-up area. HYDE provides data on land use including pasture areas, irrigated crops and rainfed crops. The HYDE dataset covers 10,000 BC to 2017 at the following time intervals: every 1000 years from 10,000 BC to 0 AD, every 100 years from 0 AD to 1700 AD, every 10 years from 1700 AD to 2000, and every year from 2000 to 2017. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Solid Waste Generation
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows solid waste generation, in millions of metric tons per year, at the national level in 2016. Solid waste management is a universal issue that affects daily health, productivity and the cleanliness of communities. Waste management is an expensive and complicated operation, which creates challenges to local administrations. Collecting waste management data is essential to creating policy and plans. With accurate data on waste generation and composition, governments can allocate realistic budgeting and land, and consider relevant technologies and partners for management strategies. 

  
  
The World Bank created this dataset by compiling the best available municipal solid waste management data for 217 countries in 2016. This dataset defines municipal solid waste as residential, commercial, and institutional waste. Industrial, medical, hazardous, electronic, and construction and demolition waste are reported separately from total national waste generation to the extent possible.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The World Bank Group compiled solid waste management data from the best available sources and publications. Every effort has been made to verify sources and find the most recent information available. Estimated data is calculated in the case of missing data for 31 countries in the Sub-Saharan Africa region and 8 countries in other regions.
  
  

This methodology uses the World Bank’s dataset on gross domestic product (GDP) per capita based on purchasing power parity (PPP) in 2011 international dollars in conjunction with United Nations population statistics. 
  
  

It is assumed  that waste generation is linked to two factors:
- **GDP growth**: As a country advances economically, its per capita waste generation rates increase. Economic growth is reflected using GDP per capita. 
- **Population growth**: As a country’s population grows, the amount of total waste generated rises. 

  
  
If waste generation data for a country had been reported for 2016, the original data was used.
When this data was not available, a regression model was developed to estimate the expected growth in a country’s waste generation rate, based on GDP per capita. The adjusted per capita waste generation rate for 2016 is multiplied by the population in 2016. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/handle/10986/30317).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for country level waste composition, collection, treatment and disposal, and municipal waste management financials are available from the data provider. Because urban data is essential for decision-making and benchmarking, the data provider also reports data from 367 cities. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Temperature Suitability for Disease-Carrying Mosquitoes
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the number of months per year when disease transmissions by two of the most common disease-carrying mosquitoes is possible, under current conditions, as well as in the years 2050, and 2080. The two mosquitoes are *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus*. They transmit diseases to humans such as zika, dengue, chikungunya, and yellow fever. The baseline data used to represent current conditions is calculated using climate data from the years 1960-1990. In addition to the current temperature suitability for disease-carrying mosquitoes, the researchers used four climate change scenarios to predict where temperatures will be suitable for mosquitoes to thrive in the years 2050 and 2080.

  
  
The dataset was published by researchers from the University of Florida, Georgetown University, the University of Maryland, Stanford University, and Virginia Polytechnic and State University. The dataset has global coverage with a 5 arc minute resolution. 

  
  
According to the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/neglected_diseases/vector_ecology/mosquito-borne-diseases/en/), millions of people die each year from mosquito-borne diseases. Temperature is the main factor in mosquito survival and disease transmission. This dataset is crucial because governments and health organizations can use it to prevent and prepare for the viruses.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers used a model to predict disease transmission by fitting the thermal responses of mosquitoes as results of several parameters. The parameters included temperature, mosquito traits such as biting rate per mosquito and mosquito mortality rate,  human population size, and human recovery rate. This model of disease transmission was based on experiments and validated with empirical data.

  
  
As for temperature, current mean monthly temperature data was derived from the WorldClim dataset. To predict future temperatures, researchers used four general circulation models (GCMs) that are most commonly used by studies forecasting species distributional shifts. Each of the four models can respectively be forecasted for four representative concentration pathways (RCPs): RCP 2.6, RCP 4.5, RCP 6.0, and RCP 8.5. These RCPs are standardized scenarios in predicting how future climate will respond to emission output. RCP 2.5 represents the best-case scenario for mitigation and adaptation, and RCP 8.5 represents the worst-case, business-as-usual fossil fuel emissions scenario. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the other three general circulation models (GCMs) besides the Had-GEM2-ES model is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Air Quality: Methane (CH₄) Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic methane (CH₄) emissions in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Methane is a powerful, short-lived greenhouse gas, [emitted as a result of](https://scied.ucar.edu/methane) raising cattle and other ruminant animals, rice production, landfills, and energy generation. Methane is also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue.  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b).

title: Subnational Infant Mortality
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes estimated infant mortality rates (IMR) for 234 countries and territories at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds (about one kilometer at the equator) for the year 2015. 143 countries are recorded with subnational units and 91 countries include only national units. IMR is defined as the number of children who die before their first birthday for every 1,000 live births. IMR can be used as a proxy measurement for poverty and wellbeing within a population. This dataset can also be useful for a wide user community in interdisciplinary studies of health, development, sustainability, and the environment. 

  
  
This dataset was compiled by the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) of Columbia University and is managed by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Infant mortality rate (IMR) data were either acquired or calculated by CIESIN. Acquired means that IMRs were collected from trusted sources. Calculated by CIESIN means that IMRs were calculated by taking the number of infant deaths, dividing them by the number of live births, and multiplying the results by 1,000. 

  
  
Researchers collected the most recent IMR data from national offices, Demographic Health Surveys (DHS), Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS) and other sources. Data collected from national offices included information from either a national Human Development Report, National Statistical Office (NSO), or ministry of health. Since the IMR input data spanned from 2006 to 2014, researchers adjusted the rate for the year 2015 based on the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation. 

  
  
Boundary data came from the IMR data source when possible and when not available the Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4), was used. Against the boundary data, IMR data were assigned to grid cells at a spatial resolution of 30 arc-seconds to allow for easy integration with other spatial data like demographic and environmental datasets. 				
			
  
  
Water features were collected from GPWv4 and categorized as no population or uninhabited areas. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/set/povmap-global-subnational-infant-mortality-rates-v2/docs).  
  
### Additional Information
