title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Oxide (NOₓ) Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, animal agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Nitrogen oxides are a family of highly reactive air pollutants, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. Nitrogen oxides are also an important precursor to ground-level ozone (O₃), an air pollutant and a major component of smog, which can worsen bronchitis and asthma and damage lung tissue. “Nitrogen oxides” is used to collectively describe the larger group of similar pollutants, which includes nitrogen dioxide, nitrous acid, and nitric acid.  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. title: Air Quality: Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) global anthropogenic shows sulfur dioxide (SO₂) emissions in 2018 for the agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes sectors. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Sulfur dioxide is a colorless air pollutant with a strong odor. The gas is a respiratory irritant that can harm human health. According to the [Australian Department of Environment and Energy](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-sulfur-dioxide-so2), sulfur dioxide irritates the nose, throat, and airways. It can cause shortness of breath, coughing, wheezing, or a tight feeling around the chest. High concentrations of sulfur dioxide can affect lung function, worsen asthma attacks, and worsen existing heart disease in sensitive groups.  
  
Most sulfur dioxide emissions come from the burning of coal, oil, or gas for electricity and transportation; these fossil fuels contain sulfur, which is emitted as sulfur dioxide when burned. Sulfur dioxide does not contribute to global warming, but it reacts easily with other substances to form harmful compounds such as sulfuric acid and small sulfate particles. When sulfur dioxide reacts with water and oxygen, it [creates acid rain](https://www.epa.gov/acidrain/what-acid-rain). Acid rain has a number of [environmental impacts](https://www.ucsusa.org/clean-energy/coal-and-other-fossil-fuels/hidden-cost-of-fossils), including making lakes, rivers, wetlands, and other water bodies more acidic, which can be harmful to fish and other aquatic wildlife.   
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS Global Anthropogenic Emissions for [black carbon](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6bf069ff-a3b6-4b58-b4b8-eb1ac6354e89), [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), and [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. CAMS global anthropogenic emissions was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.  Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 x 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 x 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 data sets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions for the year 2018. For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information

title: Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector
description:
### Overview  
  
The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset estimates the share of household income that is spent on various types of products and services. Spending was analyzed for four consumption segments: lowest, low, middle, and higher. The four levels of consumption segments were based on income per capita:  
  
- Lowest: below $2.97 per capita a day  
  
- Low: between $2.97 and $8.44 per capita a day  
  
- Middle: between $8.44 and $23.03 per capita a day  
  
- Higher: above $23.03 per capita a day  
  
This dataset shows the percent of the household income that is spent on each type of product or service within each of these consumption segments.  
  
This dataset was developed by the World Bank Group as part of its Global Consumption Database. The data covers both urban and rural households in developing countries and is reported at the national level for the year 2010.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Distribution of Consumer Spending by Sector dataset was developed using multiple different surveys, depending on data availability, including household budget survey, living standard measurement surveys, and various kinds of country-specific socioeconomic surveys. All surveys measure consumption at the household level; however, different surveys collected data over different time periods. Some conducted surveys over a period of 12 months to account for seasonality, while others collected data over a shorter period (a few weeks or a few months). Most surveys rely on the "recall method," in which households are asked to report what they can recall spending over a given period. The choice of recall period may have a significant impact on the level of consumption reported by the households.  
  
Data was collected for households in various developing countries. These households were categorized by their consumption segments for the Global Consumption Database. The consumption segments are based on the global income distribution data, which rank the global population by income per capita. The lowest consumption segment corresponds to the bottom half of the global distribution, or the 50th percentile and below; the low consumption segment to the 51st-75th percentiles; the middle consumption segment to the 76th-90th percentiles; and the higher consumption segments to the 91st percentile and above. The purchasing power parity (PPP) US dollar threshold was converted into annual expenditure in local currency (as of 2010).  
  
The Global Consumption Database draws on a diverse array of data surveys, so standardization was applied, to the extent possible, through a six-step process. The first step consisted of annualizing each household's consumption or expenditure data for each commodity. The second step was to detect and fix outliers. The third step was to map commodities found in each survey dataset to a standard classification of products and services. In the fourth step, extrapolations were done to convert all consumption and population data to a common reference year. In the fifth and sixth step, the resulting data was compared with data from other sources and used to generate a standard set of tables for each country showing consumption and demographic patterns across consumption segments.   
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Fires
description:
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS.  The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot /fire pixels. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: com.032 Belt and Road Initiative Coverage (BRI)
Carbon Footprint by City
description:
The Global Gridded Model of Carbon Footprints (GGMCF), created by the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU), shows a gridded estimate of carbon emissions across 189 countries for the year of 2013 with a 250 square meter resolution. The GGMCF was built in four steps:    
  
  

(1) National Carbon Footprints (CFs) of consumption (*CFn*) for 189 countries covering ~100% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions were taken from the Eora multi-region input-output (MRIO) database for the year 2015.    
  
  

(2) For the EU, UK, USA, Japan, and China, existing subnational CF models were used to disaggregate *CFn* into subnational regions *CFr*, where the regions *r* range in size from postcode to province. In steps 3 and 4 these subnational regions are treated the same as countries. The term 'regions' is used to mean the collection of disaggregated subnational regions plus countries which are not disaggregated.   
  
  

(3) Within each region the *CFr* was disaggregated between urban vs rural residents according to the difference in urban vs rural resident expenditure patterns and the total urban vs rural population. For 76 countries (a mixture of developed and developing coutnries, driving 19% of global CO2 emissions) no comparative expenditure data were available. In these countries all households were assumed to have a national average expenditure pattern.    
  
  

(4) CFs of grid cells within a region were calculated by further disaggregating step 3 using gridded population maps and gridded income data. The first step involved in identifying the urban and rural grid cells and subsequently distributing the total urban and rural footprint on the basis of the share of aggregate purchasing power in each cell. Urban cells were identified using the GHS-SMOD layer of urban areas (high and low density population clusters). GHS-SMOD uses a clustering algorithm to identify urban areas as clusters of contiguous cells within a total population and population density above the specified thresholds. Aggregate purchasing power per grid cell was determined by multiplying the population in the cell by the mean purchasing power at that location. Carbon footprints of cities are then defined as the CF of those cells in teh GHS-SMOD layer that are high-density clusters of contiguous grid cells with ≥1500 inhabitants/km2 and within a minimum population of 50,000.

title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of black carbon in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning, and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.”  
  
Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution.  
  
Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic.

title: Kenya and Ethiopia Groundwater Sensor Status
description:
Data for groundwater collected by in-situ borehole sensors has recently become available via two USAID funded programs. Designed to address information gaps in water service delivery and enable improved response to broken pumps, sensors measuring groundwater pump function have been installed across Kenya and Ethiopia. The sensors (SweetSense Inc. Portland, Oregon, United States www.sweetsensors.com) provide high temporal resolution data on borehole usage and report over cellular and satellite networks as a means to directly measure water service delivery. Here, we use this “Internet of Things” network to estimate groundwater usage across the region and correlate the data to satellite remote sensing as a means to quantify borehole usage and to document relationships between direct extraction of groundwater (borehole use) and estimates of surface water availability (rainfall): https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969719306941?via%3Dihub

title: Aqueduct Coastal Flood Risk
description:
### Overview  
  
Coastal flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by coastal flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by coastal floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.0009‬%) to extremely high (>0.2%).

  
  
Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by storm surge), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.”  Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on the population impacted by coastal floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods  (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Coastal hazard maps were derived using Global Tide and Surge Reanalysis (GTSR) [(Muis et al., 2016)](https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms11969) datasets from 1974-2014.The coastal flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’x5’ (regridded to 30”x30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30”. Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the FLOPROS model.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods.

  
  
Finally, raw coastal flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw coastal flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 to 9 in 1,000,000 people
- Low to medium (1-2): 9 in 1,000,000 to 7 in 100,000 people
- Medium to high (2-3): 7 in 100,000 to 3 in 10,000 people
- High (3-4): 3 in 10,000 people to 2 in 1,000 people
- Extremely high (4-5): > 2 in 1,000 people

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Access to Electricity (Rural)
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. The data represents electricity access in the rural population of each country.

  
  
Access to electricity is crucial to improving the standard of living and is one of the most obvious indications of a country’s energy poverty status. Securing electricity services while decarbonizing power systems is a key challenge for developing countries, as electricity generation from fossil fuels contributes to climate change.

  
  
While this dataset shows access to electricity at the national level, Resource Watch also shows data for the percentage of [urban](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1ad53858-f5da-47cb-8006-5b4aa5aad589) and [national](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012a-Access-to-Electricity) population with access to electricity.

  
  
This dataset comes from a Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) database from the SE4ALL Global Tracking Framework led jointly by the World Bank, the International Energy Agency (IEA), and the Energy Sector Management Assistance Program (ESMAP).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Electrification data is collected from industry, national surveys, and international sources. Data generally comes from nationally representative household surveys like national censuses. Survey sources include Demographic and Health Surveys (DHSs) and Living Standards Measurement Surveys (LSMSs), Multi-indicator Cluster Surveys (MICSs), the World Health Survey (WHS), other nationally developed and implemented surveys, and various government agencies (for example, ministries of energy and utilities).

title: Aqueduct Untreated Connected Wastewater
description:
### Overview  
  
Untreated connected wastewater measures the percentage of domestic wastewater that is connected through a sewerage system and not treated to at least a primary treatment level. Higher values indicate higher percentages of point source wastewater discharged without treatment. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<30%) to extremely high (>100%).

  
  
Wastewater discharge without adequate treatment could expose water bodies, the general public, and ecosystems to pollutants such as pathogens and nutrients. The indicator compounds two crucial elements of wastewater management: connection and treatment. Low connection rates reflect households’ lack of access to public sewerage systems; the absence of at least primary treatment reflects a country’s lack of capacity infrastructure, institutional knowledge) to treat wastewater. Together these factors can indicate the level of a country’s current capacity to manage its domestic wastewater through two main pathways: extremely low connection rates (below 1 percent), and high connection rates with little treatment.  Values are available per country. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Sewerage connection and wastewater treatment data come from a white paper published by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI) and Veolia (Xie et al. 2016). In brief, Xie et al. aggregate three of the leading research papers on country-level connection and treatment rates into one data set through a hierarchical methodology. The data includes the percentage of households connected to sewerage systems (percent connected), and the percentage of wastewater connected left untreated (i.e., not treated using primary, secondary, or tertiary treatments) (percent untreated).  
  
The calculation is based on the Yale Environmental Performance Index’s Wastewater Treatment (WWT) indicator [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). WWT examines the performance of wastewater treatment  [(Wendling et al. 2018)](https://epi.envirocenter.yale.edu/node/36476). The untreated, connected wastewater indicator reverses the WWT to instead examine the hazard.  
  
The first step in the calculation was to group all countries with a household sewage connection rate of less than 1% into the “Low to no wastewater connected” category.  
  
For all remaining countries, the percent of wastewater treated to at least primary treatment (100% - percent of untreated wastewater) was calculated. This was multiplied by the household connection rate to find the percent of treated connected wastewater. Next, the percent of treated connected wastewater was subtracted from 100% to find the percent of untreated connected wastewater. 
  
  
Finally, raw untreated connected wastewater values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw untreated connected wastewater values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.  
  
- Low (0-1): < 30%  
  
- Low to medium (1-2): 30 - 60%  
  
- Medium to high (2-3): 60 - 90%  
  
- High (3-4): 90 - 100%  
  
- Extremely high (4-5): 100%  
  
- Low to no wastewater (5): -1

title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Depletion
description:
### Overview  
  
Baseline water depletion measures the ratio of total water consumption to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies.  A higher ratio indicates larger impact on the local water supply and decreased water availability for downstream users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<5%) to extremely high water stress (>75%). Total water consumption includes domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include the impact of upstream water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water depletion values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). 

  
  
Baseline water depletion is similar to baseline water stress; however, instead of looking at total water withdrawal (i.e. all water removed from source), baseline water depletion is calculated using consumptive withdrawal only (i.e. water withdrawn but not returned to source).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water depletion is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total consumption and available water per sub-basin time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2 run. 

  
  
The model was first used to calculate a time series of water depletion per catchment per month. To calculate water depletion, total water consumptions were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. This results in 12 monthly time series of water depletion per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled.

  
  
Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2019 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water depletion in January’s from 1979 to 2019. This was repeated for every month, and then averaged into an annual value.  All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%. 

  
  
Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water depletion of -1.

  
  
Finally, raw baseline water depletion values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water depletion values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.
- Low (0-1): < 5%
- Low to medium (1-2): 5 - 25%
- Medium to high (2-3): 25 - 50%
- High (3-4): 50 - 75%
- Extremely high (4-5): > 75%
- Arid and low water use: -1 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Aqueduct Riverine Flood Risk
description:
### Overview  
  
Riverine flood risk measures the percentage of the population expected to be affected by riverine flooding in an average year, accounting for existing flood-protection standards. Higher values indicate that a greater proportion of the population is expected to be impacted by riverine floods on average. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<0.1%) to extremely high (>1%).

  
  
Flood risk was assessed using hazard (inundation caused by river overflow), exposure (population in flood zone), and vulnerability. The existing level of flood protection was also incorporated into the risk calculation. It is important to note that this indicator represents flood risk not in terms of maximum possible impact but rather as average annual impact. The impacts from infrequent, extreme flood years were averaged with more common, less newsworthy flood years to produce the “expected annual affected population.”  Values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on the population impacted by riverine floods were provided by Aqueduct Floods (Ward et al. forthcoming). Flood risk was simulated using a cascade of models within the Global Flood Risk with IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) modeling framework [(Winsemius et al. 2013)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-17-1871-2013). Riverine hazard maps were derived using PCR-GLOBWB 2 inputs from 1960-1999. The riverine flood hazard is represented by inundation maps showing the flood extent and depth for floods of several return periods (2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500, and 1000 years) at a horizontal resolution of 5’ x 5’ (regridded to 30” x 30”). Exposure is represented by gridded maps of 2010 population count per cell at a horizontal resolution of 30” x 30". Vulnerability is represented as a binary condition: people are either affected or they are not. Estimates of flood protection standards come from the [FLOPROS model](https://doi.org/10.5194/nhess-16-1049-2016). 

  
  
The expected annual affected population was calculated using a risk curve [(Meyer et al. 2009)](https://doi.org/10.1897/IEAM_2008-031.1). To create the curve, the return periods were first converted into probabilities (i.e., 1/return period) and then plotted on the x-axis against the impacted population. Next, flood protection (return year converted to probability) was added to the graph as a vertical line. All impacts that fell to the right of the flood protection line (i.e., impacted by smaller floods) were assumed to be protected against floods and were removed from the calculation. The expected annual affected population was calculated by integrating the area under the curve to the left of the flood protection line.

  
  
The expected annual affected population was divided by total population to calculate the percent of the population expected to be affected annually by riverine floods.

  
  
Finally, raw riverine flood risk values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw riverine flood risk values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 to 1 in 1,000 people
- Low to medium (1-2): 1 in 1,000 to 2 in 1,000 people
- Medium to high (2-3): 2 in 1,000 to 6 in 1,000 people
- High (3-4): 6 in 1,000 people to 1 in 100 people
- Extremely high (4-5): > 1 in 100 people

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Access to an Improved Water Source (National)
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017, at the country level. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water.

  
  
WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average was calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria (accessibility and availability).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS).  
  
### Additional Information

title: Aqueduct Unimproved or No Drinking Water Access
description:
### Overview  
  
Unimproved/No drinking water acess reflects the percentage of the population collecting drinking water from an
unprotected dug well or spring, or directly from a river, dam, lake, pond, stream, canal, or irrigation canal [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)]([https://washdata.org/data). Specifically, the indicator aligns with the unimproved and surface water categories of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP)—the lowest tiers of drinking water services. Higher values indicate areas where people have less access to safe drinking water supplies. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<2.5%) to extremely high water stress (>20%). The JMP statistics have been disaggregated from the country level to the sub-basin scale (HydroBASIN level 6) using gridded urban and rural population data.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Data for this indicator came from the 2015 drinking water access rates published by JMP [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)]([https://washdata.org/data) for urban and rural populations per country. Specifically, this indicator used the unimproved and no surface water statistics. 

  
  
First, country level data were matched to the Aqueduct sub-basin scale using a one-to-one geospatial intersection between Aqueduct sub-basins and countries (henceforth called intersect). 

  
  
Next, the gridded 2010 population data [(van Vuuren et al. 2007)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/2006/DownscalingDriversOfGlobalEnvironmentalChangeScenarios) was parsed into urban and rural classes using a 2010 urban extent data layer [(van Huijstee et al. 2018)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/towards-an-urban-preview). The total urban and rural populations were then summed per intersect.

  
  
Within each intersect, the urban and rural rates of access were multiplied by the urban and rural populations, respectively, and then were added together to find the number of people with access to unimproved/no drinking water. Results were aggregated up from the intersect scale to the HydroBASIN 6 scale. 

  
  
Within each HydroBASIN 6 sub-basin, the population with access to unimproved/no drinking water was divided by the total population to find the percent of population with access to unimproved/no drinking water. 

  
  
Finally, raw unimproved/no drinking water access values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw unimproved/no drinking water access values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 2.5%
- Low to medium (1-2): 2.5 - 5.0%
- Medium to high (2-3): 5.0 - 10.0%
- High (3-4): 10.0 - 20.0%
- Extremely high (4-5): >20.0%

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Mangrove Forests
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the global extent of mangroves for 1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2015 and 2016. This is the first global map of mangrove extent produced using an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, using a combination of optical and radar satellite data.

  
  
Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage.
Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded.  Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology.

  
  
The dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The mangrove maps were derived in two steps: 1) generation of a baseline map of global mangrove extent for the year 2010 and 2)  detection of changes between the 2010 baseline and each of the other six years.
  
  
**2010 global mangrove extent baseline map:**
  
  
The 2010 baseline map was derived by the Random Forest Classification algorithm that used  a combination of L-band radar (ALOS PALSAR) and optical (Landsat-5, -7) satellite data. Approximately 15,000 Landsat scenes and 1,500 ALOS PALSAR (1 x 1 degree) mosaic tiles were used to create optical and radar image composites covering the coastlines along the tropical and sub-tropical coastlines in the Americas, Africa, Asia, and Oceania.
  
  
The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017).
  
  
Classification accuracy of the 2010 baseline dataset was assessed with approximately 53,800 randomly sampled points across 20 randomly selected regions. Overall accuracy was 95.25 %, while User’s and Producer’s accuracies for the mangrove class were estimated at 97.5% and 94.0%, respectively.
 
  
  
**1996, 2007, 2008, 2009, 2015 and 2016 maps of mangrove extent and changes:**
  
  
The maps for the other six years were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996), ALOS PALSAR (2007, 2008 & 2009) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2015 & 2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new yearly extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0 %. 


  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669).

title: Access to an Improved Water Source (Rural)
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the percentage of people using drinking water from an improved source that is accessible, available when needed, and free from contamination. It provides values for the years 2000 to 2017 for rural populations. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), safely managed drinking water is defined as an improved water source that is accessible on premises, available when needed and free from fecal and priority chemical contamination. Improved water sources include piped water, boreholes or tubewells, protected dug wells, protected springs, and packaged and delivered water.

  
  
WHO and UNICEF’s Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene prepared this dataset. Access to safe drinking water is a human right, not a privilege, for everyone. Access to safe water can reduce illness and death from disease, improve health, reduce poverty, and lead to socioeconomic development. Yet many countries still lack access to safe drinking water. Children are especially vulnerable to deaths and illnesses related to lack of access to proper drinking water services. In addition, women and girls are almost two and a half times more likely than men and boys to fetch water, reducing their time for other activities, such as attending school. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was developed based on administrative sources, national censuses, and nationally representative surveys. A weighted average was calculated to aggregate subnational data to the national level. There are three criteria for an improved water source: (1) accessibility: water should be accessible on the premises, (2) availability: water should be available when needed, and (3) quality: water supplied should be free from contamination. The WHO/UNICEF JMP provides national estimates only when data is available on drinking water quality and at least one of the criteria (accessibility and availability).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://databank.worldbank.org/reports.aspx?source=2&type=metadata&series=SH.H2O.SMDW.ZS).

title: Aqueduct Unimproved or No Sanitation Access
description:
### Overview  
  
Unimproved/No sanitation access reflects the percentage of the population using pit latrines without a slab or platform, hanging/bucket latrines, or directly disposing human waste in fields, forests, bushes, open bodies of water, beaches, other open spaces, or with solid waste [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)](https://washdata.org/data). Specifically, the indicator aligns with the unimproved and open defecation categories of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP)—the lowest tiers of sanitation services. Higher values indicate areas where people have less access to improved sanitation services. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low (<2.5%) to extremely high water stress (>20%). The JMP statistics have been disaggregated from the country level to the sub-basin scale (HydroBASIN level 6) using gridded urban and rural population data.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Data for this indicator came from the 2015 sanitation access rates published by JMP [(WHO and UNICEF 2017)](https://washdata.org/data) for urban and rural populations per country. Specifically, this indicator used the unimproved and open defecation statistics. 

  
  
First, country level data were matched to the Aqueduct sub-basin scale using a one-to-one geospatial intersection between Aqueduct sub-basins and countries (henceforth called intersect). 

  
  
Next, the gridded 2010 population data [(van Vuuren et al. 2007)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/2006/DownscalingDriversOfGlobalEnvironmentalChangeScenarios) was parsed into urban and rural classes using a 2010 urban extent data layer [(van Huijstee et al. 2018)](https://www.pbl.nl/en/publications/towards-an-urban-preview). The total urban and rural populations were then summed per intersect.

  
  
Within each intersect, the urban and rural rates of access were multiplied by the urban and rural populations, respectively, and then were added together to find the number of people with access to unimproved/no sanitation. Results were aggregated up from the intersect scale to the HydroBASIN 6 scale. 

  
  
Within each HydroBASIN 6 sub-basin, the population with access to unimproved/no sanitation was  divided by the total population to find the percent of population with access to unimproved/no sanitation. 

  
  
Finally, raw unimproved/no sanitation access values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw unimproved/no sanitation access values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.
- Low (0-1): < 2.5%
- Low to medium (1-2): 2.5 - 5.0%
- Medium to high (2-3): 5.0 - 10.0%
- High (3-4): 10.0 - 20.0%
- Extremely high (4-5): >20.0%

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Infrastructure Investment Outlook
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Global Infrastructure Hub (GI Hub) shows national infrastructure investment gaps in 2015 U.S. dollars for the following sectors: energy, telecommunications, airports, ports, rail, road, and water. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total sectors.  
  
An investment gap represents the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued.The investment gap of a country where the investment trends meet their future investment needs is zero.  
  
This dataset was developed by the Global Infrastructure Hub. The data covers a total of 56 countries for the years 2016 to 2040.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Global Infrastructure Outlook was calculated using a “top-down” approach, beginning with existing cross-country datasets on infrastructure spending and filling in data gaps, where necessary. Sources for the initial cross-country datasets include the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Infrastructure in Latin America (INFRALATAM), and Eurostat.  
  
The infrastructure investment gap for each year was calculated as the difference between the amount of money a country would need to invest in infrastructure to match the performance of other countries within the same income group and the amount that countries would be likely to spend if trends continued for that year.  
  
Gaps in national data were filled using data from national statistics agencies and major infrastructure companies. In areas where no data sources could be identified, econometric estimation was used to compute values. In countries where a time series existed but was incomplete, further manipulation was often required to fill in the gaps in that series. For data gaps in the middle of a time series, interpolation was used to fill the gaps. When data was missing from the beginning or the end of the time series, forecasting and/or backcasting were used to develop a longer time series.  
  
In the case where data was attributed to a broader sector, secondary data sources were used to align the data with the preferred sector definition. In some countries, data related to investment in utilities was used to attribute the investment into more detailed sectors like water and energy. For example, if energy accounts for 60% of the country's utilities investment, then 60% of the utilities investment would be allocated to the energy sector.  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://cdn.gihub.org/outlook/live/methodology/Global+Infrastructure+Outlook+-+July+2017.pdf).

title: Annual Internal Displacement from Natural Disasters
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to natural disasters worldwide each year. “Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence.
  
  

Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from natural disasters may have been displaced by the following types of events:
  
  
- Geophysical - earthquakes, mass movements, volcanic activity
  
  
- Meteorological - storms, extreme temperatures
  
  
- Hydrological - flooding, landslides, wave action
  
  
- Climatological - wildfires
  
  

Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement.
  
  

This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [conflict](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=most-viewed&sortDirection=-1) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis.  
  
### Methodology  
  
lDMC monitors displacements due to natural disasters on an event-by-event basis. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people who were displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology).

title: Aqueduct Groundwater Table Decline
description:
### Overview  
  
Groundwater table decline measures the average decline of the groundwater table as the average change for the period of study (1990-2014). The result is expressed in centimeters per year (cm/yr). Higher values indicate higher levels of unsustainable groundwater withdrawals. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low risk of decline (<0 cm/yr) to extremely high risk of decline (>8cm/yr). Values are available per aquifer as defined by the [World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Groundwater table decline is one of those indicators and was calculated by coupling PCR-GLOBWB 2 with MODFLOW to account for lateral groundwater flow processes. This indicator used gridded 14 years of monthly groundwater heads between January 1990 and December 2014.

  
  
In mountainous areas, very deep groundwater influences the averages in mountainous cells and is not representative. These cells were therefore discarded from the calculations following the method in [de Graaf et al. (2015)](https://doi.org/10.5194/hess-19-823-2015). 

  
  
After masking the mountainous areas, the results were aggregated to groundwater aquifers derived from the [WHYMAP data set (BGR and UNESCO 2018)](https://www.whymap.org/whymap/EN/Home/whymap_node.html). 

  
  
Next, the monthly results were fit with first-order regression. The slope of this regression line (cm/yr) indicates the existence of a downward (or upward) trend. The trend was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R-squared) and the p value. If R-squared was greater than or equal to 0.9 and the p value was less than or equal to 0.05, the trend was accepted. 

  
  
Finally, raw groundwater table decline values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw groundwater table decline values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0 cm/yr
- Low to medium (1-2): 0 - 2 cm/y
- Medium to high (2-3): 2 - 8 cm/yr
- High (3-4): 4 - 8cm/yr
- Extremely high (4-5): > 8 cm/yr

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Aqueduct Interannual Variability
description:
### Overview  
  
Interannual variability measures the average between-year variability of available water supply, including both renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Higher values indicate wider variations in available supply from year to year. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low variability (coefficient of variation <0.25) to extremely high variability (coefficient of variation >1.0). Interannual variability values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Interannual variability is one of those indicators and was calculated using the available water supply time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2. 

  
  
Interannual or between-year variability is defined as the coefficient of variation (CV) of available water from year to year for each sub-basin. The CV was calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) of the available water across years by the mean. The CV per sub-basin was determined for each individual month, as well as annually.

  
  
Finally, raw interannual variability values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw interannual variability values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0.25
- Low to medium (1-2): 0.25 - 0.50
- Medium to high (2-3): 0.50 - 0.75
- High (3-4): 0.75 - 1.0
- Extremely high (4-5): > 1.0

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: [Archived] Annual Fishing Activity
Seychelles Storm Surge and Sea Level Rise Exposure
description: This dataset was developed in 2019 by a team of researchers at the University of Michigan. The map shows the geographic distribution of an index developed to represent the exposure of Mahé’s coastline to the impacts of a storm surge event. Due to the minimal record of storm surge data in Seychelles, the difficulty of gauging how global climate change could increase the probability of a storm surge occurring, and the fact that data parameters typically used in storm surge prediction models weren’t made available to the research team, this data set identifies the regions that would be most exposed to the impacts of a storm surge, rather than the likelihood of a storm surge occurring. Considering these existing constraints, this model is processes-based and not calibrated by existing storm surge data; therefore, it is purely theoretical. The data was created in ArcGIS using a multi-criteria analysis model with elevation, slope, topographic wetness index, cost distance from river, soil type, and vegetation cover as criteria of interest. These variables were scaled, weighted, arranged into a pairwise comparison matrix, assigned relative importance, put into an Analytic Hierarchy Process program to calculate weighted sums, and ultimately produce a storm surge exposure index. A more comprehensive explanation of how this index was created can be found in the report linked below.

title: Unemployment Rate
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the estimated unemployment rate in 208 countries from 1991 to present and is updated annually. The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labor force that is without work but available for and seeking employment. The unemployment rate is an indicator of an economy’s efficiency and effectiveness to absorb its labor force. High and consistent unemployment suggests serious inefficiencies in resource allocation. 

  
  
The dataset is published by the International Labour Organization (ILO), through its Department of Statistics (ILOSTAT). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Country-level estimations of unemployment rates came from several data sources. Nationally representative labor force surveys were first consulted for this data. In the case that this survey data was not available, other sources like population censuses and nationally reported estimates were used. In cases of missing values, an ILO econometric model was used. This model ensured that data was comparable across countries and over time by accounting for differences in data sources, the scope of coverage, methodology, and other country-specific factors. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.ilo.org/ilostat-files/Documents/TEM.pdf).

title: Groundwater Vulnerability to Floods and Droughts
description:
The German Federal Institute for Geosciences and Natural Resources (BGR) partnered with UNESCO's International Hydrological Programme and the International Association of Hydrogeologists to coordinate the World-wide Hydrogeological Mapping and Assessment Programme (WHYMAP). The Map of Global Groundwater Vulnerability (GWV) to Floods and Droughts at the scale of 1:25,000,000 is a WHYMAP product that rates groundwater systems on a scale of 1 to 7 according to their vulnerability to drought and flood events. Vulnerability is defined as a system's sensitivity to natural and/or human impacts, and the ability of the system to cope with these impacts. This information can be used to prioritize which groundwater resources can be relied on in case of a natural disaster.

The maps of groundwater systems were sourced from national, regional, and global sources. Many aquifer boundaries were sourced from the WHYMAP Groundwater Resources Map (GRM). The GRM includes major groundwater basins, areas with complex hydrogeological structures, and local and shallow aquifers. These were complemented by aquifers in fluvial deposits of large rivers from the Geological Map of the World, aquifers in carbonate rocks—usually karstified—from the World Map of Carbonate Rock Outcrops, and the WHYMAP database for aquifers with nonrenewable groundwater. The extent of the impact of different natural disasters on aquifers and their groundwater resources differs depending on factors such as the origin of the disaster, its intensity and frequency, the hydrogeological conditions and geographical position of the aquifer (coastal area or a floodplain), and other factors affecting vulnerability (shallow or deep, whether groundwater is nonrenewable). The GWV uses a simplified version of the DRASTIC index for assessing groundwater vulnerability, measuring aquifer vulnerability according to the type of aquifer and the aquifer’s groundwater recharge rate. Aquifer types are assessed according to the map sources mentioned above. Groundwater recharge rates are calculated using the WaterGAP hydrogeological model and categorized as < 20 mm/year, 20-100 mm/year, or > 100 mm/year. 

A total vulnerability range (TVR) is assigned to each aquifer based on its type and recharge rate. Aquifer type is weighted more than rate of recharge in this calculation, since aquifers in carbonate rocks (often karstified) or in fluvial deposits of large rivers and shallow and local aquifers are all highly vulnerable to natural disasters—particularly floods, storms, and tsunamis—and are also highly vulnerable to droughts in arid and semiarid regions. Natural disasters include 1) hydro-climatic events (floods, droughts, storms); 2) geological events (earthquakes, volcanic activity); and 3) events caused by a combination of hydroclimatic and geological factors (tsunamis, landslides). The GWV focuses on hydroclimatic events, and the vulnerability of each aquifer is assessed for floods and droughts. The map assigns 7 categories of vulnerability based on the combination of flood and drought vulnerability (low, low; low, moderate; etc). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Ecological Footprint
description:
The Ecological Footprint of Consumption data set, released by the Global Footprint Network, defines the area used to support a defined population’s consumption. The consumption Footprint in global hectares (ha) includes the area needed to produce the materials consumed and the area needed to absorb the carbon dioxide emissions. The consumption footprint of a nation is calculated in the National Footprint Accounts as a nation’s primary production footprint plus the footprint of imports minus the footprint of exports, and is thus, strictly speaking, a footprint of apparent consumption. The national average of per capita consumption footprint is equal to a country’s consumption footprint divided by its population. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Cities with Bus Rapid Transit
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from Global BRT Data shows cities that have active bus rapid transit (BRT) systems and the year in which they commenced.  
  
Global BRT Data collects information on BRT and bus priority systems in cities around the world. BRT systems are characterized by median-aligned and segregated bus lanes, preboard fare collection, and platform-level boarding. Bus priority systems are similar in that they include dedicated bus lanes, but they may not include all of the features necessary to be classified as a BRT system.  
  
The Bus Rapid Transit Locations dataset is managed and updated monthly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) Brazil Ross Center for Sustainable Cities. The dataset covers 171 cities globally from 1968 to 2019.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Bus Rapid Transit dataset was created by Global BRT Data. The data is collected and aggregated from various sources, including transit agencies or associations of transit agencies, government, researchers, and nongovernmental organizations.  
  
The data may be collected from websites, publications, conversations with experts, or direct observations. In instances where sources of published data contradict each other, Global BRT Data defers to data from transit agencies, governments, or peer-reviewed publications. The most current data available is used whenever possible.

title: Roads
description:
The Global Roads Open Access Data Set, Version 1 (gROADSv1) was developed under the auspices of the CODATA Global Roads Data Development Task Group. The data set combines the best available roads data by country into a global roads coverage, using the UN Spatial Data Infrastructure Transport (UNSDI-T), Version 2, as a common data model. All country road networks have been joined topologically at the borders, and many countries have been edited for internal topology. Source data for each country are provided in the documentation, and users are encouraged to refer to the readme file for use constraints that apply to a small number of countries. Because the data are compiled from multiple sources, the date range for road network representations ranges from the 1980s to 2010 depending on the country (most countries have no confirmed date), and spatial accuracy varies. The baseline global data set was compiled by the Information Technology Outreach Services (ITOS) of the University of Georgia. Updated data for 27 countries and 6 smaller geographic entities were assembled by Columbia University's Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN), with a focus largely on developing countries with the poorest data coverage. description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](f3855c03-ef91-47a5-8167-69c8625f0978) as a replacement.**_
  
The GRanD (v1) 2011 data set is produced with a consortium of partners led by the Global Water System Project in Bonn, Germany. The data incorporates dam point location and reservoir polygons from a variety of sources, creating a global, harmonized account of dams and reservoirs with a storage capacity of more than 0.1 km³. Smaller dams and reservoirs were added if data were available, or if the dam is of particular socioeconomic importance.   
  
There are strong connections between the GRanD data set and the HydroSHEDS database (metadata available through Resource Watch). When multiple dams are associated with one reservoir polygon, the dam with the highest expected rate of outflow from the reservoir, as measured by the HydroSHEDS digital elevation model and flow accumulation measures, is chosen as the main dam. The main source of GRanD reservoir polygons is the SRTM Water Body Database (SWBD), another link between the GRanD and HydroSHEDS data sets. The original dam and reservoir data sets did not include explicit polygon information for many reservoirs. The participating consortium of partners worked to identify reservoir polygons using the SWBD and other tools. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: [Archived] Political Rights and Civil Liberties Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](8eafc054-a350-43b5-af61-a64a9a7f8ffe) as a replacement.**_
  
Freedom in the World is Freedom House’s flagship annual report, assessing the condition of political rights and civil liberties around the world. It is composed of numerical ratings and supporting descriptive texts for 195 countries and 14 territories. Freedom in the World has been published since 1973, allowing Freedom House to track global trends in freedom over more than 40 years. External analysts assess the 209 countries and territories using a combination of on-the-ground research, consultations with local contacts, and information from news articles, nongovernmental organizations, governments, and a variety of other sources. Expert advisers and regional specialists then vet the analysts’ conclusions. The final product represents the consensus of the analysts, advisers, and Freedom House staff. For each country and territory, Freedom in the World analyzes the electoral process, political pluralism and participation, the functioning of the government, freedom of expression and of belief, associational and organizational rights, the rule of law, and personal autonomy and individual rights. A country or territory is assigned 2 ratings (7 to 1)—one for political rights and one for civil liberties—based on its total scores for the political rights and civil liberties questions. Each rating of 1 through 7, with 1 representing the greatest degree of freedom and 7 the smallest degree of freedom, corresponds to a specific range of total scores. The average of a country’s or territory’s political rights and civil liberties ratings is called the Freedom Rating, and it is this figure that determines the status of free (1.0 to 2.5), partly free (3.0 to 5.0), or not free (5.5 to 7.0). title: Glacier Locations
description:
The GLIMS: Global Glacier Database managed by the NSIDC is an international collaborative project that includes more than 60 institutions worldwide. Its goal is to create this globally comprehensive inventory of land ice including measurements of glacier area, geometry, surface velocity, and snow line elevation. To perform these analyses, the GLIMS project uses satellite data, primarily from the Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection Radiometer (ASTER) and the Landsat Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (ETM+), as well as historical information derived from maps and aerial photographs. The analysis results are submitted to the GLIMS database at the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) in Boulder, CO. The GLIMS database is designed to be a logical extension of the World Glacier Inventory (WGI) of the World Glacier Monitoring Service (WGMS) and stores the full complement of the WGMS-defined glacier characteristics. Each analysis received by the GLIMS team at the NSIDC is ingested into the GLIMS Glacier Database. New glacier data are continually being added to the database. description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c66d7f3a-d1a8-488f-af8b-302b0f2c3840) as a replacement.**_
  
In response to growing concerns from private sector actors around water availability, water quality, climate change, and increasing demand, World Resources Institute developed Aqueduct Global Maps to help decision-makers identify areas with higher exposure to water-related risks. Aqueduct employs the composite index approach as a robust communication tool to translate hydrological data into intuitive indicators of water-related risks. 12 indicators were grouped into a framework identifying spatial variation in water risks for 15,006 subcatchments. The 12 global indicators (baseline water stress, interannual variability, seasonal variability, flood occurrence, drought severity, upstream storage, groundwater stress, return flow ratio, upstream protected land, media coverage, access to water, and threatened amphibians) were grouped into 3 categories of risk (physical quantity, quality, and regulatory and reputational risk) and 1 overall score. For 6 of the 12 indicators, an ensemble of time series estimators, spatial regression, and a sparse hydrological model was used to generate novel data sets of water supply and use. The remaining 6 indicators were adapted from existing publications. Aggregation methods were chosen to maximize transparency and communicability, and to allow for dynamic weighting to reflect different users’ sensitivities to water-related risks. Catchments with less than 0.012 m/m²/year of withdrawal and 0.03 m/m²/year of available blue water were masked out as “arid and low water use.” Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description:

This data set was generated by Aberystwyth University and soloEO within the framework of the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) project, which is a part of the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency’s Kyoto and Carbon Initiative and the Mangrove Capital Africa Programme coordinated by Wetlands International and financed by DOB Ecology. The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on a randomly sample of 38 million points using the mangrove masks (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. title: Climate Change Impacts on Crop Production
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows potential climate change impacts on world crop production and yield from 1970-2000  to  2080 under different emissions scenarios. The impact under different emissions scenarios is reported as the percentage change from this baseline. 

  
  
This dataset includes the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B.  This dataset is an update to a major crop modeling study by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The initial study was published in 1997, based on output of the HadCM2 model forced with greenhouse gas (GHG) concentration from the IS95 emission scenarios in 1997. Results of the initial study are presented in “Potential Impacts of Climate Change on World Food Supply: Data Sets from a Major Crop Modeling Study,” released by the NASA Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (SEDAC) in 2001. The co-authors developed and tested a method for investigating the spatial implications of climate change on crop production. The Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer dynamic process crop growth models were specified and validated for 127 sites in the major world agricultural regions. Results from the crop models, calibrated and validated in the major crop-growing regions, were then used to test functional forms describing the response of yield changes in the climate and environmental conditions as a percent change by country.   

  
  
The baseline year for crop yield changes is the average yield simulated under current climate (1970-2000 baseline). The resulting yield change data was then fed into trade models to assess impacts on prices and overall food production. Optimal yield is the potential yield not limited by water or fertilizer and without management constraints. Adapted yields are evaluated in each country as a fraction of the potential yield. The weighting factor combines the ratio of current yields to current yield potential and the economic limitation of the economic country’s agricultural systems. This updated version is based on HadCM3 model output along with GHG concentrations from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES). The crop yield estimates incorporate some major improvements: (1) consistent crop simulation methodology and climate change scenarios; (2) weighting of model site results by contribution to regional and national, and rainfed and irrigated, production; (3) quantitative foundation for estimation of physiological CO₂ effects on crop yields; (4) explicit consideration of adaptation; and (5) reporting of results by country rather than by Basic Linked System region. For full documentation, please read the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0959378003000827?via%3Dihub).   
  
### Additional Information

Additional data is available from the data provider for the years 2020, 2050, and 2080; the crops maize, rice, wheat, and grain; and the emissions scenarios from the Special Report on Emissions Scenarios (SRES) A1F1, A2A, A2B, A2C, B1A, B2A, and B2B. description:

The Global Human Settlements Grid (GHS), produced by the European Commission Joint Research Centre (EC JRC), highlights areas with a dense population and a high degree of built-up land. It assesses the REGIO-OECD “degree of urbanization” model using as input the population grid cells in 4 epochs (2015, 2000, 1990, and 1975). Each km2 grid cell has been generated by integration of built-up areas produced from Landsat image and population data derived from the Center for International Earth Science Information Network Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (CIESIN GPW v4). These data are divided into 3 discrete categories: urban centers, urban cluster, and rural areas. Urban centers, or high density clusters, are defined as “contiguous cells (4-connectivity, gap filling) with a density of at least 1,500 inhabitants/km² or a density of built-up greater than 50%, and a minimum of 50,000 inhabitants” per cluster. Urban clusters are lower-density clusters including towns and suburbs, defined as contiguous grid cells with a population of at least 300 inhabitants per km² or a density of built-up greater than 50% and a minimum of 5,000 inhabitants. Rural areas are defined as grid cells outside high-density clusters and urban clusters. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set.
