description:
The Terrestrial Ecoregions data set released by The Nature Conservancy (TNC), and updated in 2019 from compilations of previous studies, classifies land into 14 major habitat types (MHTs). MHTs reflect groupings of ecoregions with similar biological, chemical, and physical characteristics. The MHTs refer to the dynamics of ecological systems and the broad habitat structures that define them. These groupings can provide a structured framework for examining and comparing the diversity of life in terrestrial systems.   
  
MHTs are broadly broken down by latitude, ranging from boreal and tundra, temperature, and tropical regions. Temperate and tropical forests are further broken down into broadleaf and conifers. These regions are also distinguished by moisture level, ranging from desert, xeric, and dry, to moist habitats. Finally, shrublands are distinguished by elevation, from high altitude montane shrublands to flooded lowlands. The ecoregions, originally developed by Olson and Dinerstein (2002), Bailey (1995), and Environment Canada (Wiken 1986), were modified by TNC. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset shows the change in the average number of days of extreme heat at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme heat day is a day where the maximum temperature is greater than the 99th percentile maximum temperature during the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. Temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, an increased quantity of extreme heat days can lead to human and ecosystem threats caused by more frequent, more intense, and longer heat waves.
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The average number of extreme heat days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily maximum temperature values for a given year and summing the number of days where the maximum temperature was greater than the 99th percentile temperature during the baseline period. The number of extreme heat days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in extreme heat days. Positive values indicate that the number of extreme heat days is increasing, while negative values indicate that the number is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme heat days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme heat days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), and [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

title: Projected Change in Heating Degree Days
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4ca6826c-718d-457d-b4e2-e9277d7ed62c), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

title: Fishery Production
description:
### Overview  
  
The Fishery Production dataset on Resource Watch shows annual time series data of national aquaculture, capture, and total fishery production beginning in 1950. The data displayed cover capture fishery production related to catch of fish, crustaceans, molluscs and other aquatic animals taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. The data also cover aquaculture fishery production related to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Quantities are given in metric tons (=1000 kg).

  
  
The fisheries and aquaculture sector contributes significantly to food security and nutrition, especially in some of the world’s most food-limited regions, while simultaneously supporting the livelihood of hundreds of millions of people around the world. It is critical to ensure fisheries are managed responsibly and sustainably around the world. This requires standardized, reliable and up-to-date information on fishery production and supply chain, as well as the consideration of social and economic aspects, for making sound policy and assessing the performance of responsible fisheries and aquaculture management systems. Furthermore, timely, trustworthy data are crucial for demonstrating progress towards the [2030 UN Agenda for Sustainable Development](https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/development-agenda/). 

  
  
Attaining the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) will require a solid framework of indicators and statistical data to monitor progress, inform policy and ensure accountability of all stakeholders. The FAO works to achieve food security for all, and as the custodian agency of four indicators under SDG14, the FAO has an obligation to accelerate the global momentum to secure healthy and productive oceans. Underpinning these efforts is the need to rely on high quality national, regional and global statistics, while ensuring these data are freely accessible to all. To meet this need, the FAO provides the only source of global statistics on capture fisheries and aquaculture production—a unique global asset for sector analysis and monitoring.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data on Fisheries and Aquaculture Production are sourced annually from relevant national offices concerned with fishery statistics. Information is collected by means of a system of standardized forms, which list for each country the relative species items and fishing areas breakdown. In the case of some "aquatic products," data are also obtained from trade associations or other specialized international organizations to which data are also submitted. In this way the statistics are reviewed by subject matter specialists. Data concerning the nominal catch of certain major groups are generally reviewed in collaboration with the regional agency concerned. For example, data on tuna provided by the national correspondents are often replaced by the "best scientific estimates" produced by regional bodies collecting tuna catch statistics.         

  
  
For the period 1950–1995, capture and aquaculture were compiled together in the total production statistics. However, capture and aquaculture production quantities have since been extended back to 1950. Capture data relate to the nominal catches of fish, crustaceans, molluscs, aquatic mammals, other aquatic animals, residues (used for fishmeal and fish oil production) and plants. Catches from capture production are taken for commercial, industrial, recreational and subsistence purposes from inland, brackish and marine waters. Data include all quantities caught and landed for both food and feed purposes but exclude discards. Aquaculture data relate to the farming of aquatic organisms including fish, molluscs, crustaceans and aquatic plants. Farming implies some form of intervention in the rearing process to enhance production, such as regular stocking, feeding, protection from predators, etc. Farming also implies individual or corporate ownership of the stock being cultivated. For statistical purposes, aquatic organisms which are harvested by an individual or corporate body which has owned them throughout their rearing period contribute to aquaculture while aquatic organisms which are exploitable by the public as a common property resource, with or without appropriate licenses, are the harvest of fisheries.

  
  
Catches of fish, crustaceans and molluscs are expressed in live weight, that is, the nominal weight of the aquatic organisms at the time of capture. The harvest of aquatic plants is given in wet weight. Data are given in metric tons (=1000 kg), except those for whales, seals and crocodiles, which are given in numbers.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.fao.org/cwp-on-fishery-statistics/handbook/capture-fisheries-statistics/en/).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows FAO yearbook data for [ocean-sourced dietary energy and protein supply](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/foo061rw0-Blue-Food-Supply).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for species and fishing areas as well as data on commodities, trade, catches, number of fishers, and consumption are provided by the FAO fisheries division. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Projected Coral Bleaching
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset represents climate model projections of the year in which severe coral bleaching conditions will begin occurring twice per decade and ten times per decade (i.e., annually). The 4 kilometer (km) resolution projections are global, running from 2000 through 2100. Coral communities will start to change when bleaching becomes more frequent than twice per decade: corals susceptible to bleaching will be less common and the structural complexity of many coral reefs will decline. These changes will occur even more rapidly when bleaching events begin to occur annually.

  
  
These projections are based on future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 8.5. The RCP 8.5 scenario presumes no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. More information on these scenarios can be found [here](http://tntcat.iiasa.ac.at:8787/RcpDb/dsd?Action=htmlpage&page=about).

  
  
Mass coral bleaching events due to unusually warm ocean water have increased in frequency and severity, and have become one of the most significant contributors to the deterioration of the world's coral reefs. Furthermore, bleaching events are expected to become more frequent and more severe in the decades ahead. Thermal stress that persists for several weeks with ambient water temperatures as little as 1 to 2 °C above a coral’s thermal tolerance level has been shown to cause bleaching, often on broad geographical scales. Corals can die if thermal stress is severe or long-lasting or if it leads to disease in the colony. Extensive bleaching events have dramatic long-term ecological and social impacts, including loss of reef-building corals, changes in benthic habitat, changes in associated fish populations and economic loss. Even under favorable conditions, it can take decades for severely bleached reefs to fully recover. As the climate continues to warm, bleaching is a major threat to the future of coral reefs.

  
  
There is great variation in the projected timing of when severe bleaching conditions will become an annual occurrence in most coral reef regions. These large variations can even be seen within a single country’s coral reefs. Reefs projected to experience annual severe bleaching 10 or more years later than other reefs in the same country or territory are considered to be relative refugia: they may provide refuge for aquatic creatures living in surrounding areas with higher levels of bleaching. These relative refugia should therefore be conservation priorities. The projected timing of annual severe bleaching varies by 10 or more years in 71 of the 87 countries and territories with at least 500 square kilometers of reef area. This suggests that these projections should be taken into consideration in most reef areas during conservation and management planning.

  
  
Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Ensembles of climate models were used to generate projections of the year when severe coral bleaching events will start to occur annually, and of changes in aragonite saturation state. The models were used to generate projected monthly data for the following variables: sea surface temperature (SST), surface pressure of carbon dioxide (CO₂), pH, and salinity. Each model independently generated monthly data for the listed variables, and these model outputs were then adjusted to the mean (within the annual cycle) of observations of SST based on the [OISST V2 1982‐2005 climatology](https://www.ncdc.noaa.gov/oisst/optimum-interpolation-sea-surface-temperature-oisst-v20). 

  
  
The sea water temperature stress that triggers bleaching is measured in degree heating weeks (DHWs). One degree heating week is equal to one degree above the long-term average summer maximum temperatures for one week. Severe bleaching is common when thermal stress exceeds 8 DHWs.

  
  
Both bleaching frequency projections have been produced for emissions scenarios RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 (for a total of four projections). RCP8.5 is a "business-as-usual" scenario that assumes emissions increase unabated. At time of dataset production in May of 2016, emissions concentrations were greater than what RCP8.5 had projected for 2016. RCP4.5 assumes emissions stabilize just after 2100 due to successful implementation of climate policies that reduce emissions.

  
  
These projections are unique in that they have been produced through statistical downscaling so have high resolution (4km) relative to raw climate model data (~1x1°), i.e. relative to the projections [here](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/climate/projections/piccc_oa_and_bleaching/index.php). The final outputs represent the ensemble average, with 33 climate models from the [Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, Phase 5 (CMIP5)](https://pcmdi.llnl.gov/mips/cmip5/) of the [International Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)](http://www.ipcc.ch/) used for RCP8.5 and 35 used for RCP4.5.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only the subset of the dataset corresponding to severe bleaching under the RCP 8.5 scenario. The full dataset includes equivalent data layers about the onset of 2x and 10x per decade bleaching under the RCP 4.5 scenario. Projection results are available in the form of Google Earth files, map images, and ArcGIS-compatible spatial data. The projections can also be viewed on [the UNEPLive site](http://uneplive.unep.org/) under the Coral Reefs theme. The [About page](http://uneplive.unep.org/theme/index/19#about) on UNEPLive also describes the main findings of the research project and discusses the conservation, management and policy applications of the downscaled projections. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_010_projected_coral_bleaching).

title: Ocean Health Index
description:
The Ocean Health Index, developed by the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), measures the global state of the world's oceans. By providing a tool for the ongoing assessment of ocean health, the index can inform policy decisions about how to use or protect marine ecosystems.   
  
The Ocean Health Index uses data from global databases to annually assess 221 regions, including all coastal countries, territories, and the Antarctic. The Index is comprised of ten overarching goals that represent the wide range of benefits a healthy ocean can provide: Food Provision, Artisanal Fishing Opportunities, Natural Products, Carbon Storage, Coastal Protection, Tourism & Recreation, Coastal Livelihoods & Economies, Sense of Place, Clean Waters, and Biodiversity.   
  
Four dimensions are measured and scored for each goal: status, trend, pressures, and resilience. Present status is a goal’s current value compared to its reference point. Trend is the average percent change of a goal’s status over the most recent five years. Pressures are the ecological and social factors that decrease status. Resilience includes the ecological factors and social initiatives (policies, laws, etc.) that increase status by reducing or eliminating pressures.   
  
Scores for the Trend, Pressures and Resilience dimensions are combined as Like Future Status, an indicator of what the status score is likely to be in five years. The Goal Score is the average of the scores for Present Status and Likely Future Status. Status (including Trend) thus makes up 83% of the goal score, while Pressures and Resilience each contribute 8.5%. A region's score, which ranges from 0-100, is the average of its goal scores. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Aridity
description:
The Consultative Group for International Agricultural Research Consortium for Spatial Information (CGIAR-CSI) supported the development of the Global-Aridity Database. This database is designed for use in models of sustainable development, biodiversity and environmental conservation, poverty alleviation, and adaption to climate change globally, in particular in developing countries, and provides data for each month between 1970 and 2000 at a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds. This data set is the aridity index (AI), which is calculated as the ratio of mean annual precipitation to mean annual potential evapotranspiration (PET), using data from the WorldClim Global Climate Database. The yearly precipitation values are available directly from the WorldClim database, and the PET values are derived from a selection of WorldClim variables. PET is a measure of the rate at which water evaporates from the Earth's surface into the atmosphere. It is influenced by several factors, including solar radiation, temperature, air humidity, and wind speed. Other contributing factors include the leaf area index of an area, as water pooling on top of leaves and tree canopies can lead to faster evaporation than if precipitating water entered the soil layer. title: Human Development Index
description:
The Human Development Index (HDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, a sufficient education, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The HDI is calculated for 188 countries annually. title: Cities with Bus Rapid Transit
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from Global BRT Data shows cities that have active bus rapid transit (BRT) systems and the year in which they commenced.  
  
Global BRT Data collects information on BRT and bus priority systems in cities around the world. BRT systems are characterized by median-aligned and segregated bus lanes, preboard fare collection, and platform-level boarding. Bus priority systems are similar in that they include dedicated bus lanes, but they may not include all of the features necessary to be classified as a BRT system.  
  
The Bus Rapid Transit Locations dataset is managed and updated monthly by the World Resources Institute (WRI) Brazil Ross Center for Sustainable Cities. The dataset covers 171 cities globally from 1968 to 2019.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Bus Rapid Transit dataset was created by Global BRT Data. The data is collected and aggregated from various sources, including transit agencies or associations of transit agencies, government, researchers, and nongovernmental organizations.  
  
The data may be collected from websites, publications, conversations with experts, or direct observations. In instances where sources of published data contradict each other, Global BRT Data defers to data from transit agencies, governments, or peer-reviewed publications. The most current data available is used whenever possible.

title: Political Rights and Civil Liberties Index
description:
Freedom in the World is Freedom House’s flagship annual report, assessing the condition of political rights and civil liberties around the world. It is composed of numerical ratings and supporting descriptive texts for 195 countries and 14 territories. Freedom in the World has been published since 1973, allowing Freedom House to track global trends in freedom over more than 40 years. External analysts assess the 209 countries and territories using a combination of on-the-ground research, consultations with local contacts, and information from news articles, nongovernmental organizations, governments, and a variety of other sources. Expert advisers and regional specialists then vet the analysts’ conclusions. The final product represents the consensus of the analysts, advisers, and Freedom House staff. For each country and territory, Freedom in the World analyzes the electoral process, political pluralism and participation, the functioning of the government, freedom of expression and of belief, associational and organizational rights, the rule of law, and personal autonomy and individual rights. A country or territory is assigned 2 ratings (7 to 1)—one for political rights and one for civil liberties—based on its total scores for the political rights and civil liberties questions. Each rating of 1 through 7, with 1 representing the greatest degree of freedom and 7 the smallest degree of freedom, corresponds to a specific range of total scores. The average of a country’s or territory’s political rights and civil liberties ratings is called the Freedom Rating, and it is this figure that determines the status of free (1.0 to 2.5), partly free (3.0 to 5.0), or not free (5.5 to 7.0). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Road Traffic Death Rates
description:
The traffic deaths rate data produced by the World Health Organization (WHO) give mortality data from road traffic injuries. To estimate road traffic fatal injury, countries were classified into 4 groups as follows: (1) Countries with death registration data completeness of at least 80%. For this category, one of the following data points was used: death registration, projection of the most recent death registration, reported death, or projected reported deaths. (2) Countries with other sources of information on cause of death. This group includes India, Iran, Thailand, and Vietnam. For these countries, a regression method was used to project forward the most recent year for which an estimate of total road traffic deaths was available. (3) Countries with population less than 150,000 and without eligible death registration data. For these countries, the deaths reported in the survey were used directly, without adjustment. (4) Countries without eligible death registration data. For these countries, a negative binomial regression model was used. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Malaria Extent
description:
The Malaria Extent dataset is provided by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) and shows the estimated proportion of 2-10 year olds in the general population that are infected with P. falciparum at any one time at a global scale. Malaria is a disease caused by parasites that are transmitted to humans by Anopheles mosquitoes. Two related parasite species cause the majority of disease and death from malaria: Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax. In areas affected by malaria, children and pregnant women are especially vulnerable, a condition further compounded by poverty. MAP conducted surveys to collect data on malaria cases. Each survey included in the MAP parasite database has been disaggregated to individual sites (geographical points), individual dates (if the same site was sampled repeatedly), and individual parasite species. Conversely, individual-level survey data have been aggregated up to the community level at a particular site and time. MAP data spans 2000-2017. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average maximum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the maximum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average maximum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average maximum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCAdata on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily maximum temperature data over a given year. The average annual maximum temperatures were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average maximum temperature.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average maximum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual maximum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c985d4f6-9a03-4158-9955-e9f96db109ab), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).   
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original LOCA dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.

(2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the U.S.
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows LOCA RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a9567364-e5ba-415e-a834-310e279326b6), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/4c6ba704-12f3-4954-92af-6c248c584233), [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7ec68890-34a9-427c-907e-2f646f0dd9c8), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/412a8589-4887-44f2-9f45-3db5fb3937e7), [Projected Change in Dry Spells in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cd91e8d6-2e3d-46c1-9601-0dd7f524c7ba), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/09e43293-98f1-4618-8e7e-d9f72cd5a4d7), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/9e9b465a-bb0f-4047-ad72-9b8fabc0fd09), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6114c6fa-0ca6-4e06-ae23-413be0677503), [Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the U.S.](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c5cbedcd-8cf5-4140-ac21-6791f6786f22).

title: Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the U.S.
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDD are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in heating degree days.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Conflict Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
The Conflict Forecast dataset categorizes areas by their modeled risk of conflict over the following 12 months. Each district is labeled with one of the following: emerging conflict, ongoing conflict, or peace.    
  
 Conflict is defined by the subnational administrative district (ADM-2), forecasted to have at least 10 fatalities in the next 12 months using a random forest machine model that learns from past records and optimizes its predictive power. The forecast incorporates frequently updated environmental variables, including water indicators, in order to capture the many stressors that may lead to conflict. Updated forecasts are released on a quarterly basis.   
  
  This forecast was produced by researchers at the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the Hague Center for Strategic Studies (HCSS) under the Water, Peace, and Security Partnership (WPS).  
  
### Methodology  
  
This model forecasts conflict up to a year in advance using a random forest machine learning model. It was measured with the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) data over a 12-month period. Conflict is defined as organized violence resulting in at least 10 fatalities. Machine learning techniques are adept at detecting subtle or complex patterns within large volumes of data without requiring a priori instructions or a theoretical framework. Since conflict literature does not offer a clear consensus on what factors contribute to violence, nor on the causal pathways to conflict, machine learning was identified as a viable means of establishing quantitative linkages between local conditions and the subsequent emergence (or continuation, or cessation) of conflict. 
  
  

The data used as indicators in the model capture a wide range of factors—from socioeconomics to governance to biophysical phenomena—and are correspondingly collected at a variety of geographic and temporal resolutions.
In order to utilize and analyze them in concert, data was reconciled to a common unit of analysis: the ADM-2 month.  Only districts with at least three years of recorded organized violence within the selected conflict database were eligible for inclusion in the modeling process.  Currently, the geographic scope is limited to the following regions: Africa, Asia, and the Middle East.
  
  

The model used historical data to learn to “predict” past conflict outcomes based on past conditions. The model was then applied to a separate tranche of more recent historical data and used its performance on this validation data to estimate the model’s predictive power on “true” forecasts made based on current conditions.  When applied to test data, the model captures 86 percent of future conflicts. The model’s conflict signal is noisy, with half of conflict predictions representing false positives.  
  
### Additional Information

title: Environmental Performance Index
description:
The Environmental Performance Index (EPI), produced by the Yale Center for Environmental Law and Policy (YCELP) and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CEISIN), scores countries from 0 to 100 according to each country's relative performance on a set of environmental indicators. High scorers exhibit long-standing policies and programs to protect public health, preserve natural resources, and decrease greenhouse gas
emissions.   
  
The index is built from 32 national-level indicators relevant to environmental issues, grouped into 11 issues, which are themselves divided into 2 overarching themes: (1) ecosystem vitality and (2) environmental health as it applies to human health. Multiple other data sets were employed to provide context before whittling down to those 32. Each country's value for each indicator is scaled between 0 and 100 to reflect the proximity of its performance in that indicator to best and worst performances. The best performance can either be a statistical measure—such as the 95th percentile of the distribution of all countries' scores—or a scientifically determined target, such as the World Health Organization's designation of safe and dangerous amounts of particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) in the air we breathe. Setting the target for worst performance follows a similar logic. 1st or 5th percentile was often used depending on the distribution of the underlying data.   
  
The 32 indicators, each scored between 0 and 100, are then weighted and aggregated to produce the overall EPI score for a country. The weights used to calculate EPI scores reflect a mixture of emphases determined by subjective best judgment, data quality, and analysis of global trends. A "materiality threshold" is used to determine whether an indicator should count toward a given country's score. Landlocked countries, for example, are not rated according to their marine protected areas or the health of their fisheries. When these indicators are removed, the remaining indicators receive proportionally higher weights in calculating the country total EPI.   
  
The datasets used to calculate EPI come from trusted third-party sources like international governing bodies, nongovernmental organizations, and academic research centers. title: Host Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons
description:
### Overview  
  
The Host Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons dataset shows the populations of concern that are living in each country worldwide. This dataset utilizes a subset of the categories used in the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees’ (UNHCR) definition for populations of concern and includes refugees, asylum-seekers, internally displaced persons (IDPs), stateless persons, and others of concern. The dataset is available for every year from 1951 to 2020 at a national spatial resolution. It shows the results in millions of people.

  
  
[According to the UNHCR](https://www.unhcr.org/en-us/figures-at-a-glance.html), there are over 70 million persons forcibly displaced worldwide. This includes 25.9 million refugees, 41.3 million IDPs, 3.5 million asylum seekers, and over 3.9 million stateless people. Out of the world’s displaced people, 80% live in countries or territories affected by acute food insecurity and around 13 million are people under the age of 18. 

  
  
The dataset is part of the UNHCR’s [population statistics database](https://www.unhcr.org/refugee-statistics/). It was created as a way to provide open source data on populations of concern. Data on a person's country of residence or origin and their status (refugees, asylum seekers, internally displaced persons, etc.) are included. The UNHCR uses the information to help meet their mission of working to ensure that everybody has the right to seek asylum and find safe refuge in another country.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The UNHCR’s population statistics database provides information on people of concern’s country of residence or origin and their status. It was created and is updated using information from reliable sources including censuses, government reports, international agencies, and UNHCR estimates. The [populations of concern](https://www.unhcr.org/en-us/statistics/country/45c06c662/unhcr-statistical-online-population-database-sources-methods-data-considerations.html#refugees) used in the database include:

1. Refugees: Individuals recognized under the 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees; its 1967 protocol; the 1969 Organization of African Unity Convention Governing the Specific Aspects of Refugee Problems in Africa; the definition contained in the 1984 Cartagena Declaration on Refugees; those recognized in accordance with the UNHCR statute; individuals granted complementary forms of protection; or those enjoying temporary protection. Since 2007, the refugee population also includes people in refugee-like situations.
 
2. Asylum-seekers: Individuals who have sought international protection and whose claims for refugee status have not yet been determined, irrespective of when they may have been lodged.
 
3. Internally displaced persons (IDPs): people or groups of individuals forced to leave their homes or places of habitual residence, in particular as a result of, or in order to avoid the effects of, armed conflict, situations of generalized violence, violations of human rights, or natural or man-made disasters, and who have not crossed an international border. For the purposes of the UNHCR's statistics, this population only includes conflict-generated IDPs to whom the UNHCR extends protection and/or assistance. Since 2007, the IDP population also includes people in an IDP-like situation. For global IDP estimates, see [www.internal-displacement.org](https://www.internal-displacement.org/).
 
4. Returned refugees: Former refugees who have returned to their country of origin spontaneously or in an organized fashion but are yet to be fully integrated. Such return would ideally take place in conditions of safety and dignity.
 
5. Returned IDPs: IDPs who were beneficiaries of the UNHCR's protection and assistance activities and who returned to their areas of origin or habitual residence during the year.
 
6. Stateless persons: Defined under the 1954 Convention Relating to the Status of Stateless Persons as those not considered as nationals by any state under the operation of its law. In other words, they do not possess the nationality of any state. UNHCR statistics refer to persons who fall under the agency’s statelessness mandate because they are stateless according to this international definition, but data from some countries may also include persons with undetermined nationality.
 
7. Others of concern: Individuals who do not necessarily fall directly into any of the groups above, but to whom the UNHCR extends its protection and/or assistance services, based on humanitarian or other special grounds. 

  
  
The dataset was created by adding these individual categories together to show the populations for each country that hosts refugees. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows UNHCR data on the [Origin Countries of Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a8b5296-d283-4832-9be1-edd760bbb58f).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Further data on returned refugees and returned IDPs are available, as well as the status of current asylum seekers shown as monthly and yearly values. Additionally, data for every year between 1951 and 2017 are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Gender Gap Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Gender Gap Index quantifies the gaps between women and men in four key areas: health, education, economy, and politics. Data is available from 149 countries for select years between 2010-2021. Scores are based on the level of access women have to resources and opportunities relative to men. Countries are given a score from 0-1. A score of 1 indicates full equality between women and men and a score of 0 indicates full inequality. The Gender Gap Index is published annually by the World Economic Forum (WEF) and is designed to capture the magnitude of gender-based disparities and track progress over time.

Gender equality is a necessity for a peaceful, prosperous and sustainable world. Women represent half of the world’s population but continue to be underrepresented in leadership and in the workplace. According to the 2021 Gender Gap Index, only 27% of global managerial positions were held by women in 2021. The largest gap between women and men was in political empowerment, where only 26.1% of about 35,500 parliament seats and 22.6% of over 3,400 ministers globally are held by women. The Gender Gap Index serves as a benchmark for comparing countries and their progress to gender equality over time. Based on current trends, the WEF estimates that it will take 135.6 years to close the global gender gap. However, the 2021 Gender Gap Index shows that many countries have made significant progress towards closing the gender gap. These countries include Iceland, Finland, Norway, New Zealand, Sweden, Namibia, Rwanda, and Lithuania.

The WEF Centre for the New Economy and Society published the Gender Gap Index. The WEF is an international NGO founded in 1971. Focused on public-private cooperation, the WEF brings together political, business and cultural leaders at their annual meetings, workshops and seminars. The WEF’s primary aim is to drive positive change for the world by conducting research, producing data and leading collaborative projects and initiatives. The Centre for the New Economy and Society is focused on closing economic gender gaps, fostering diversity and promoting inclusive growth.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Gender Gap Index quantified the gaps between men and women across four subindexes: economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment. Indicators were scored within each subindex. The Gender Gap Index was based on three underlying concepts that determined how indicators were chosen, how the data was treated and how the index can be used. These concepts can be thought of as the “rules” for how the subindexes were scored.
  
  
First, the index measured gender-based gaps in access to resources and opportunities in countries, rather than the actual levels of the available resources and opportunities. This rewarded countries with smaller gaps in access to these resources, regardless of the overall level of resources. Second, the index evaluated countries based on outcomes rather than inputs. Inputs – indicators related to country-specific policies, rights or customs – were not included in the index. For example, the gap between women and men in high-skilled jobs (an outcome indicator) was measured, but the length of maternity leave (a country-specific policy) was not. Third, the index evaluated countries based on their proximity to gender equality, rather than their level of women’s empowerment. The index rewarded countries in which outcomes for women equaled those for men, but it neither rewarded nor penalized countries in which women outperformed men. 

  
  
The four subindexes were scored based on the following indicators: 
- Economic participation and opportunity: This subindex measured gender-based gaps in workforce participation, remuneration and advancement. The remuneration gap was measured by the ratio of estimated female-to-male earned income and a qualitative assessment of wage equality for similar work. The advancement gap was captured through two hard data statistics: the ratio of women to men among legislators, senior officials and managers, and the ratio of women to men among technical and professional workers. Data was provided by the [International Labour Organization ILOSTAT database](https://ilostat.ilo.org/) and the WEF. 
- Educational attainment: Gender-based gaps in educational attainment were measured with the ratio of women to men enrolled in primary, secondary and tertiary education. The ratio of female to male literacy was also used as an indicator of a country’s long-term ability to educate women and men. Data was provided by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Institute for Statistics Education Indicators database](http://uis.unesco.org/).
- Health and survival: The differences between women’s and men’s health were measured using the sex ratio at birth and the gap between women’s and men’s healthy life expectancy. Sex ratio at birth is the measure of male births for every female birth and was included to capture the phenomenon of [“missing women.”](https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2015/10/where-are-all-the-women/) This refers to the observation of a low ratio of women to men, particularly in countries with a strong son preference. Data for this subindex was provided by the [United Nations (UN) World Population Prospects dataset](https://population.un.org/wpp/) and the [World Health Organization (WHO) Global Health Observatory database](https://www.who.int/data/gho).
- Political empowerment: The gap between women and men at the highest level of political decision-making was measured by the ratio of women to men in ministerial positions and the ratio of women to men in parliamentary positions. The ratio of women to men in terms of years in executive office (prime minister or president) for the last 50 years was also included. Data was provided by the Inter-Parliamentary Union [Women in National Parliaments](http://archive.ipu.org/wmn-e/classif.htm).  [Women in Politics](https://www.ipu.org/resources/publications/infographics/2020-03/women-in-politics-2020) datasets and the WEF. 

  
  
All data was converted to female-to-male ratios. Ratios were then truncated at the “equality benchmark”. The equality benchmark was 1 for all indicators except the two in the health subindex. The sex ratio at birth equality benchmark was 0.9445 and the healthy life expectancy benchmark was 1.06. Truncating ratios at 1 assigns the same score to a country that has reached equality between women and men (a ratio of 1) and one in which women have surpassed men (a ratio greater than 1). This method measured how close women were to achieving equality with men in a country, but did not reward or penalize countries with a gender gap in the opposite direction. The total score for each subindex was a weighted average of the scores for each indicator. A weighted average was used to make sure each indicator had the same relative impact on the total score.The overall score for each country was a simple average of the subindex scores. A score of 0 indicated complete inequality between women and men and a score of 1 indicated complete equality.  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://reports.weforum.org/global-gender-gap-report-2018/measuring-the-global-gender-gap/).
