title: Daily Imagery
description:
### Overview  
  
The Daily Imagery dataset shows near real-time global satellite imagery from the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership (SNPP) satellite. SNPP passes over each pole 14 times per day and crosses the equator at 01:30 local time. VIIRS contains a radiometer that creates imagery by collecting wavelengths of light in the visible bands of the electromagnetic spectrum. The imagery created is at a spatial resolution of 250 meters (m) and has been updated daily since 2015.

  
  
The Daily Imagery dataset can be used for fire and air quality monitoring, along with flood and sea ice mapping. In addition, long-term records of global daily imagery data can contribute to scientists’ understanding of climate change, earth’s atmosphere, natural disasters and weather predictions.

  
  
The SNPP satellite is a joint mission from the North American Space Administration (NASA) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Association (NOAA). It serves as an improvement to the previously launched Earth Observing System (EOS) Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) and is part of the future [Joint Polar Satellite System (JPSS)](https://www.jpss.noaa.gov/mission_and_instruments.html).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Daily Imagery dataset was created with data collected by the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) instrument on board the joint NASA/NOAA SNPP satellite. The SNPP satellite passes above or nearly above both poles on each revolution.

  
  
For this dataset VIIRS collected imagery in the “true color” spectral band, which is a combination of wavelengths similar to what the human eye would see. The bands of light collected were in the VIIRS I and M bands. The I band utilizes a high-resolution 375 m sensor that collects red light, while the M band utilizes a moderate-resolution 750 m sensor that collects blue and green light. After the spectral band data was collected it was compiled to create a 250 m RGB (Red, Green, Blue) composite image of the earth.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Nighttime Imagery] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cli061nrt-Daily-Nighttime-lights) dataset from the VIIRS instrument on board the SNPP satellite.

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional satellite band data is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cli_060_viirs).

title: Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Modeled 5-day Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted ozone (O₃) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). Ground-level ozone is an air pollutant that is harmful to breathe and damages crops and other vegetation. Unlike stratospheric ozone in the upper atmosphere, which protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays and forms naturally, ground-level ozone forms when emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides react in the presence of heat and sunlight. Gasoline-burning vehicles are large sources of volatile organic compounds. Other sources include consumer products such as paints, insecticides, cleaners, as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing.  
  
According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution/health-effects-ozone-pollution), ozone irritates respiratory systems, can aggravate asthma, and can damage cells that line your lungs. Ozone may also aggravate chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and bronchitis and may cause permanent lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults.  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators.  
  
GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model.  
  
To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module.  
  
All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ecce902d-a322-4d13-a3d6-e1a36fc5573e).  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_002_gmao_air_quality).

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). NO₂ is a highly-reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid.   
  
NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2) (EPA), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development.  Even exposures to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.  
  
WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted O₃ concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO),  [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps.   
  
WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution.  
  
### Methodology  
  
WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-CO).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_038_waccm_atmospheric_chemistry_model).

title: Food Price Spikes
description:
### Overview  
  
The Alert for Price Spikes (ALPS) dataset tracks the current prices of key staple food commodities and compares them to expected prices, which are calculated based on seasonal trends. An ALPS value is assigned to a given commodity at a particular market based on how much its current price differs from the expected price. This value is used to categorize a commodity’s price into one of four categories: normal, stress, alert, or crisis.
  
  

Food prices on a local market often correlated with food security crises. Food price spikes can have devastating impacts for rural households in developing countries since they spend a large percentage of income on food. ALPS serves three main purposes for decision-making. First, it can serve as a price monitoring tool that allows users to identify price abnormalities. Second, ALPS can generate early warning information that enables users to prepare and act to reduce harm to households most vulnerable to food price fluctuations. Third, ALPS can trigger contingency planning by anticipating food price crises. 
  
  

The ALPS dataset is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP) and monitors markets spanning more than 60 countries. The time period over which prices have been tracked varies by location, but certain markets have food price data as early as 1994. The data is updated monthly for markets that are actively being monitored.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Seasonal price trends were determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Vulnerability Analysis and Mapping (VAM) Food and Commodity Price dataset. This dataset was collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. 
  
  

The ALPS indicator level was calculated in four steps:
- **Estimation of seasonal price trends**: The seasonal price trend was calculated using a linear regression of market price data over the entire period for which data was available. Both the long-term trend and monthly fluctuations, related to the production or demand of a commodity, were included in the regression.
  
  
- **Calculation of the difference between market price and estimated price**: The difference between the observed price and the expected price based on seasonal trends was calculated for each month.
  
  
- **Calculation of the ALPS indicator considering price volatility**: Each month’s difference was divided by the standard deviation of the differences over all of the recorded months, producing the value of the ALPS indicator.
  
  
- **Categorization of the ALPS indicator**: Based on the ALPS indicator value, markets were assigned to one of four situations:  (1) Normal: ALPS < 0.25; (2) Stress: 0.25 ≤ ALPS < 1; (3) Alert: 1 ≤ ALPS < 2; (4) Crisis: ALPS ≥ 2.
  
  

For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information

See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/foo_053_alerts_price_spikes). title: Recent Internal Displacement from Conflict, Natural Disasters, and Development
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced recently due to conflict, natural disasters, or development projects worldwide, and is updated daily. ”Internal displacement” refers to the forced movement of people within the country that they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change, and remain displaced within their countries of residence.
  
  

Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs can include, but are not limited to
  
  
- families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats;
  
  
- residents of neighborhoods that have become unsafe or uninhabitable due to the impacts of weather-related, geophysical, or technological hazards;
  
  
- indigenous communities forced from their ancestral lands to make way for the construction of dams and other infrastructure projects;
  
  
- families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs;
  
  
- communities whose livelihoods have been severely impacted by drought and are unable to feed their families; and
  
  
- communities from coastal, mountainous, or arid regions whose land and livelihoods were lost because of gradual environmental degradation linked to the impacts of climate change.
  
  

Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement.
  
  

This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually, aggregated to the national level. This data is available for displacements due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) and due to [conflict](https://preproduction.resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%25226974833b-004e-4b24-bdbc-ffbb779c1496%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%2522cb5daeb3-80ef-4e6e-8ca8-5ed0d6170b3b%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062b).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Country analysts monitor displacements in near real-time on an event-by-event basis after IDMC learns of their occurrence. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.internal-displacement.org/database/methodology).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/soc_062_internal_displacement). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.

title: Energy Intensity
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows energy intensity in 259 countries from 1990 to 2015. Energy intensity indicates how much primary energy (energy that comes directly from nature and has not been converted to a different form) is used to produce one unit of gross domestic product (GDP). GDP is a key economic indicator that measures the monetary value of goods and services provided within an area. Energy intensity is expressed as megajoules (MJ) of primary energy available per GDP produced, based on [purchasing power parity (PPP)](https://www.imf.org/external/pubs/ft/fandd/basics/ppp.htm) in 2011 U.S. dollars (USD). PPP is a factor used to convert local currencies to one comparable unit of measure based on the local cost of goods and services in each country.

  
  
Low energy intensity is desirable, as it means that less energy is used to produce one more unit of economic output. Having a low energy intensity indicates that a country can increase its economic growth without having to rely as heavily on energy consumption. 

  
  
The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative. The database is intended to help policymakers in government, business, and civil society work toward doubling the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene021a-Renewable-Energy-Consumption) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Energy intensity was measured as the ratio of total primary energy supply to the value added to the economy. Primary energy supply data came from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database. The value added to the economy was expressed in 2011 USD, adjusted for PPP. The data for GDP PPP came from the World Bank’s World Development Indicators. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://trackingsdg7.esmap.org/methodology).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [renewable energy consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/431f7c9e-7ef5-4f00-a5dc-8845fcb3a9a9) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data related to electricity access and renewable energy electricity is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_worldbank_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Peatlands
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset includes the most-updated effort to map the global distribution of peatlands. [Peatlands are unique and underappreciated ecosystems, rich in both carbon and biological diversity](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Peat forms when dead plants partially decay in water-saturated soils and organic matter gradually accumulates, layer upon layer, over hundreds or even thousands of years. Peatlands are important because they store soil carbon and provide water resources and habitats for a range of rare, threatened, or declining species. This dataset estimates the global peatland area to be 4.23 million square kilometers, almost 3% of the world's land area. 
  
  

This dataset was published in 2017 by researchers at the University of Leeds. It may provide a useful reference for policymakers and researchers interested in global ecosystem biodiversity, climate change, carbon cycles, and water resources. It may also help provide support for wetland protection and restoration.

  
  
### Methodology  
  
The global dataset is put together by compiling the most high quality and freely available data from a wide range of sources that describe peatland distributions at global, regional, and national levels. Data includes information derived from digitized soil maps, wetland databases, and satellite imagery.
For areas in Hokkaido (Japan), Mongolia, and North Korea, where peatland-specific datasets were not available, the authors estimated peatland extent based on the distribution of histosols derived from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2 (HWSD). 
 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0341816217303004?via%3Dihub).

title: U.S. Drought Monitor
description:
The U.S. Drought Monitor, established in 1999, is a weekly map of drought conditions produced jointly by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the National Drought Mitigation Center at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. The U.S. Drought Monitor website is hosted and maintained by the drought center.

The weekly maps are released at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Standard Time each Thursday and are assessments of past conditions based on data through 7 a.m. Eastern time (8 a.m. Eastern Daylight Time) the preceding Tuesday. The map is based on measurements of climatic, hydrologic and soil conditions as well as reported impacts and observations from more than 350 contributors around the country. Eleven climatologists from the partner organizations take turns serving as the lead author each week. The authors examine all the data and use their best judgment to reconcile any differences among sources.

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Climate Risk Index
description:
The Global Climate Risk Index identifies the extent to which countries have been affected by extreme weather events. These can be meteorological events such as tropical storms or tornados, hydrological events such as storm surges or flash floods, or climatological events such as wildfires or droughts. The index scores are derived from country’s rankings within the following indicators, and averaged according to their weighting:    
  
- Number of deaths – Weight: 1/6   
  
-  Number of deaths per 100,000 inhabitants – Weight: 1/3   
  
- Sum of losses in US$ in purchasing power parity (PPP) – Weight: 1/6   
  
- Losses per unit of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) – Weight: 1/3   
  
Lower index scores indicate countries with higher risk. Countries with high ranks in each category (low numbers) add up to low index values.   
  
The Global Climate Risk Index has been calculated for impact in 2018 and separately for the annual average impact from the past 2 decades (1999-2018). Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Crop Land Area and Production
description:
### Overview  
  
The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice,  maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2010 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. 

Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. 

The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching
and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2010 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer.

The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type:
- Irrigated – high input (I)
- Rainfed – high input (H)
- Rainfed – low input (L)
- Rainfed – subsistence (S)

The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and
country-level statistics by the overall harvested area.

The optimization module in SPAM2010 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically.

The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others):
- Administrative units
- Crop Type
- Farming system
- Adjusted harvested area
- Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system
- Crop prices
- Market accessibility in each grid
- Population density

Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2010 essential output indicators:

- Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the
pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size.
- Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop.
- Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields.

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2010 Version 2.0 has data for 36 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.

Our data catalog has previously shown data for [2005](https://bit.ly/3CjoFYc). This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed.

title: Aqueduct Baseline Water Stress
description:
### Overview  
  
Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. A higher ratio indicates more competition among users. These ratios were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low water stress (<10%) to extremely high water stress (>80%). Water withdrawals include domestic, industrial, irrigation and livestock consumptive and non-consumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include surface and groundwater supplies and the impact of upstream consumptive water use and large dams on downstream water availability. Water stress values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).   
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Baseline water stress is one of those indicators and was calculated using the gross and net total withdrawal and available water per sub-basin time series from the default model run.   
  
The model was first used to calculate a time series of water stress per catchment per month. To calculate water stress, total withdrawals were divided by the available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Net consumptive water use was subtracted from the total available renewable water supply before the ratio was calculated. The results were output in 12 monthly time series time series of water stress per sub-basin. Water resources in delta sub-basins were pooled.  
  
Next, the time series were converted into baseline values using an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression. For example, the regression output for January 2020 represents the chronic, long-term condition of water stress in January’s from 1960 to 2020. This was repeated for every month and then averaged into an annual value.  All raw values were limited to a maximum of 100% and a minimum of 0%.   
  
Sub-basins that were classified “Arid and low water use” were handled separately and were given a raw value for baseline water stress of -1.  
  
Finally, raw baseline water stress values were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw baseline water stress values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.  
  
- Low (0-1): < 10%  
  
- Low to medium (1-2): 10-20%  
  
- Medium to high (2-3): 20-40%  
  
- High (3-4): 40-80%  
  
- Extremely high (4-5): >80%  
  
- Arid and low water use (5): -1  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Built-Up Area Change
description:
### Overview  
  
The Built-Up Area Change dataset shows areas of built-up extent and change from 2000 to 2020, and the data is available at 30 m spatial resolution, globally. The dataset was created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory. Built-up lands represent the most intensive land uses of humankind in the form of cities, villages and infrastructure. Given the heterogeneous nature of built-up lands, advanced algorithms such as deep learning neural networks, which examine spatial context, are a powerful alternative to traditional per pixel classifiers. The presented maps are the first of their kind for the GLAD lab and will soon be produced at annual time-scales and temporally filtered to provide a consistent record of global built-up land development.
  
  
The Global Land Analysis and Discovery Lab (GLAD) laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes, and impacts of global land surface change. Earth observation imagery is the primary data source, and the land cover extent and change is the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Built-up land consists of human constructed land surfaces associated with infrastructure, commercial and residential land uses. The global annual built-up land extent and gain map was made using annual metrics derived from the Landsat 5, 7 and 8 satellites for 2000 through 2020. To facilitate the deep learning application, GLAD only employed interquartile metrics from the red, near-infrared and both shortwave infrared bands. Training data were primarily from the Open Street Map data base. 
  
  
Due to the contextual nature of built-up lands, particularly settlements, GLAD employed a deep learning convolution neural network algorithm. The input metrics were related to the training data through the U-Net convolutional neural network architecture, which has proven to work robustly over a variety of tasks in remote sensing ([Brandt et al., 2020](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2824-5?proof=t%29Nature), and [Feng, et al., 2018)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8573826). For parameterizing the algorithm, GLAD randomly sampled patches with a size of 128x128 pixels (each pixel corresponds to 30x30 m). Weight decay and data augmentation were utilized in the form of down sampling, rotations, and flips for the gradient-based optimization of the U-Net parameters. A moving window approach employing 10x10 degree tiles was employed to better fit to local development patterns. Final 2000 and 2020 per pixel probabilities were generated and validation data used to assist in final thresholding of the layers in depicting 2000 and 2020 extents and 2000-2020 gain in built-up lands. 
  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows datasets from the GLAD laboratory for [Cropland Extent](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/50634b51-ea2e-4cc1-9e4b-8f26a389a301), [Cropland Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ec282483-4f5c-4fb8-ace7-8e557826781a), [Tree Height Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/64a3e126-000b-46fb-aaf4-8ac765a8263b), [Water Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b83ad197-eb95-44e2-8ec3-3351ab926421), [Snow/Ice Change](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5a796ce9-71d4-42b0-922d-056a86e5eb72), and [Land Cover Map](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/06e734af-66f0-4c3e-ac71-1b99f3cbfe1d).

title: Projected Permafrost Loss
description:
Projected permafrost extents, created through the research of Chadburn et al. (2017), estimates a sensitivity of permafrost area loss to global mean warming at stabilization of 2°C. The latest climate models all predict warming of high-latitude soils and thus thawing of permafrost under future climate change, but with widely varying magnitudes of permafrost thaw. It is estimated that permafrost area will eventually be reduced by over 40% if the climate is stabilized at 2°C above preindustrial levels. This research showed that it is possible to infer the sensitivity of permafrost to future global warming by using present-day spatial distribution of permafrost and mean annual air temperature (MAAT). Permafrost extent is estimated at a 0.5 degree spatial resolution and is restricted to the Northern Hemisphere. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Observed and Potential Crop Yields
description:
The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Biodiversity Intactness
description:
### Overview  
  
The biodiversity intactness map shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in an area. This data is important because if biodiversity loss goes unchecked, it will undermine efforts toward long-term sustainable development. The data, created by [Newbold et al. (2016)](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288), represents intactness in 2005 at a 1 kilometer resolution.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Biodiversity Intactness dataset shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in samples from local terrestrial ecological assemblages. The map represents the average losses of originally present species. The datasets used 2,382,624 data points from the Projecting Responses of Ecological Diversity in Changing Terrestrial Systems (PREDICTS) database, a global database of how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human impacts. The map modeled how richness and abundance respond to land use pressures. The models included 4 pressure variables—land use, land use intensity, human population density, and proximity to the nearest road. The values of the response variables were expressed relative to an intact assemblage undisturbed by humans. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288).

title: Nighttime Lights 2012 and 2016
description:
The "Earth at Night" map images were generated by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) using the Suomi National Polar-Orbiting Partnership (Suomi NPP) satellite, managed by NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Suomi NPP observes nearly every location on Earth at roughly 1:30 p.m. and 1:30 a.m. (local time) each day, as it images the planet in vertical 3,000 km (2,000-mile) strips from pole to pole. The satellite’s workhorse instrument is the Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS), which detects photons of light reflected from the Earth’s surface and atmosphere in 22 different wavelengths. The final Earth at Night products show the areas of man-made visible and infrared light in the world at night, excluding moonlight, fires, and other natural sources of light. Areas with the brightest light points tend to be population centers and are often located in coastal areas. Earth at Night maps are available for the years 2012 and 2016, in both color and grayscale, in both JPEG and GeoTIFF formats and with resolution from 500 m to 3 km. The 2016 images were processed using a compositing technique that selected the best cloud-free nights in each month over each land mass. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Fire Weather
description:
The Fire Weather data set is derived from the Fire Weather Index (FWI) System, which was developed by the Canadian Forest Service and is the most widely used fire danger rating system in the world. The Global Fire WEather Database (GFWED) is a global database of daily FWI System calculations, produced by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Institute for Space Studies. This system combines different weather factors that may influence the start and spread of a vegetation fire and is comprised of three moisture codes and three fire behavior indices. The moisture codes describe the moisture content of three general fuel classes. The fire behavior indices describe the rate of spread, fuel consumption and intensity of a fire if it were to start. 

  
  
 The data inputs for these calculations are measurements of 12:00 local time temperature at 2 m, relative humidity at 2 m and wind speed at 10 m. Daily snow-depth and precipitation were totaled over the previous 24 hours. GFWED includes several different versions of these calculations, each of which uses a different input weather and precipitation data. The version of these calculations shown on Resource Watch uses input data from GEOS-5 for temperature, relative humidity, wind-speed and snow depth; input precipitation comes from the 'Late' version of GPM IMERG Daily Precipitation. Global daily calculations of the FWI System indices using these data inputs are available from 2015 to present with 0.1° resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Tree Height Change
description:
### Overview  
  
The global tree canopy height and change dataset at 30 m spatial resolution was developed through the integration of the [Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI)](https://gedi.umd.edu/) lidar forest structure measurements and [Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD)](https://www.usgs.gov/core-science-systems/nli/landsat/us-landsat-analysis-ready-data?qt-science_support_page_related_con=0#qt-science_support_page_related_con) time series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure, including tree canopy height between 52°N and 52°S globally. The Global Land Analysis and Discover (GLAD) team at the University of Maryland (UMD) integrated the GEDI point-based tree height measurements with the global wall-to-wall Landsat analysis-ready time-series data (Landsat ARD). The GEDI relative height at 95% (GEDI RH95) metric was used to calibrate the model. The Landsat multi-temporal metrics that represent the surface phenology serve as the independent variables for global tree height modeling. The “moving window” locally calibrated and applied regression tree ensemble model was implemented to ensure high quality of tree height prediction and global map consistency. The model was extrapolated in the boreal regions to create the global tree height prototype map. The model was applied for the years 2000 and 2020 and the maps were temporally filtered to provide a two-decade global forest structure and change metrics.
  
  
The GLAD laboratory in the Department of Geographical Sciences at UMD investigates methods, causes and impacts of global land surface change.  Earth observation imagery are the primary data source and land cover extent and change the primary topic of interest. GLAD aspires to generate new science insights concerning land resources, educate the next generation of remote sensing-based land change scientists, and disseminate land monitoring capabilities to operational settings nationally and internationally.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The year 2000 and 2020 global tree height was modeled through the integration of the Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) lidar forest structure measurements and Landsat analysis-ready data (Landsat ARD) time-series. The NASA GEDI is a spaceborne lidar instrument operating onboard the International Space Station since April 2019. It provides point-based measurements of vegetation structure between 52°N and 52°S globally [(Dubayah et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666017220300018). The GEDI relative height of returned energy (RH) metrics were filtered to exclude low quality observations and gridded to the Landsat 30-m spatial resolution. The RH metrics were compared with 90th percentile of the tree height at 30-m pixel resolution derived from the airborne lidar instruments and found that the GEDI RH95 (relative height at 95%) metric is highly correlated with the airborne lidar canopy height product. This metric was selected as the calibration data for the global tree height map. To exclude non-woody vegetation from the training,  a zero height was assigned to all GEDI observations with RH95 values below 3 meters.
  
  
A global 16-day normalized surface reflectance Landsat ARD was employed as input data for tree height modeling [(Potapov et al., 2020)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425720305381?via%3Dihub). The per-pixel 16-day time-series data were composed only of clear-sky observations during the snow-free season.  A set of annual multitemporal metrics was generated to provide consistent land surface phenology inputs for model application. To facilitate spatiotemporal consistency of the reflectance time-series, gap-filling of the missing 16-day data with data from preceding years was implemented. Annual metrics include selected ranks, inter-rank averages, and amplitudes of surface reflectance and vegetation indices values, and surface reflectance averages for land surface phenology stages defined by vegetation indices (i.e., surface reflectance for the maximum and minimum greenness periods). The Landsat metrics were augmented with elevation data.
  
  
The 2019 GEDI RH95 was used as a dependent variable and the Landsat multitemporal metrics from the same year as independent variables to calibrate the regression tree ensembles. A separate model was calibrated for each Landsat ARD tile (1×1°) using training data collected within the neighboring tiles. The prototype for the boreal tree height map, where GEDI data were absent (north of 52°N), was calibrated using training data extracted from the modeled tree height between 40°N and 52°N. To address the overestimation of tree height over wetlands and tundra, additional non-forest training was manually collected in areas indicated as treeless by the year 2010 tree canopy cover product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/).
  
  
The model calibrated for the year 2019 was applied to the multitemporal metrics for other years (2000-2003 and 2017-2020). The tree height value for the years 2000 and 2020 was calculated as the median of 2000, 2001, 2003 and 2017, 2019, 2020, respectively, unless forest loss was indicated by the forest change product [(Hansen et al., 2013)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24233722/). To reduce errors and noise in the model outputs due to remaining atmospheric contamination and differences in the radiometric resolution of Landsat sensors in 2000 and 2020, extensive filtering of the output products was implemented. Pixels that did not experience forest loss according to the Hansen et al. (2013) product and that had an overlap of ranges of tree height values for 2000-2003 and 2017-2020 intervals were considered stable forests. Manual masks were also used to clean up incorrectly mapped forest loss and gain, especially in the short seasonal forests. 
  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information

title: Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Modeled Next-day Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted carbon monoxide (CO) concentrations at Earth's surface, modeled by the Whole Atmosphere Community Climate Model (WACCM). Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless gas that is toxic when inhaled in large amounts. Carbon monoxide exposure can be fatal.  
  
According to the U.S. [Center for Disease Control](https://www.cdc.gov/co/faqs.htm) (CDC), carbon monoxide is released when fossil fuels are burned. Common household sources include grills, cars, fireplaces, and gas stoves that aren’t properly ventilated. Major sources of carbon monoxide to outdoor air include cars, trucks and other fossil-fuel-burning machinery. Breathing air with a high concentration of carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability in the bloodstream for critical organs like the heart and brain. Symptoms of carbon monoxide poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion.   
  
WACCM creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators, as well. While this dataset shows forecasted carbon monoxide concentrations, Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO),  [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO). WACCM runs the model daily, and on their website you can find forecasted concentrations for each compound up to nine days into the future at three-hour time steps.   
  
WACCM was developed by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) and the University Corporation for Atmospheric Research (UCAR). The data has global coverage at 1.9 x 2.5 degree resolution.  
  
### Methodology  
  
WACCM is a comprehensive numerical model, driven by meteorological fields from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration’s (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) Goddard Earth Observing System Model, Version 5 (GEOS-5) model. The development of WACCM is an inter-divisional collaboration that unifies modeling from the High Altitude Observatory ([HAO](http://www2.hao.ucar.edu/)), the Atmospheric Chemistry Observations and Modeling ([ACOM](https://www2.acom.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory, and the Climate and Global Dynamics ([CGD](http://www2.cgd.ucar.edu/)) Laboratory. Upper atmospheric modeling from HAO, middle atmospheric modeling from ACOM, and tropospheric modeling from CGD are combined using the NCAR [Community Earth System Model (CESM)](http://www.cesm.ucar.edu/) as a common numerical framework. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://opensky.ucar.edu/islandora/object/articles%3A12836).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows WACCM forecasts for [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-SO), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-PM-25), [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-Black-Carbon), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-O), and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit038-Air-Quality-Modeled-Forecast-WACCM-NO).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere are also produced by WACCM. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Ramsar Internationally Important Wetlands
description:
Ramsar wetlands refer to "internally important" wetlands as defined by the Convention on Wetlands and are designated by each contracting party. At the time of joining the Convention, each contracting party must designate at least one wetland site within their territory for inclusion in the List of Wetlands of International Importance (the Ramsar List). These Ramsar sites acquire a new national and international status. They are recognized as being of significant value not only for the country or the countries in which they are located but for humanity as a whole. There are currently over 2,400 Ramsar sites around the world. They cover over 2.1 million km2, an area larger than Mexico. Parties continue to designate wetlands for inclusion on the list. They select suitable wetlands for designation by referring to the criteria for identifying wetlands of international importance. The Convention has provided guidance to contracting parties on the management of Ramsar sites, in addition to its guidance on the wise use of all wetlands. The inclusion of a wetland on the list signifies the government’s commitment to take the steps necessary to ensure that the site’s ecological character is maintained. The Convention includes various measures to respond to threats to the ecological character of sites. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Wastewater Inputs in Coastal Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, maps human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. This dataset maps the locations of coastal pourpoints, where surface water empties into the ocean. At these pourpoints nitrogen and pathogens from human sewage are transported to coastal ecosystems. Nitrogen concentration at each pourpoint is measured in grams/year.

  
  
Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue, because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters.  Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management.  

  
  
The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this map of pourpoints, along with a model of nitrogen dispersion into the ocean, to inform marine conservation and public health work. The data allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources and traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
High-resolution watershed vector data and pourpoints were used with an automated flow-accumulation process to determine the boundaries for ~135,000 global basins that drain into the ocean. Population and settlement data for each basin were used to estimate the levels of nitrogen and pathogen inputs to coastal waters. Nitrogen concentrations in grams per year (g/yr) were modeled from data on three types of wastewater (treated, septic, and open defecation) and the estimated amount of nitrogen removed by each treatment type. The inputs to coastal waters at each pourpoint were determined by totaling the estimates that fell within the watershed boundary. Pourpoints that transferred less than 1 gram of nitrogen per year were discarded by the authors.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also provides data on the dispersion of nitrogen into the coastal ocean from the pourpoints in [Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/11804f04-d9c7-47b9-8d27-27ce6ed6c042) and on the size and shape of the watersheds that feed into the pourpoints in [Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/784732cc-8e7e-4dac-be51-d4506ff2ee04).

title: Renewable Energy Consumption
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows renewable energy consumption in 259 countries from 1990 to present. In this dataset, renewable energy sources are defined as hydropower, solid and liquid biofuels, wind, solar, biogas, geothermal, marine, and waste to energy. 

  
  
The dataset was published as part of the Sustainable Energy for All (SE4ALL) initiative, and the data was compiled by the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the United Nations Statistics Divisions (UNSD). IEA and UNDC are the primary developers of internationally comparable national energy statistics. This dataset tracks the progress of Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) indicator 7.2, to advance the target of increase substantially the share of renewable energy in the global energy mix by 2030. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database.  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was compiled using data from the International Energy Agency (IEA) energy statistics, complemented by the United Nations (UN) database when IEA data was not available. IEA data contained the most comprehensive and accurate data for countries that were a part of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), as well as 75 non-OECD countries. In the case of smaller non-OECD countries, extrapolations of country data provided by the UN Statistics Division were used. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.seforall.org/sites/default/files/l/2013/09/9-gtf_ch4.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [energy intensity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene029a-Energy-Intensity) and [percentage of energy consumption from renewable sources](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bced4001-425a-4fad-8c22-8214d9340ea4) data from the SE4ALL Database.

title: [Archived] Solar Energy Potential
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](2063964b-56c8-4080-b2a5-5a7710f321b9) as a replacement.**_
  
Vaisala created this global data set of average annual global horizontal irradiance (GHI, the key variable for photovoltaic (PV) projects, measured in W/m²) at a 2 arc minute resolution. Solar energy investors and project developers can use these data to identify regions of the world likely to have sufficient solar resources to make a solar generation facility a worthwhile investment. Vaisala is an industry leader in the solar resource assessment space. It has been at the forefront of research regarding the estimation of surface solar conditions to better understand and predict solar energy generation. In 2010, Vaisala produced the world's first high-resolution, globally consistent data set mapping the world's solar resource potential. The annual average GHI information from this data set is provided here at a 2 arc minute resolution and based on over a decade of half-hourly, high-resolution visible satellite imagery via the broadband visible wavelength channel. The values have been processed using a combination of peer-reviewed, industry-standard techniques and in-house, including a cloud-index algorithm that produces consistent results when used with the large number of satellites that must be combined to construct a global data set. Vaisala's complete global solar database includes 2 decades of hourly estimates of GHI, direct normal irradiance (DNI), and diffuse irradiance (DIF) and is regularly maintained and updated across 5 different versions of the data set. GHI is most relevant for fixed-panel PV installations, and DNI is most relevant for concentrated solar power (CSP) projects and PV tracking systems. This data set can be used for rapid prospecting for solar energy generation sites or conducting national or regional infrastructure, policy, or transmission planning. However, the development of specific utility-scale projects generally requires additional site-specific research after this step. The global solar data set is intended as a tool to help narrow the focus of project developers and investors to accelerate the growth of solar energy worldwide. The data set has been validated against nearly 200 publicly available ground stations around the world. For more information, please visit http://www.vaisala.com/Vaisala%20Documents/Scientific%20papers/3TIER%20Solar%20Dataset%20Methodology%20and%20Validation.pdf. title: Gridded Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
description:
Global Gridded Geographically Based Economic Data (G-Econ), Version 4, provides a measure of global cell product (GCP): estimates for the amount of gross domestic product (GDP) produced in each grid cell of a 1-degree grid of the world using 2 metrics: GCP measured in the market exchange rate (MER) from local currencies into US$, and GCP measured in purchasing power parity (PPP), which adjusts country currency GCP according to the equivalent amount of US$ needed to purchase a standardized collection of goods in the country using the country's currency. GCP is defined as the gross value added by activities in a grid cell. Gross value is calculated as the total value of the outputs of local businesses providing goods and services in the grid cell, minus the value of inputs bought by those businesses. The data and methods used to calculate local added value are different for different countries, as the data available are different for different countries. State- and county level gross value data are used whenever possible.

title: Crop Land Area and Production
description:
### Overview  
  
The Crop Land and Production dataset shows the global harvested area, production, and yield for six major crops: wheat, soybean, rice,  maize, coffee, and cotton. The dataset was derived from the 2020 Spatial Production Allocation Model (SPAM). The SPAM model aimed to disaggregate (downscale) national and sub-national crop statistics using a variety of inputs, such as cropland surface, location of irrigated areas, crop suitability and potential yields, rural population densities, production systems characteristics and crop prices. Crop data was downscaled to a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes. This spatial resolution is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. 

Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels, and increased biofuel demand. Increased demand for these resources will significantly affect land and resource use, climate change, political agendas, and technological developments. A comprehensive understanding of the current spatial distribution of the world’s crops is necessary in order to preemptively address these effects. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset can be used to understand the extent and productivity of key global crops, which will help address food crop demand and its effects. 

The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was generated by the [Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research Program on Policies, Institutions, and Markets (CGIAR-PIM)](https://pim.cgiar.org/about/). CGIAR-PIM provides support for policies that help farmers improve their lives, produce nutritious and affordable foods, and protect the soil, water and biodiversity in rural landscapes. The program is led by the [International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI)](https://www.ifpri.org/about), a CGIAR-PIM research center. IFPRI provides research-based policy solutions to sustainably reduce poverty and end hunger in developing countries. The Crop Land Area and Production dataset was part of the larger SPAM dataset, which was developed for the HarvestChoice research initiative. Conducted by IFPRI, [HarvestChoice](https://www.ifpri.org/project/harvestchoice) generated knowledge products to help guide strategic investments to improve the well-being of poor people in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia through more productive and profitable farming.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The main purpose of SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics (e.g., harvested area, production quantity, and yield) by different farming systems and to further allocate such disaggregated statistics into spatially gridded units. The whole procedure entails a data fusion approach that combines information from different sources and at different spatial scales by deploying various matching
and calibration processes. Then all the data elements are processed by the optimization model, which generates results at the grid level. There are three submodules in a standardized SPAM model: disaggregation, optimization, and allocation. The SPAM2020 is conceptualized based on this general setting, while it adds further methodological and data improvements, which mainly include the update of base year, the expansion of subnational administrative-unit coverage, the extension of crop list, and the substitution of the latest hybrid cropland map as the basic allocation layer.

The first step for SPAM is to disaggregate crop statistics of agricultural production (e.g., the yield, harvested area, and total production) by administrative-unit levels (k), crop type (j), and farming system (l) from coarser scale to finer scale. The four production systems were defined by water and management type:
- Irrigated – high input (I)
- Rainfed – high input (H)
- Rainfed – low input (L)
- Rainfed – subsistence (S)

The four conceptualized farming systems are mainly delineated by the water supply system and inputs used by farmers, despite global data on farming system shares for each crop being largely absent. For a small number of large countries, e.g., Brazil, China, India, Russia, the United States, the authors have data on farming system shares at the ADM1 level. For the other countries the authors assigned the national farming system shares to each ADM1 level and then adjusted individual ADM1 farming system shares in light of the supporting evidence. For irrigated farming systems, the crop-specific shares are derived by dividing the harvested area cultivated under full control irrigation obtained from [Global Information System on Water and Agriculture (AQUASTAT)](https://www.fao.org/aquastat/en/), [MIRCA](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1029/2008GB003435), and
country-level statistics by the overall harvested area.

The optimization module in SPAM2020 is almost the same as that in previous versions. The authors applied a cross-entropy process in the General Algebraic Modeling System (GAMS), which ensures that the optimization procedure iterates until a solution is found. Once the allocation is successful, meaning that an optimal or locally optimal solution has been found, the routine immediately returns the allocated physical area by grid, crop and farming system, and the program continues with post-processing automatically.

The SPAM model used additional biological and economic inputs to allocate the statistics within each pixel. Input data included (among several others):
- Administrative units
- Crop Type
- Farming system
- Adjusted harvested area
- Total suitable area in each grid by crop and farming system
- Crop prices
- Market accessibility in each grid
- Population density

Our data catalog provides three of the SPAM2020 essential output indicators:

- Harvested Area: also measured in hectares, harvested area is at least as large as physical area but sometimes more since it also accounts for multiple harvests of a crop on the same plot. Like for physical area, the harvested area is calculated for each production system, and the sum of all harvested areas of all production systems in a pixel amounts to the total harvested area of the
pixel. The sum of all the harvested areas of the crops in a pixel can be larger than the pixel size.
- Production: for each production system and crop, production is calculated by multiplying the area harvested by its corresponding yield. It is measured in metric tons. The total production of a crop includes the production of all production systems of that crop.
- Yield: is the amount of production per harvested area and measured in kilograms per hectare. It is a measure of productivity. The total yield of a crop, when considering all production systems, is the weighted average of the four systems’ yields.

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/articles/12/3545/2020/essd-12-3545-2020.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Spatially-Disaggregated Crop Production Statistics Data for 2020 Version 3.0 has data for 36 other crops (42 total). The full dataset also includes physical area and value of production for all 42 crops. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.

Our data catalog has previously shown data for [2005](https://bit.ly/3CjoFYc). This dataset was archived because the methodology has been changed.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/foo_005_rw2_crop_area_production).

title: U.S. Monthly Precipitation Normals
description: The Parameter-elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model (PRISM) Climate Group monthly climate normals are baseline data sets describing average monthly conditions over the most recent three full decades. The most recent PRISM normals are for the period 1981-2010. Spatial climate data sets for mean monthly precipitation and minimum and maximum temperature were developed for the conterminous United States. These 30-arcsec (∼800-m) grids are the official spatial climate data sets of the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The PRISM interpolation method was used to develop data sets that reflected, as closely as possible, the current state of knowledge of spatial climate patterns in the United States. PRISM calculates a climate–elevation regression for each digital elevation model (DEM) grid cell, and stations entering the regression are assigned weights based primarily on the physiographic similarity of the station to the grid cell. Factors considered are location, elevation, coastal proximity, topographic facet orientation, vertical atmospheric layer, topographic position, and orographic effectiveness of the terrain. Surface stations used in the analysis numbered nearly 13,000 for precipitation and 10,000 for temperature. Station data were spatially quality controlled, and short-period-of-record averages adjusted to better reflect the 1981–2010 period.
