title: Crop Suitability Classes
description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the Fourth theme, Suitability and Attainable Yield, is displayed here. It combines multiple inputs ranging from climatic conditions, water supply, and agricultural input levels to spatially map the suitability of 4 different crops globally. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616).

​​Information on the current and future use of land resources are important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on current crop suitability and assess its potential impact from climate change. Coffee, Cotton, Dryland Rice, and Wetland Rice are important commodities around the globe and the Crop Suitability Class provides important spatial information on where these commodities will thrive or face challenges in future timeframes and under different climate scenarios. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security.

The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data is derived from multiple climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the Fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps.
 
The Suitability Class sub-theme falls under Theme Four of the outputs and Module V of the modeling framework. Module V integrates results from the first four modules and combines agro-climatic potential yields with soil and terrain evaluation results. This Module identifies in each grid cell its respective soil types and slope classes and then assesses and assigns a suitability rating and simulated potential yield. Results are then aggregated and mapped for each historic and future 30-year period by crop, input level, and water source and have a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator).
 
Suitability classes are calculated from the normalized Suitability Index (SI), where:
           
SI = 100 x (90 x VS + 70 x S + 50 x MS + 30 x mS + 15 x VmS + 0 x NS) / 0.9
 
SI values can range from 0 to 10,000 and the acronyms that are underlying suitability classes are defined as follows: VS = very suitable, S = suitable, MS = moderately suitable, mS = marginally suitable, VmS = very marginally suitable, and NS = not suitable. These six categories represent the shares of area extents of the different suitability classes in a grid cell. SI is calculated for each of the 53 crops by the level of input, management, and water supply system. The resultant SI in each grid cell is then grouped into eight classes depicting the aggregate crop suitability as:
- Very high: SI > 8,500
- High: 7,000 < SI ≤ 8,500
- Good: 5,550 < SI ≤ 7,000
- Medium: 4,000 < SI ≤ 5,500
- Moderate: 2,500 < SI ≤ 4,000
- Marginal: 1,000 < SI ≤ 2,500
- Very marginal: 0 < SI ≤ 1,000
- Not suitable: SI = 0
 
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Crop Suitability Index full dataset has data for 53 crops, additional timeframes (1961-1990, 1971-2000, and 2071-2100), RCPs (2.6 and 6.0), water supply (rainfed all phases, gravity irrigation), a low input level option, and a without CO2 fertilization option. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/blob/master/foo_067_rw0_crop_suitability_class).

Tree Cover
description:
### Overview  
  
The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity.

  
  
The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. 

  
  
The following steps were taken to pre-process the images:
  
  
1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed.
  
  
2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water.
  
  
3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another.

  
  
Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) and [Tree Cover Gain](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) from the same dataset. 

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and 2019 is available from the data provider. 
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. 
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_001_rw2_tree_cover).

title: Vulnerability to Climate Change Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The University of Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative (ND-GAIN) produces an annual index that measures a country’s vulnerability to climate change along with its readiness to respond and adapt. The index assesses 192 countries annually from 1995-2019. The index is on a scale from 0-100, with higher numbers indicating that the country is better poised to respond to climate disruptions. 

Every country around the world will experience and respond differently to climate disruptions. Due to the unique socioeconomic and geographic locations of each country, some will be more vulnerable from the impacts of climate change and will have differing capacities to adapt. ND-GAIN’s index combines a vulnerability score with a readiness score to assess each country. Vulnerability measures a country's exposure, sensitivity, and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change. Readiness measures a country's ability to leverage investments and convert them to adaptation actions. This index provides a standardized way to estimate a country's adaptation risk and opportunity.

ND-GAIN is a program within the Notre Dame Environmental Change Initiative with the goal of heightening awareness and understanding of adaptation, providing products and services to spur action, and enhance investments in vulnerable communities.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The ND-GAIN index measures both a country's vulnerability to climate change and its readiness to take adaptation actions. Vulnerability is assessed by considering six sectors: food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure. Each sector is composed of six indicators (36 total) that relate to three components: exposure, sensitivity, and adaptive capacity.                 
- Exposure measures the extent to which society and its supporting sectors are stressed by future climate conditions. 
- Sensitivity relates to the degree to which people and the sectors they depend on are affected by climate related disturbances.
- Adaptive capacity measures the ability of society to respond and decrease the negative consequences of climate related events.

Similarly, readiness is assessed by three core components - economic readiness, governance readiness, and social readiness - and nine indicators to produce an overall readiness metric that gauges a country's ability to leverage investments and adaptation actions.
- Economic readiness represents the investment environment which is needed to marshal funds from the private sector.
- Governance readiness relates to the conditions (stability of society, institutional arrangements) that contribute to investment risk.
- Social readiness measures the social conditions that enable society to make efficient and equitable use of and benefit from an investment.

74 data sources are used to construct the 45 indicators that make up the readiness and vulnerability scores. 20 indicators come directly from raw data sources, the other 25 are computed by the underlying data. The following steps outline how the index is created:
  
  
1. Collect the raw data and process
  
  
2. Interpolate missing data or denote certain indicators as “missing” for specific countries
  
  
3. Identify the baseline minimum and maximum values from the raw data
  
  
4. Define a reference point for each indicator (e.g. reference point for child malnutrition is 0%) 
  
  
5. Scale the raw data to score, from 0 to 1,  to allow for comparison
  
  
6. Compute the vulnerability and readiness scores
  
  
7. Compute ND-GAIN and scale scores to give a value from 0 to 100 (higher values representing greater readiness and lower vulnerability)

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The ND-GAIN dataset also includes data for each vulnerability sector (food, ecosystem services, health, human habitat, infrastructure, water), readiness sector (economic, governance, social), all 45 indicators, and trends. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on WRI’s data catalog. See the documentation on how we processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_029_rw2_vulnerability_to_climate_change).

title: Agricultural Trade Statistics
description:
### Overview  
  
The Agricultural Trade data and statistics compiled by the Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) are key economic indicators, used to track trade flows between nations. Metrics are aggregated annually at the country level. The dataset comprises four categories: import quantity, import value, export quantity, and export value, and are available for all food and agricultural products for each country in the world. Quantity data is measured in weight (tonnes), while value is measured in 1,000 United States Dollars (USD).

  
  
Agricultural commodity flows are especially important for actors along the agricultural supply chain. The metrics included in this dataset are standardized across countries, enabling comparisons to be made. This provides important information about what commodities are in surplus/deficit at the national level and elucidate linkages in the global flow of agricultural goods.

  
  
The FAO has an institutional mandate to “collect, analyze, interpret, and disseminate information relating to nutrition, food and agriculture.” A primary purpose of this dataset is to ensure that there is a source of current, relevant, and reliable statistics for crop and livestock products that is applicable on the global scale.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The FAO collects trade data from various entities including the United Nations Statistics Division (UNSD), Eurostat, and other national authorities. Trade data is collected, processed, and disseminated according to the standards outlined by the International Merchandise Trade Statistics (IMTS) [Methodology](https://unstats.un.org/unsd/trade/default.asp). The database includes annual information on the import quantity, export quantity, import value, and export value of all crop and livestock products for all countries in the world. Our data catalog only shows certain products that are derived from three crops: coffee, cotton, and rice. Additionally, only data from 1990 to 2020 is shown here , as it provides a firm historical understanding of these metrics.
 
  
  
Trade quantity refers to the net weight (in tonnes) of the commodity and excludes containers. Export quantities are defined by IMTS methodology as the physical quantity of crop products originating or manufactured in and shipped out of the reporting country and include [re-exports](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports). Import quantity is essentially the reverse: referring to the import of products for domestic consumption or processing within that country and includes re-imports. Trade values (measured in one thousand USD) are reported as the value of the products or goods as well as the value of the services performed to deliver the goods from border to border. Trade data is compiled by the domestic customs office.
 
  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://unstats.un.org/wiki/display/comtrade/Re-exports+and+Re-imports).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for every year between 1961 and 2020 and more crops and livestock products are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
See the documentation on how our team retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_039_rw0_agricultural_trade_statistics). This data has been mapped on our data catalog by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Volcano Frequency and Distribution
description:
The Global Volcano Hazard Frequency and Distribution data are created by the World Bank Group, the Columbia University Center for Hazards and Risk Research (Columbia CHRR), and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN). The data are released in a 2.5 minute gridded data set based on the National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC) Volcano Database spanning the period 1979 through 2000. This database includes nearly 4,000 volcanic events categorized as moderate or above (values 2 through 8) according to the Volcano Explosivity Index (VEI). Most volcanoes are georeferenced to the nearest 10th or 100th of a degree, with a few to the nearest 1,000th of a degree. To produce the final output, the frequency of a volcanic hazard is computed for each grid cell, with the data set consequently being classified into deciles (10 classes consisting of an approximately equal number of grid cells). The higher the grid cell value in the final output, the higher the relative frequency of hazard posed by volcanoes. This data set is the result of collaboration between the CHRR and CIESIN. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: [Archived] Cumulative Climate Impacts on Marine Ecosystems
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](85a08a4d-9336-4d18-9aaa-b7cb97bc6abf) as a replacement.**_
  
This cumulative impact index ranging from ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change) for the impact of climate change on oceans was calculated using sea surface temperature (SST), ocean productivity measured by chlorophyll (CHL), and ocean circulation by Ramirez et al. (2017). The data to calculate were from the longest time series of remote-sensing records (annual composites) on SST (1980-2014), CHL (1979-2014), and marine currents (1980-2014) available to provide finest-scale measurements of the impacts of climate change on the marine environment globally.   
  
Pixel basis, least-squares linear regression of annual information from SST, CHL, and the eastern and northern components of water speed were used for deriving the significance of temporal trends and its magnitudes (slopes; that is, annual changes in target features) over the past 3 decades. CHL data were sourced online as annual composites, whereas data on SST and marine currents were obtained on a monthly basis and averaged yearly to generate a linear relationship to extract slopes. This calculation was repeated for every pixel of the globe. These magnitudes were combined to obtain the spatially explicit Cumulative Impact Index.   
  
Different layers were first resampled following a bilinear interpolation procedure to match the spatial resolution of the coarsest SST product (that is, 1° grid). Absolute values for the slopes of obtained trends (a proxy to the magnitude of environmental changes) were then standardized to the maximum value to make all variables comparable. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value. In this way, researchers obtained a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (no change) to 1 (maximum change), thereby providing information about spatial heterogeneity in the magnitude of environmental changes and highlighting those marine areas that have undergone the largest changes in their environmental conditions. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Satellite Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: NO₂ Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) density in the troposphere. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of NO₂ between Earth’s surface and the top of the troposphere. The NO₂ density is reported with units of moles of NO₂ per square meter of air (mol/m²).

  
  
Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) is one of the most common compounds in the nitrogen oxides (NOx) group. Other nitrogen oxides include nitric acid (HNO₃) and nitric oxide (NO). NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides, meaning if NO₂ is present it is likely other nitrogen oxides are as well. NO₂ is primarily created by the burning of fuel, which can be from cars, trucks and buses, power plants, and off-road equipment. Breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the human respiratory system. Acute exposures can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms, like coughing, wheezing or difficulty breathing. Longer chronic exposures to elevated concentrations of NO₂ may contribute to the development of asthma and potentially increase susceptibility to respiratory infections. People with asthma, as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system. The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as NO₂, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI). 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI NO₂ dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. The data was retrieved and analyzed using a 3 step process. 

  
  
1. Total NO₂ slant column density was determined from radiance and irradiance spectra measured by TROPOMI. It was analyzed using a Differential Optical Absorption Spectroscopy (DOAS) method. NO₂ slant column density is the amount of NO₂ found along an average path taken by photons traveling from the sun to the satellite sensor.

  
  
2. Slant column density data was then separated into stratospheric and tropospheric categories based on information coming from the satellite’s data assimilation system. Stratospheric data was then removed from the dataset.

  
  
3. Tropospheric slant column density was converted into tropospheric vertical column density and the average NO₂ density for the entire vertical column was calculated. This was determined by applying an appropriate air mass factor (AMF) and actual, daily information on the vertical distribution of NO₂ calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model. The altitude-dependent AMF used depended on the satellite geometry, terrain height, cloud fraction and height, and surface albedo.

  
  
The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Total Column”.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_035_tropomi_atmospheric_chemistry_model).

title: [Archived] Water Stress Country Ranking
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](47053e23-7808-40d9-b4ae-1af73c5c8bab) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating for countries and water basins at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available water and estimates the degree to which freshwater availability is an ongoing concern in a region. The dataset’s main focus is to include detailed and accurate information for the world’s 100 most populous river basins, as they are often areas where water stress is a large concern. Additionally, researchers grouped the final dataset into water usage by different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand where water stress in an area is coming from. The dataset was calculated by comparing weighted averages of water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high.
  
  
Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production.
  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments creating water use policies. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers created this global dataset to include the 100 most populous river basins and all countries. Baseline water stress was calculated by dividing the weighted average water withdrawals in a region by the total blue freshwater available. To create the weighted average water withdrawals researchers used information on water withdrawals and divided each region into grid cells. Each grid cell was given a different weight based on the water withdrawals and water available within it. The grid cells were then combined to encompass different regions shown in the final dataset. Researchers further separated the dataset to view water usage in three different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial).
  
  
Baseline water stress values were grouped into five categories when mapped: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high. The water stress scores for each category are as follows: Low <1, low to medium 1-5, medium to high 5-10, high 10-20, and extremely high >20. Each category represents the risk of water stress in the area. Data for country boundaries was taken from the Natural Earth Data 10m Admin 0 – Countries dataset. Data on the extent of the 100 most populous river basins was taken from HydroSHEDS 30s Basin Outlines and Gridded Population of the World, v3, Future Estimates 2010 datasets. Gridded weights and source indicators (baseline water stress) were calculated using Aqueduct Global Maps 2.0.
  
  
The final dataset was created in tabular format and projected on a global map of the earth at a national scale. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset.  
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for flood occurrence from 1985 to 2011 and drought severity from 1091 to 2008 is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Minimum Annual Arctic Sea Ice Extent
description:
This minimum annual Arctic sea ice extent data is derived from the monthly sea ice extent data produced by the NSIDC, which show monthly averages of sea ice extent in the Arctic and Antarctic. Sea Ice Index products are derived from 2 data sets: the Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations and the Sea Ice Concentrations from Nimbus-7 SMMR and DMSP SSM/I-SSMIS Passive Microwave Data. These satellite passive microwave-derived data sets are used to generate the monthly images and numbers that comprise the Sea Ice Index record of sea ice extent and concentration from November 1978 to present. Median extents are calculated using a 30-year reference period of 1981 through 2010. The data are produced in a consistent way that makes the monthly index time-series appropriate for use when looking at long-term trends in sea ice cover. title: Annual Surface Temperature Anomalies
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the average annual surface air temperature anomaly from 1850 to present, compared to a 1951-1980 baseline time period. In other words, this dataset shows how much cooler or warmer each year is compared to the average surface air temperature from 1951-1980. This dataset is available at 1 degree (°) spatial resolution and  covers increasing amounts of the Earth’s surface: approximately 57% in 1850, 75% in 1880, 95% in 1960, and 99.9% by 2015. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C). 
  
  

Surface air temperature is defined as the temperature of the air near the surface of the earth and is generally measured by weather stations. Surface air temperatures are influenced by solar radiation, weather, surface materials, topography, and climate. Surface air temperature anomalies are used to track the change in surface air temperature from a baseline, in this case a 30 year average temperature from 1951-1980. Short-term changes in surface air temperature can have an impact on plants, animals, and humans in those areas. Long-term changes in surface air temperature are used to measure climate change and global warming ([Berkeley Earth](https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2019-259/)). Climate change is a long-term change in the average weather patterns that have come to define Earth’s local, regional and global climates. Global warming is the long-term heating of Earth’s climate system observed since the pre-industrial period (between 1850 and 1900) due to human activities, primarily fossil fuel burning, which increases heat-trapping greenhouse gas levels in Earth’s atmosphere ([NASA](https://climate.nasa.gov/resources/global-warming-vs-climate-change/)). 
  
  

This dataset was created by combining the Berkeley Earth [monthly land surface air temperature estimates](http://static.berkeleyearth.org/papers/Methods-GIGS-1-103.pdf)  with the Hadley Centre Sea Surface Temperature 3 dataset ([HadSST3](https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/data/external/hadsst-4-global-sea-surface)). Berkeley Earth was founded in 2010 with the goal of addressing the major concerns of climate change skeptics regarding global warming and the land surface temperature record. Berkeley Earth uses this dataset to measure changes in global air surface temperature and climate change.  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset has been created by Berkeley Earth by combining the Berkeley Earth [monthly land surface air temperature estimates](http://static.berkeleyearth.org/papers/Methods-GIGS-1-103.pdf) with the [HadSST3](https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/data/external/hadsst-4-global-sea-surface) sea surface temperature dataset. 
  
  

To develop the monthly land surface air temperature estimates, Berkeley Earth developed a new mathematical framework for producing maps and large-scale averages of temperature changes from weather station data for the purposes of climate analysis. They preliminarily merged weather station datasets, combining 1.6 billion temperature reports from 16 pre-existing data archives. After eliminating duplicate records, the current archive contains over 39,000 unique weather stations. Berkeley Earth then applied weighted sampling and spatial interpolation to this dataset to convert individual weather station measurements to a global map of average land temperature.
  
  

The sea surface air temperature dataset from HadSST3 was interpolated using a [Kriging-based approach](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/earth-and-planetary-sciences/kriging) to increase the spatial resolution and fill in missing data. After interpolation, the Berkeley Earth monthly land surface air temperature estimates were merged with the HadSST3 dataset using the fraction of land to water in each grid cell (typically reported with a 1° spatial resolution). When the land surface temperature and sea surface temperature are combined, Berkeley Earth creates two versions of the final dataset, based on how air temperature is measured in areas with sea ice. One version records the temperature as the air temperature over sea ice, referred to as, “Average Temperature with Air Temperatures at Sea Ice”, and the other records the temperature as the sea surface temperature under sea ice, referred to as, “Average Temperature with Water Temperatures at Sea Ice”. The user can choose between the two options, and the choice of how to assess the temperature of areas with sea ice coverage has a notable impact on global anomalies over past decades due to rapid warming of air temperatures in the Arctic. 
  
  

Then, Resource Watch created the Annual Surface Temperature Anomalies dataset by taking the yearly average of the combined Berkeley Earth and HadSST3 monthly datasets. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://essd.copernicus.org/preprints/essd-2019-259/).   
  
### Additional Information  
  
Additional data on monthly average air surface temperature anomalies is also available from Berkeley Earth, along with higher resolution versions for select geographies and the original weather station data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. Resource Watch created the annual average surface air temperature dataset by averaging monthly surface air temperature anomaly measurements. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on Github

title: Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents
description:
### Overview  
  
The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset shows the location of selected incidents that have occured from 1957 to present. The dataset shown on Resource Watch includes oil spills, chemical spills, and other incidents in which the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R) has been active in assisting with the incident response. The dataset includes United States waters and some international locations show as point locations.

  
  
OR&R is the federal U.S. government organization with expertise in preparing for, evaluating, and responding to threats to coastal environments, including oil and chemical spills, releases from hazardous waste sites, and marine debris. They are responsible for responding to and providing scientific support to federal on-scene coordinators for these incidents. The dataset is intended to provide public access to the history of incidents that have occured. It can be used to show trends and the long term effects of spills.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Oil and Chemical Spill Incidents dataset was created by using data from reports created by NOAA's Office of Response and Restoration (OR&R). These reports are present for all oil, chemical, and other incidents that OR&R provided scientific support for. From each report the name, date, location (longitude/latitude), type of threat, and a brief description were cataloged in the Raw Incident dataset.

title: [Archived] Tree Cover Gain
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](d305958d-3468-4a35-9660-5e18aa3e3190) as a replacement.**_
  
This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and  the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, measures areas of tree cover gain across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at 30 × 30 m resolution, displayed as a 12-year cumulative layer. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. Over 600,000 Landsat 7 images were compiled and analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis. The clear land surface observations (30 × 30 m pixels) in the satellite images were assembled, and a supervised learning algorithm was then applied to identify per pixel tree cover gain. Tree cover gain was defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. The tree cover canopy density of the displayed data is >50%. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Food Price Spikes
description: The Alert for Price Spices (ALPS) is generated by the World Food Programme (WFP). This alert indicates when prices of key staple food commodities have deviated from seasonal trends, and by how much. Early detection of food price increases can alert the international community to the possibility of current and future food insecurity in a region.    Seasonal price trends are determined through reference to monthly commodity prices recorded in the WFP's Food and Commodity Price Database, which is collected by WFP country offices, national government agencies, and partner organizations. A linear regression is used to determine the contributions that 2 components make to seasonal price trends: the month of the year (related to harvest times) and the overall passage of time (related to population growth, inflation rates, etc.).    The current ALPS value for a food commodity is the number of standard deviations the current price is above the commodity's expected price for that month. Based on this ALPS value, markets are assigned to 1 of 4 situations, where all nominal values are measured in standard deviations from the seasonal mean price:     Normal, ALPS < 0.25  Stress, 0.25 < ALPS < 1  Alert, 1 < ALPS < 2  Crisis, ALPS >= 2 Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Riverine Nitrogen (N) and Phosphorus (P) Input, Retention, and Export
description:
The Integrated Model to Assess the Global Environment—Global Nutrient Model (IMAGE-GNM) is a global distributed, spatially explicit model using hydrology as the basis for describing nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) delivery to surface water, transport, and in-stream retention in rivers, lakes, wetlands, and reservoirs. It is part of the integrated assessment model IMAGE, which studies the interaction between society and the environment over prolonged time periods. In the IMAGE-GNM model, grid cells receive water with dissolved and suspended N and P from upstream grid cells; inside grid cells, N and P are delivered to water bodies via diffuse sources (surface runoff, shallow and deep groundwater, riparian zones, litterfall in floodplains, atmospheric deposition) and point sources (wastewater); N and P retention in a water body is calculated on the basis of the residence time of the water and nutrient uptake velocity; subsequently, water and nutrients are transported to downstream grid cells. Differences between model results and observed concentrations for a range of global rivers are acceptable given the global scale of the uncalibrated model. Sensitivity analysis with data for the year 2000 showed that runoff is a major factor for N and P delivery, retention, and river export. For both N and P, uptake velocity and all factors used to compute the subgrid in-stream retention are important for total in-stream retention and river export. Soil N budgets, wastewater, and all factors determining litterfall in floodplains are important for N delivery to surface water. For P the factors that determine the P content of the soil (soil P content and bulk density) are important factors for delivery and river export. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Wind Energy Potential
description:
Vaisala created this global data set of average annual wind speeds at 80 m above the Earth's surface, a common height for wind turbines when the data set was originally created in 2008. The map resolution is 2 arc minutes and average wind speeds are measured in m/s. These data can be used to identify regions of the world likely to have sufficient wind resources to make wind energy generation a worthwhile investment. Vaisala pioneered the use of numerical weather prediction (NWP) models for producing realistic wind flows around the world to better understand and predict wind energy generation. NWP models are physically based and use powerful supercomputers to simulate the interaction between the entire atmosphere and the Earth's surface, even in places where no direct observations are available. This methodology captures the myriad processes responsible for wind—from jet-level dynamics to surface-level processes—and creates a more robust and accurate wind climatology. In essence, the models use numerical methods to obtain approximate answers to mathematical equations that describe the physics and dynamics of the atmosphere. To solve these equations for different locations on the globe, the atmosphere is divided into many small elements, both horizontally and vertically. The model computes what happens within each model element and how much mass, energy, and momentum is exchanged between the model elements. In 2008, with the release of its global wind data set, Vaisala was the first to map global wind potential at high resolution by using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and conducting a 10-year computer simulation at a 2 arc minute (approximately 5 km) resolution. This data set can be used for rapid prospecting for wind energy generation sites or conducting national or regional infrastructure, policy, or transmission planning. However, the development of specific utility-scale projects requires additional site-specific research after this step. The global wind data set is intended as a tool to help to narrow the focus of project developers and investors to accelerate the growth of wind energy worldwide. The data set was validated against publicly available wind speed observations from more than 4,000 globally distributed meteorological stations from the National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP) Automated Data Processing (ADP) surface observations data set. For more validation information, please visit http://www.vaisala.com/en/energy/Documents/WEA-ERG-3TIER-Global%20Wind%20Dataset.pdf. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: [Archived] Observed and Potential Crop Yields
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](01ae2fd7-b818-429f-a27e-a36c8def971a) as a replacement.**_
  
The Yield Gap and Potential Yield for Major Crops data set was created by EarthStat, the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment and the Land Use (UMN IonE), and the Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC) for 16 major crops. Yield gaps are defined as the difference between observed crop yields and the potential yield at the same location. Yield gaps were estimated by comparing observed yields to potential yields determined by identifying high-yielding areas within zones, or bins, of similar climate. To classify climates, 2 parameters, which are known to be fundamental drivers of plant growth, were used to describe a region's climate: growing degree days (GDD) and a crop soil moisture index (the ratio of actual evapotranspiration to potential evapotranspiration). For each climate zone and each crop, a table was generated containing the yield, harvest area, and latitude/longitude position information for each grid cell included in the distribution. The data were sorted from the grid cells by their yield values, ranking them from lowest to highest yield. The grid cells' respective harvest areas were then accumulated until arriving at the statistical information of interest: the mean, median, and 90th percentile yields. The percentage of a crop's harvested area was calculated to define a percentile yield value. The data draw on average of census data between 1997 and 2003 and are shown as 2000 at a 5 minute x 5 minute spatial resolution. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. To produce the final output, the frequency of an earthquake hazard is calculated for each grid cell, and the resulting grid cells are then classified into deciles (10 classes consisting of an approximately equal number of grid cells). title: Historical Sea Ice Medians
description:
### Overview  
  
The Historical Sea Ice Medians dataset shows monthly median sea ice extent over the period of 1981-2010. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments for both the Arctic and Antarctic regions. Satellite data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Gridded ice concentration estimates were used to define the ice edge position that is typical for each month. This dataset shows the maximum (blue line) and minimum (yellow line) sea ice extent, and the typical sea ice extent for each month in between. In the Arctic, sea ice normally reaches its maximum extent in March and its minimum extent in September. Antarctic sea ice extent peaks in September and reaches its minimum in February. The lines in this dataset represent how sea ice expands and retreats between its maximum and minimum extent.

  
  
This dataset is the [baseline](https://nsidc.org/data/noaa/baseline-change) for sea ice index products from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). Climate baselines are used as a historical reference to current trends and anomalies. A three-decade time period is ideal because it averages out short-term variability. This dataset can be used to understand how polar sea ice extent and melting season are changing. Antarctic sea ice behaves differently than Arctic sea ice, largely because the two regions have different land-ocean configurations. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has declined since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. Comparing current sea ice extent data to this baseline dataset can help define the rates and locations of sea ice retreat. 

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Historical Sea Ice Medians were generated from data collected by five sensors:
- [Nimbus-7](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987
- [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991
- DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995
- DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007
- DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to December 2017

  
  
The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. The SMMR sensor collected data on alternate days and the SSM/I and SSMIS sensor collected data on a daily basis. Daily satellite measurements were averaged each month to eliminate errors and smooth variations caused by short-term weather conditions. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell.

  
  
Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Median ice extents were calculated by applying the 15% cutoff to all gridded concentration data for each month between 1981 and 2010. Cells that classified as ice more than 50% of the time from 1981-2010 were designated as ice; cells that classified as ice less than 50% of the time were designated as water. This was done on a monthly basis: for example, the data from every January from 1981-2010 was analyzed together to create a single January dataset. Each month’s gridded concentration data was mapped and a contour line was drawn to mark the ice edge. This contour line represents the median sea ice extent. Because the sea ice extent varies considerably from year to year, the median extent is a better representation of the sea ice extent over time. The workflow was applied to both the Arctic and Antarctic regions.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).

title: Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maize, Rice, Soybean, and Wheat Yield Trends dataset shows the average annual change in crop yield from 1989-2008. Agricultural crop yield is the amount of crop harvested per area of land. It is used to measure a crop’s performance. This study used approximately 1.8 million agricultural census reports from 13,500 political units around the world to determine how crop yield changed over time. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes, which is approximately 10 kilometers x 10 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.”
  
  
Together, maize, rice, soybean, and wheat account for nearly two-thirds of global agricultural calories. Global demand for these crops is rising as a result of diet shifts, rising population levels and increased biofuel demand. In order to meet projected demand, [crop production needs to double by 2050](https://www.nature.com/articles/ncomms2296#MOESM1532). Improving crop yield, instead of clearing new land for agriculture, is one of the preferred solutions. In many areas, yield is stagnant or has collapsed entirely. Understanding where improvement is most needed can guide new agricultural investments. It is also important to identify and continue improving yield of high-performing crops and regions.  

  
  
This dataset was produced by EarthStat, a collaboration between the Global Landscapes Initiative (GLI) at the University of Minnesota’s Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE) and the Land Use and Global Environment (LUGE) lab at the University of British Columbia (UBC). EarthStat’s mission is to provide data on the global food system to help others make science-based decisions. The GLI is a scientific initiative that develops and applies tools to characterize global land use and evaluate global agricultural supply and demand trends. The LUGE lab is a research group that studies links between land use, global environmental change, and food security.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Approximately 1.8 million census reports were used to determine yield of the four crops for the years between 1989 and 2008. Crop yield is the ratio of production (kilograms) and harvested area (hectares). According to the UN’s [Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)](http://www.fao.org/waicent/faostat/agricult/pr_ele-e.htm), production is the amount of crop harvested. The harvested area is the area from which the crop is gathered. National-level data used in this study was provided by the [FAO](http://www.fao.org/faostat/en/#home), who collects data from the member countries’ statistical offices. At the time of the study, the FAO had crop data for 226 nations. In addition to national-level data, the study also used subnational data for the 51 countries that account for more than 70% of global production/harvested area for each of the four crops. Data was available at the state/province level for all 51 countries and county/district/município/department level for an additional 17 countries. This data was collected from these countries’ agricultural and statistical bureaus. 

  
  
According to the data provider, studies have used linear regression to project future crop yields. As such, the annual crop yields in this study (one data point per year) were linearly regressed to calculate the average change in yield from 1989-2008. A linear regression is a line modeled to fit the shape of a group of data points. The slope of the line gives the rate of change–in this case, the average yield change over the observed period. This calculation was performed for each crop at each political unit. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0066428#pone.0066428.s017).

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. title: Earthquakes
description:
### Overview  
  
The Earthquakes dataset shows all earthquakes that have occurred within the last seven days, earthquakes with a magnitude of 5.0+ within the last 30 days, and significant earthquakes within the last 30 days. Earthquakes are deemed significant based on a combination of their magnitude, number of Did You Feel It (DYFI) responses, and Prompt Assessment of Global Earthquakes for Response (PAGER) alert level. The dataset shows earthquakes that have occurred globally and is updated within 15 minutes of an earthquake’s occurrence. The location of each earthquake is designated by longitude and latitude and listed with its magnitude.

  
  
The dataset is part of the Earthquake Hazards Program created by the United States Geological Survey (USGS) with assistance from contributing government agencies around the world. The Earthquake Hazards Program works to provide and apply relevant earthquake science information and knowledge for reducing deaths, injuries, and property damage from earthquakes through understanding of their characteristics and effects and by providing the information and knowledge needed to mitigate these losses. This dataset serves as a way to track and understand where earthquakes occur, which is integral in mitigating earthquake hazards for the future.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The USGS created this dataset by collecting and compiling near-real-time seismological information, alerts, and reports of earthquakes from over 100 contributing institutions and government agencies around the world. Seismological information was largely collected by remote sensors placed and monitored by these groups. The USGS then utilized the information collected to calculate the significance level for each earthquake. An earthquake’s significance was determined by using the following formula based on magnitude (mag), PAGER alert level (pager), and Did You Feel It Score (DYFI):

  
  
Significance = max(mag_significance, pager_significance) + dyfi_significance

  
  
mag_significance = magnitude  x  100  x  (magnitude / 6.5)
  
  
pager_significance = red is 2000, orange is 1000,  yellow is 500, and green is 0
  
  
dyfi_significance = min(num_responses, 1000)  x  (max_cdi / 10)
  
  
Any event that received a significance score over 600 was considered a significant event in the dataset. 
  
  
PAGER is an automated system that rapidly estimates earthquake shaking and the scope and impact of earthquakes around the world. PAGER delivers rapid estimates of the total number of people and settlements exposed to a wide range of shaking from light to catastrophic. Additionally, it provides estimates of potential fatalities, as well as the approximate economic impact an earthquake may cause. PAGER alert levels are assigned as follows:
- Red = 1000+ fatalities and $1 billion+ estimated losses
- Orange = 100-999 fatalities and $100 million - $1 billion estimated losses
- Yellow = 1-99 fatalities and $1 million - $100 million estimated losses
- Green = 0 fatalities and less than $1million estimated losses
  
  
Did You Feel It (DYFI) is a program run by the USGS. It is a system that was developed to tap the abundant information available about earthquakes from the people who experience them. It is made up of an online questionnaire where people provide a description of what they experienced, the effects of the earthquake, and the extent of damage. For each earthquake the responses are aggregated for users in each community and a single intensity score is assigned, called “Community Decimal Intensity” (CDI), to that community.
  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data specifically for the U.S.z on all earthquakes that have occurred over the last 1 day, 7 days, and 30 days is available. Further data on each earthquake’s depth of occurrence, Did You Feel It score, ShakeMap score, and PAGER alert level is also available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/dis_001_significant_earthquakes). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map this data for display on Resource Watch.

title: Female & Male Population Densities
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010. It uses national censuses and population registers for the year 2010. The global data is presented as gridded raster data with a 30 arc second resolution (about 1 km at the equator). This dataset was created by Columbia University’s Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) and is the fourth version and 11th revision of the Gridded Population of the World (GPWv4) estimates.  
  
GPWv4 consists of estimates of age and sex disaggregated population as counts (number of persons per pixel) and densities (number of persons per km²).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPWv4): Basic Demographic Characteristics, Revision 11 provides estimates of population counts by age and sex for the year 2010, consistent with national censuses and population registers. To estimate the male and female populations by age in 2010, the proportions of males and females in each five-year age group from ages 0-4 to ages 85+ for the given census year were calculated. These proportions were then applied to the 2010 estimates of the total population to obtain 2010 estimates of male and female populations by age.   
  
In some cases, the spatial resolution of the age and sex proportions was coarser than the resolution of the total population estimates to which they were applied. The population density rasters were created by dividing the population count rasters by the land area raster. The data files were produced as global rasters at 30 arc second (about 1 km at the equator) resolution. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data on male and female counts, and distribution of populations disaggregated by age, is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Water Stress Country Ranking
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the baseline water stress rating at a national scale. Baseline water stress is a measure of the level of competition for available freshwater. The dataset was calculated by comparing water withdrawals in a region to the quantity of water available. Higher water stress values indicate that there is more competition among people for available freshwater. The dataset was grouped by water usage for different sectors (agricultural, domestic, and industrial) to help understand which sectors had the greatest impact on water stress. The results were projected on a global map in five water stress risk categories: low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high.
  
  
Understanding water stress is integral for human wellbeing. Water is a limited resource and a necessity for life. Water stress can have serious environmental consequences, with damage occurring to natural ecosystems reliant on a steady water supply. Additionally, water stress can lead to human and business conflicts, particularly between industrial and agricultural users that rely on water supply for production.
  
  
This dataset was created by the World Resources Institute (WRI) to assist companies, investors, and governments in creating water use policies.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Water Stress Country Ranking is based on baseline water stress measurements. Baseline water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Gridded output data from the [PCRaster Global Water Balance](https://gmd.copernicus.org/articles/11/2429/2018/) (PCRGLOBWB 2) hydrological model was used for both water withdrawal and available water. The water withdrawal output data from PCRGLOBWB 2 included monthly data from January 1960 to December 2014 for four sectors: domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock. Output data for available water was also available over the same time frame. Data from the model was then aggregated spatially to the sub-basin level using the World Wildlife Fund’s (WWF) [HydroBASINS level 6](https://hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) hydrological sub-basins. Next, the data was regressed at the sub-basin level using an ordinary least square (OLS) regression with a trailing moving window size of 10 years to reduce noise in the data. This process resulted in gross water withdrawal and available water for each month for each sub-basin in the dataset. 
  
  
Next, the overall baseline water stress per month, per year, per sub-basin was determined. This was done by dividing the gross total water withdrawal by the difference between the available water and consumptive water withdrawal. This resulted in 12 time series of baseline water stress for each sub-basin: one time series for each month, with each time series spanning the years 1960-2014. Then, a single baseline water stress value for each month in each sub-basin was calculated by fitting a second OLS regression to each of the 12 time series and using the value for 2014 as the baseline water stress for that month. While the 2014 regression value is used, this value actually represents the baseline value, rather than an estimate of the water stress in 2014.
  
  
To compute national baseline water stress scores, the sub-basins had to be aggregated to a national scale. Aggregation was made possible by following the steps outlined on page 4 of the [2013 version](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct_coutnry_rankings_010914.pdf) of the methodology. This resulted in raw country score percentages in which water stress was classified as follows:
- Low (0-1): <10%
- Low to medium (1-2): 10-20%
- Medium to high (2-3): 20-40%
- High (3-4): 40-80%
- Extremely high (4-5): >80%
  
  
Each category represents the risk of water stress in the country. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://files.wri.org/s3fs-public/aqueduct-30-updated-decision-relevant-global-water-risk-indicators_1.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [interannual variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat052-Aqueduct-Interannual-Variability) and [seasonal variability](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/wat053-Aqueduct-Seasonal-Variability) in water supply from the same dataset.  
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional information on drought risk and riverine flood risk is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_036_rw1_water_stress_country_ranking). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: National Infant Mortality
description:
The 'mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is the number of infants dying before reaching one year of age, per 1,000 live births in a given year.  The main sources of mortality data are vital registration systems and direct or indirect estimates based on sample surveys or censuses. A "complete" vital registration system - covering at least 90 percent of vital events in the population - is the best source of age-specific mortality data. Estimates of neonatal, infant, and child mortality tend to vary by source and method for a given time and place. Years for available estimates also vary by country, making comparisons across countries and over time difficult. To make neonatal, infant, and child mortality estimates comparable and to ensure consistency across estimates by different agencies, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), which comprises the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank Group, the United Nations Population Division, and other universities and research institutes, developed and adopted a statistical method that uses all available information to reconcile differences. The method uses statistical models to obtain a best estimate trend line by fitting a country-specific regression model of mortality rates against their reference dates.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.  
  
### Additional Information

title: Fertility Rates
description:
The Fertility rate, total (births per woman) data set released on the World Bank data catalog, represents the number of children that would be born to a woman if she were to live to the end of her childbearing years and bear children in accordance with age-specific fertility rates of the specified year.  Data is collected from the "World Population Prospects" of the United Nations Population Division,Census reports and other statistical publications from national statistical offices, "Demographic Statistics" of Eurostat, the "Population and Vital Statistics Report" of the United Nations Statistical Division, theU.S. Census Bureau's  International Database, and the Statistics and Demography Programme of the Secretariat of the Pacific Community.  Total fertility rates are based on data on registered live births from vital registration systems or, in the absence of such systems, from censuses or sample surveys. The estimated rates are generally considered reliable measures of fertility in the recent past. Where no empirical information on age-specific fertility rates is available, a model is used to estimate the share of births to adolescents. For countries without vital registration systems fertility rates are generally based on extrapolations from trends observed in censuses or surveys from earlier years.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

description: GADM is a spatial database of the location of the world's administrative areas (or adminstrative boundaries) for use in GIS and similar software.
