title: Arctic Sea Ice Extent
description:
### Overview  
  
The Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Arctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Arctic region. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand the current Arctic sea ice extent. Typically, Arctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in March and minimum in September. However, Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property - albedo -  keeps polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns.

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Arctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset.  

  
  
The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. 

  
  
Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data

title: [Archived] Tree Cover
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](027799db-c161-462a-9c20-aeb97b84e06e) as a replacement.**_
  
This data set, a collaboration between the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and NASA, displays tree cover over all global land (except for Antarctica and a number of Arctic islands) for the year 2000 at 30 × 30 m resolution. This layer displays all vegetation greater than 5 m in height with >30% canopy density. Data in this layer were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. The clear surface observations from over 600,000 images were analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis, to determine per pixel tree cover using a supervised learning algorithm. title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of PM2.5 for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to a 24-hour average.

  
  
PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) the size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even go into the bloodstream.  The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world.

  
  
These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/).
Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md).  
 
   
  
Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). 
 
  
  
Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry.  The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions.
 
  
  
The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/403726e5-6852-49f4-9dce-b82b599b09fc) and [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/8ee6a93b-ab7a-41a8-95f5-3d684626d9ea).

title: Agro-Ecological Zones
description:
### Overview  
  
The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 (GAEZ v4) dataset assesses current and future agricultural resources and their potential. It is a standardized framework allowing for the characterization of climate, soil, and terrain conditions that are relevant for agricultural production. Data from the First Theme, Land and Water Resources, is displayed here and allows for the uniform classification of [biophysical](https://dictionary.cambridge.org/dictionary/english/biophysics) resources that are relevant for agricultural production systems. Outputs are presented at 5 arc minutes resolution, which is approximately 9 km x 9 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

​​Information on the current and future use of land resources is important for agricultural decision-making with implications on food security, sustainability of land and water resources, and agricultural development and policies. The GAEZ v4 dataset brings together multiple data sources to provide information on the biophysical limitations of land, current crop suitability, and information on how different agricultural resources may be impacted by climate change. Understanding what changes may occur in the future will enable different actors the ability to increase resilience, develop techniques or policies to alleviate potential challenges, and maintain food security.

The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations (FAO) together with the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA) began developing the GAEZ modeling framework in the early 1980s to provide current data on the state of agricultural resources. It has since expanded to support sustainable agricultural development and provide key information on current and future risks to agricultural production, crop development, land productivity, and impacts from climate change.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Multiple datasets were used as inputs to the GAEZ v4 modeling framework and provide data on historic and future climate attributes, soil and terrain resources, land cover, protected land, biodiversity areas, water resources, administrative units, population, and livestock. Historical climate data comes from the Climatic Research Unit TS v3.21 datasets which include monthly climate information. Future climate data for AEZ is derived from climate model outputs for four (2.6, 4.5, 6, 8.5) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) from the fifth Assessment Report (AR5) of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

Data processing was broken into several steps and seven main modules summarize the necessary steps within the GAEZ v4 modeling framework. Outputs from each of the modules are categorized into six main themes: 1) Land and Water Resources, 2) Agro-climatic Resources, 3) Agro-climatic Potential Yield, 4) Suitability and Attainable Yield, 5) Actual Yields and Production, and 6) Yield and Production Gaps.
 
The Agro-Ecological Zones (AEZ) sub-theme outputs fall under the first Theme, Land and Water Resources, and provides an inventory of land resources for the assessment of land productivity under specific agro-ecological conditions. Thermal and moisture layers are combined with broad categories of soil and terrain qualities allowing for the identification of land areas with biophysical constraints. 

A rigorous methodology and set of explicit principles are followed to assemble the AEZ classes and definitions. The following principles ensure that: 1) the map classes align with major climate zones based on the baseline historical period of 1981-2010, 2) map classes reflect broad ranges of the length of growing period boundaries, and 3) AEZ classes have generalized information about the prevailing soil and terrain limitations that are derived from GAEZ v4 terrain and soil resources inventories. The final AEZ layer has 57 different classes that are mapped at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (approximately 9 km at the equator).
 
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.fao.org/3/cb4744en/cb4744en.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Our data catalog shows only a subset of the dataset. The Global Agro-Ecological Zoning version 4 Agro-Ecological Zones data has additional data for 2071-2100 and additional RCPs (2.6 and 6). For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Migrant Deaths
description:
The Missing Migrants Project by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) counts migrants who have died or gone missing at the external borders of states, or in the process of migration toward an international destination. The IOM defines a migrant as any person who is moving or has moved across an international border or within a state away from his or her habitual place of residence. Data are obtained from local authorities (coast guards, sheriff’s offices, medical examiners), interviews with survivors provided by IOM field offices, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and media reports. The count excludes deaths that occur in immigration detention facilities, during deportation, or after forced return to a migrant’s homeland, as well as deaths more loosely connected with migrants’ irregular status, such as those resulting from labor exploitation. Migrants who die or go missing after they are established in a new home are also not included in the data, so deaths in refugee camps or housing are excluded. This approach is chosen because deaths that occur at physical borders and while en route represent a more clearly definable category and inform which migration routes are most dangerous. title: Climate Hazard Indicators (Extreme rainy days) Historical and SSP scenarios - Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu
description:
### Overview
 
 
The dataset includes five major climatic indicators viz. annual values for minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), total precipitation (mm/year), and the number of rainy days (represented as integers) for two Indian states, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. It features decadal averages from 2020-2100 for Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs), including SSP5-8.5, which reflects a high emissions scenario, and SSP2-4.5, representing moderate challenges to both mitigation and adaptation. Additionally, the dataset provides historical data for all the five indicators averaged over the period from 2005 to 2014.
 
 
### Methodology
 
 
**Pre-Processing**: The decadal time periods were labeled as follows: 2020-2029 as 2020, 2030-2039 as 2030, 2040-2049 as 2040, 2050-2059 as 2050, 2060-2069 as 2060, 2070-2079 as 2070, 2080-2089 as 2080, and 2090-2099 as 2090.
 
 
**Layers of interest**: Annual averages of minimum temperature (℃), maximum temperature (℃), mean temperature (℃), Annual total precipitation (mm/year), and the annual total number of rainy days (represented as integers).
 
 
**Data**: The ERA5 reanalysis dataset (ECMWF 2022), a satellite data product of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts with a spatial resolution of 31 kilometers (km), is used as a reference dataset. The ensemble of downscaled daily time series outputs from global climate models (GCMs). These time series include the historical years covered by the observation time series as well as the specified future years of interest. We have used the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 product, which includes outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models at approximately 25 km spatial resolution.
 
 
### Estimation Methods
 
 
Out of the 35 models, we select the top 3 climate models that perform best for a specific weather variable in a particular geographic region, and present the ensemble mean of these models. The ERA5 dataset is used as a reference, and the comparison is made for the historical period between 1980 and 2014. After selecting the models, we apply a calibration/bias correction procedure to the future time series of the models. This involves aligning the model's frequency distribution with the historical data by shifting the percentiles of the model's distribution. For instance, if the 20th percentile of the model data corresponds to the 30th percentile of the observations, then the 30th percentile of the calibrated model data will match the 20th percentile of the uncalibrated model data.
 
 
For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Wong, T., and P Switzer. 2023. 'Estimating future local climate hazard probabilities.' Technical Note. Washington, DC: World Resources Institute. Available online at: doi.org/10.46830/writn.22.00074.v2.
 
 
### Description of the Layers
 
 
**Annual Maximum Temperature (℃)**: The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Minimum Temperature (℃)**: The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Mean Temperature (℃)**: The daily mean temperature is calculated by averaging the daily minimum and maximum temperatures. The annual mean temperature is obtained by averaging the daily mean temperatures over the course of a year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Total Precipitation (mm/year)**: The daily precipitation values are summed over the entire year to calculate the annual total precipitation. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
**Annual Rainy Days (represented as integers)**: A rainy day is defined as a day with precipitation exceeding 2.5 mm (as per the India Meteorological Department). The total number of rainy days in a year is calculated by summing the rainy days throughout the year. The decadal average is the average of the annual values across 10 years.
 
 
### Visualizing the Data
 
 
The data is provided at a 25-km resolution and is presented as a raster with a time slider with a separate layer for each variable. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shade (indicating low values) to darker shade (representing higher values).

title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description:
### Overview  
  
Biodiversity hotspots, a classification system created by the Critical Ecosystem Partnership Fund (CEPF), include some of our planet’s most biologically diverse yet threatened terrestrial areas. An area is qualified as a hotspot if it contains at least 1,500 species of vascular plants found nowhere else on Earth (known as “endemic” species) and it has lost at least 70 percent of its primary native vegetation. Between 1988 and 2016, 36 biodiversity hotspots have been identified globally.   
  
### Methodology  
  
Hotspots were defined by Norman Myers in 1988 when he published a seminal paper identifying 10 tropical forest “hotspots.” These regions were characterized both by exceptional levels of plant endemism, meaning plants found nowhere else on Earth, and serious levels of habitat loss. Conservation International (CI) adopted Myers’s hotspots as its institutional blueprint in 1989. In 1999, CI undertook a global review, which introduced quantitative thresholds for the designation of biodiversity hotspots and resulted in the identification of 25. 

  
  
In 2005, an additional analysis brought the total number of biodiversity hotspots to 34, based on the work of nearly 400 specialists. In 2011, the Forests of East Australia were identified as the 35th hotspot by a team of researchers from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization working with CI. In February 2016, the North American Coastal Plain was recognized as meeting the criteria and became the world’s 36th hotspot. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Gender Development Index
description:
The Gender Development Index (GDI), published by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), measures gender gaps in human development achievements by accounting for disparities between women and men in 3 basic dimensions of human development using the same component indicators as in the Human Development Index (HDI). The HDI is a summary measure of average achievement in key dimensions of human development: a long and healthy life, being knowledgeable, and a decent standard of living. The HDI is the geometric mean of normalized indices for each of the 3 dimensions. The health dimension is assessed by life expectancy at birth; the education dimension is measured by mean of years of schooling for adults aged 25 years and more and expected years of schooling for children of school-entering age. The standard-of-living dimension is measured by gross national income per capita. The HDI uses the logarithm of income to reflect the diminishing importance of income with increasing gross national income (GNI). The scores for the 3 HDI dimension indices are then aggregated into a composite index using geometric mean. The GDI is the ratio of the HDIs calculated separately for females and males using the same methodology as in the HDI. It is a direct measure of gender gap, showing the female HDI as a percentage of the male HDI. The GDI is calculated for 161 countries in 2015 and shows how much women are lagging behind their male counterparts in each dimension of human development. It facilitates understanding of the real gender gap in human development achievements and is useful in designing policy tools to close the gap. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: World Database on Protected Areas
description:
The World Database on Protected Areas (WDPA) is the most comprehensive global spatial data set on marine and terrestrial protected areas available. Protected area data are provided via Protected Planet, the online interface for the WDPA. The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data are provided as shapefiles and updated monthly.   
  
Not all protected areas receive the same degree of protection. While some have strict guidelines designed to preserve intact ecosystems, others allow for sustainable land use, often including limited resource extraction. In addition, not all countries use the same terminology when designating a protected area. Universal management categories are designated by the IUCN that stipulate the level of protection for most protected areas. These categories are defined as follows:   
  
(Ia) Strict Nature Reserves: protected areas designed to preserve biodiversity and all geological features. Limited human use (e.g., scientific study, education) is allowed and carefully monitored. Strict nature reserves are often used to understand the impact of indirect human disturbance (e.g., burning fossil fuels) because of the area’s high level of preservation.   
  
(Ib) Wilderness Areas: protected areas managed to preserve ecosystem processes with limited human use. Wilderness areas cannot contain modern infrastructure (e.g., a visitor’s center), but they allow for local indigenous groups to maintain subsistence lifestyles. These areas are often established to restore disturbed environments.   
  
(II) National Parks: protected areas designed to preserve large-scale ecosystems and support human visitation. With conservation as a priority, these areas allow infrastructure and contribute to the local economy by providing opportunities for environmental educational and recreation.   
  
(III) National Monuments or Features: areas established to protect a specific natural feature (e.g., cave, grove) or human-made monument with significant historical, spiritual, or environmental importance and the immediate surroundings. Accordingly, natural monuments or features are typically smaller in area and have high human impact resulting from visitor traffic.   
  
(IV) Habitat and Species Management Areas: areas designed to conserve specific wildlife populations and/or habitats. Habitat and species management areas often exist within a larger ecosystem or protected area and are carefully managed (e.g., through hunting abatement or habitat restoration) to conserve a target species or habitat.   
  
(V) Protected Landscapes and Seascapes: protected areas with ecological, biological, or cultural importance that have been shaped by human use of the landscape. Protected landscapes and seascapes typically cover entire bodies of land or ocean and allow for a number of for-profit activities (e.g., ecotourism) in accordance with the region’s management plan.   
  
(VI) Protected Areas with Sustainable Use of Natural Resources: areas designed to manage natural resources and uphold the livelihoods of surrounding communities. These regions have a low level of human occupation, small-scale developments (i.e., not industrial), and part of the landscape in its natural condition.

title: Aqueduct Seasonal Variability
description:
### Overview  
  
Seasonal variability measures the average within-year variability of available water supply, including both renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Higher values indicate wider variations of available supply within a year. These values were then converted into risk scores based on the thresholds defined in the methodology. These risk scores range from low variability (coefficient of variation <0.33) to extremely high variability (coefficient of variation >1.33). Seasonal variability values are available per sub-basin (HydroBASIN level 6).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Aqueduct used the global hydrological model, PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB
2), to calculate five indicators. Seasonal variability is one of those indicators and was calculated using the available water supply time series from the default PCR-GLOBWB 2. 

  
  
Seasonal or within-year variability is defined as the coefficient of variation (CV) of available water between months in a year for each sub-basin. The CV was calculated by dividing the standard deviation (SD) of the available water supply within a year by the year’s mean available water supply.

  
  
Finally, raw baseline seasonal variability were converted to risk scores between 0 and 5, based on quantiles. These scores were placed into categories indicating how high the risk for this indicator is. The thresholds for raw seasonal variability values and the corresponding risk scores that were used in each category are defined below as Risk Category (Risk Scores): Raw Value Thresholds.

- Low (0-1): < 0.33
- Low to medium (1-2): 0.33 - 0.66
- Medium to high (2-3): 0.66 - 1.0
- High (3-4): 1.0 - 1.33
- Extremely high (4-5): > 1.33

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.wri.org/publication/aqueduct-30).

title: Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Fully and Highly Protected Marine Areas dataset as shown on Resource Watch presents marine protected areas (MPAs) that are fully or highly protected. The [Marine Protection Atlas (MPAtlas)](https://mpatlas.org/) uses the [World Database on Protected Areas](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas) as a starting point, then assesses the current protection status of listed MPAs based on additional sources and research. This global dataset was first created in 2020 and in the future will be regularly updated, as new MPAs are created, protections change, and currently designated areas are implemented.

  
  
MPAs are essential for safeguarding biodiversity and the health of marine ecosystems. They provide sanctuary for species to mature and reproduce, and they help restore healthy populations within and beyond their borders. MPAs also build resilience against threats such as climate change and pollution by maintaining vital natural processes, storing carbon, buffering coastlines, and ensuring sustainable food supplies for coastal communities. However, different MPAs may offer different levels of protection, from minor restrictions to the full exclusion of most commercial activity. Robust scientific evidence indicates that no-take zones (where no extractive activities are allowed) and highly protected areas yield the greatest conservation benefits.

  
  
The MPAtlas brings together the best available information on marine protection around the world, so that the marine conservation community can work together to protect at least [30% of the world's oceans by 2030](https://www.campaignfornature.org/science-page). This more detailed approach to MPA data provides a more nuanced look at progress toward conservation goals and the outcomes that can be expected from existing protections.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
MPAtlas takes the WDPA as its starting point and examines the listed MPAs in depth, adding to or replacing WDPA records with information from original research using more detailed or up-to-date sources, such as national or regional databases, official documentation, or management plans. These additions can include more accurate spatial data, such as the addition of boundaries for individual zones within an MPA. It can also include more detailed information about site regulations and management, both of which are directly related to conservation outcomes.

  
  
MPAtlas coverage numbers differ from those of other sources for two primary reasons:
1. MPAtlas attempts to identify and distinguish protected areas that are legally designated but are still awaiting implementation from those that are fully in effect on the water. The project also identifies committed or proposed protected areas that have not yet achieved legal or authoritative recognition.
2. MPA coverage data is reported by protection level, as no-take and fully and highly protected areas are those which afford the greatest conservation benefits. The project accomplishes this by conducting detailed assessments using widely-accepted, scientifically-based criteria for measuring an MPA’s protection level and associated conservation outcomes. Detailed information about the assessment process [can be found here](https://marine-conservation.org/mpatlas-assessments/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://mpatlas.org/methods).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [the full WDPA](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007-World-Database-on-Protected-Areas_replacement) and [the MPA subset](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/bio007b-Marine-Protected-Areas), on which the MPAtlas is based.

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the Marine Protected Atlas. The MPAtlas includes all MPAs in the WDPA, but because these are already mapped elsewhere, Resource Watch displays only those MPAtlas entries with confirmed partial or complete protections from fishing and extractive commercial activity.

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in extreme precipitation is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average days of extreme precipitation during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
  
  
### Additional Information

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) as a replacement.**_
  
This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, the U.S. Geological Survey, and  the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, measures areas of tree cover gain across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at 30 × 30 m resolution, displayed as a 12-year cumulative layer. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+) sensor. Over 600,000 Landsat 7 images were compiled and analyzed using Google Earth Engine, a cloud platform for Earth observation and data analysis. The clear land surface observations (30 × 30 m pixels) in the satellite images were assembled, and a supervised learning algorithm was then applied to identify per pixel tree cover gain. Tree cover gain was defined as the establishment of tree canopy at the Landsat pixel scale in an area that previously had no tree cover. Tree cover gain may indicate a number of potential activities, including natural forest growth or the crop rotation cycle of tree plantations. The tree cover canopy density of the displayed data is >50%. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Tree Cover Gain
description:
### Overview  
  
The Tree Cover Gain dataset measures areas of tree cover gain from 2001 through 2012. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Gain is mapped for all areas that did not have tree cover in 2000 and had ≥ 50% cover in 2012. Longer-lived regrowing stands of tree cover that did not begin as non-forest within the study period were not mapped as forest gain. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.
  
  
Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the gain in tree cover of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity.


  
  
The dataset has been created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. 

  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. 

  
  
The following steps were taken to pre-process the images:
  
  
1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed.
  
  
2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water.
  
  
3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another.

  
  
Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover gain. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Tree Cover](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/027799db-c161-462a-9c20-aeb97b84e06e) and the [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) from the same dataset. 
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and the reference multispectral imagery from 2019 is available from the data provider.

title: Tsunamis
description:
The Global Historical Tsunami Database released by NOAA provides information on over 2,400 tsunamis from 2100 BC to the present in the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans; and the Mediterranean and Caribbean Seas. The database includes 2 related files. The first file includes information on the tsunami source such as the date, time, and location of the source event; cause and validity of the source; tsunami magnitude and intensity; maximum water height; total number of fatalities, injuries, houses destroyed, and houses damaged; and total damage estimate (in U.S. dollars). The second related file contains information on the runups (the locations where tsunami waves were observed by eyewitnesses, reconnaissance surveys, tide gauges, and deep-ocean sensors), such as name, location, arrival time, maximum water height, and inundation distance, as well as socioeconomic data (deaths, injuries, damage) for the specific runup location. title: Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density of Carbon Monoxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Carbon Monoxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA).

  
  
According to the [U.S. Center for Disease Control (CDC)](https://www.cdc.gov/co/faqs.htm), CO is released when fossil fuels are burned. Common household sources include grills, cars, fireplaces, and gas stoves that aren’t properly ventilated. Major sources of CO to outdoor air include cars, trucks and other fossil-fuel-burning machinery. Breathing air with a high concentration of carbon monoxide reduces oxygen availability in the bloodstream for critical organs like the heart and brain. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain, and confusion. As stated by [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)](http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), the CO values in Mexico City have been decreasing over the last years, complying with the levels set by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the World Health Organization (WHO). The main source of CO in the MCMA is fossil-fuel-burning related to transport, making this pollutant a good indicator to monitor transport-related emissions in the region. Showcasing the spatial distribution of CO in the MCMA will  provide insight about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models.The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles.

  
  
The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset is comprised of the following models:
  
  
Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates  temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators..
  
  
Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate CO levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution.
  
  
Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)](https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) forecast ](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), [Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone  (O₃)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538), [Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide  (NO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/918ba6bc-69ed-44fb-9b29-5fb445fdfef6), and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e)

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes the outputs for their weather model as well as the measurements of the Mexico City Weather Monitoring System (SIMAT) using their air quality index. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Accessibility to Cities
description:
### Overview  
  
Accessibility to cities quantifies the time it takes to travel to the nearest urban center via surface transport as of 2015. The dataset uses data on roads, railways, rivers, water bodies, and foot travel on different land cover types. It also includes information on topographical conditions (slope angle and elevation) and additional time for crossing national borders. The dataset was sourced from a variety of resources that each specialize in a specific mode of land transportation.

  
  
The data was created with the goal of understanding how travel time varies for different urban centers. Urban centers typically have higher concentrations of important resources and infrastructure than rural regions. Improving accessibility to these resources is integral to improving equality around the world. 

  
  
The dataset was created by the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) with travel time in minutes at a 30 arc second spatial resolution (approximately 1 km at the equator).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers first created a model that calculated the travel time for each pixel (1 km²) on earth. It was based on travel time information on roads, railways, and bodies of water. Additionally, information on land cover types, topographic conditions (slope and elevation), and national borders were included, as they usually affect travel time.  An algorithm was then applied to the model to determine the fastest travel times between destinationsThe road and railway datasets were created by merging Open Street Map (OSM) data with a distance-to-roads product derived from the Google roads database from November 2016 and March 2016. Data on river travel was taken from CIA World Data Bank II vector rivers dataset, lake travel from global surface-water occurrence dataset, and ocean travel from the automatic Identification System (AIS) and Voluntary Observing Ship (VOS) program. Undeveloped land was given a baseline speed of movement (by foot) using the MODIS MCD12Q1 land cover product. The final data was adjusted to account for topographical properties using Global Multi-resolution Terrain Elevation Dataset 2010 (GMTED2010) and a one hour travel penalty was added for any border crossing.

  
  
An urban center is defined as a contiguous area with 1,500 or more inhabitants per km² or a majority of built-up land cover coincident with a population center of at least 50,000 inhabitants. Cities were identified using the above assumption based on the Global Human Settlement Grid of High-Density Land Cover (GHS-HDC) data set and country borders were taken from the UN Global Administrative Units Layer (GAUL). Because cities are typically clusters of many cells rather than individual points, they are effectively treated as polygons when calculating travel time from a given point. The accessibility surface map was generated using the cumulative cost function within Google Earth Engine. The map was validated by testing its travel time calculations between 53,091 points compared to travel time estimates calculated by Google Maps. 

  
  
The final accessibility map was presented in raster format with a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds (around 1 km at the equator). For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature25181).

Volcano Eruptions
description:
### Overview  
  
The Volcano Eruptions dataset shows the location of currently active and historically active volcanoes since the Holocene Epoch. The Holocene Epoch is a geological time period that began over 10,000 years ago. 
  
  
This dataset was created as a way of better understanding Earth's active volcanoes and their eruptions. Volcanoes were a key component in forming the landscapes we see today and in the present time they can have serious impacts for people living in close proximity to them. Understanding active volcanoes, their trends, and how to predict them serves as a way of protecting people and understanding how the Earth was formed.
  
  
The data is taken from the Volcanoes of the World database, which is part of the Global Volcanism Program (GVP) run by the Smithsonian Institution. The mission of GVP is to document, understand, and disseminate information about global volcanic activity.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Volcanoes of the World database was created and is continually updated by GVP with information from organizations around the world. During the early stages of an eruption anywhere in the world GVP acts as a clearinghouse of reports, data, and imagery. After GVP staff verifies the information, it is added to the Volcanoes of the World database. The database is made available to the public and updated approximately every 1-3 months.
  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: [Archived] Environmental Performance Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](faaf0a0f-7475-49f3-bb8b-68edfaad4b77) as a replacement.**_
  
The Environmental Performance Index (EPI), produced by the Yale Center for Environmental Law and Policy (YCELP), Data-Driven Yale, and the Columbia University Earth Institute Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CEISIN), scores countries from 0 to 100 according to each country's relative performance on a set of environmental indicators. A score of 100 means that the country ranks above a high-quality benchmark for all its indicators. A score of 0 means that the country ranks below some low-quality benchmark for all its indicators. The index is built from 19 national-level indicators relevant to environmental issues, grouped into 9 issues, which are themselves divided into 2 overarching themes: (1) ecosystem vitality and (2) environmental health as it applies to human health. Multiple other data sets were employed to provide context before whittling down to those 19. Each country's score for each indicator is scaled between 0 and 100 to reflect the proximity of its score in that indicator to a high-quality benchmark. The high-quality benchmark can either be a statistical measure—such as the 95th percentile of the distribution of all countries' scores—or a scientifically determined target, such as the World Health Organization's designation of safe and dangerous amounts of particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5) in the air we breathe. The 19 indicators, each scored been 0 and 100, are then combined with each other to produce the overall EPI score for a country. The indicators are weighted differently depending on the relative reliability of the data that underpin them. A "materiality threshold" is used to determine whether an indicator should count toward a given country's score. Landlocked countries, for example, are not rated according to their marine protected areas or the health of their fisheries. When these indicators are removed, the remaining indicators receive proportionally higher weights in calculating the country total EPI. The EPI uses both primary and secondary data. Primary data come from human-administered surveys or technological monitoring schemes, including data derived from satellites. Secondary data include country-collected statistics, but only when those statistics are submitted to an independent international organization that enforces data reporting and quality requirements. Modeled data are also included. The 2016 global data set is retrieved from the Global Metrics for the Environment—2016 Environmental Performance Index Report. title: Oil Palm Concessions
description:
### Overview  
  
The Oil Palm Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and the Solomon Islands. Concession name, company and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Oil Palm Concessions dataset. Oil Palm Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset is updated monthly. 

  
  
Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil produced from the fruits of the oil palm tree. According to the [World Wildlife Fund (WWF)](https://www.worldwildlife.org/industries/palm-oil), oil palm is a highly productive crop and grows only in tropical regions. Palm oil does not require refrigeration and is used in food products, cosmetics and detergents. However, oil palm farming contributes to deforestation and the release of harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. [According to a study from the European Commission](http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/14868/), oil palm farming is responsible for 8% of global agriculture-related deforestation. Deforestation from oil palm farming is most prevalent in Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia. Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of oil palm plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. 

  
  
The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near real-time. This information is critical to ending illegal deforestation and fires, and promoting sustainable practices. It can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. Additionally, farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The term “oil palm concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. GFW generated the Oil Palm Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and Solomon Islands. Most locations in the dataset include the company, concession name and concession area (ha). 

  
  
Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies and public documents. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. Data from the public domain (company websites, news reports, NGOs) was used for countries where data was not readily available from government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information such as company and concession name was added to the polygons as attributes. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=oilpalm). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Air Quality: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Satellite Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: CO Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of carbon monoxide (CO) densities in the total atmospheric column. Each value shown in the dataset represents the density of CO found between Earth’s surface and the top of the atmosphere. The CO density is reported with units of moles of CO per square meter of air (mol/m²).

  
  
Carbon monoxide (CO) is a colorless, odorless gas that can be harmful when inhaled in large amounts. CO is released during combustion, so the largest outdoor sources of CO are cars, trucks and other vehicles, and machinery that burn fossil fuels. Breathing air with a high concentration of CO reduces the amount of oxygen that can be transported in the bloodstream to critical organs like the heart and brain. At very high levels, which are possible indoors or in other enclosed environments, CO can cause dizziness, confusion, unconsciousness, and death. Very high levels of CO are not likely to occur outdoors. However, when CO levels are elevated outdoors it can be of particular concern to people with preexisting heart disease. These people already have a reduced ability for getting oxygenated blood to their heart. They are especially vulnerable to the effects of CO when exercising or under increased stress. In these situations, short-term exposure to elevated CO may result in reduced oxygen to the heart accompanied by chest pain also known as angina.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as CO, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).   
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI CO dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. CO data was collected by determining the amount of sunlight reflected by the troposphere in the 2.3 µm spectral range of the solar spectrum. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that CO molecules produce in the atmosphere. The CO data collected using this method was then input into the Shortwave Infrared CO Re- trieval (SICOR) algorithm created by the Netherlands Institute for Space Research. Along with CO data, the following information was input into SICOR:

  
  
- Relative profile of CO and water in the atmosphere for a given region
  
  
- Solar/viewing geometry and geo-location of the S5P satellite
  
  
- Temperature, water vapor/pressure profiles, and geo-potential height of the S5P satellite
  
  
- Estimate of methane (CH₄) abundance as calculated by the TM5-MP global chemistry transport model

  
  
CH₄ estimates were required as CH₄ is used to help filter out the presence of clouds in the model. The algorithm further takes into consideration cloud cover by changing the column sensitivity (altering the minimal amount of light reflection within the column required to determine CO density) according to the light path created by cloud cover. The final results produced by the algorithm were tropospheric vertical column density of CO and the average CO density for the entire vertical column.

  
  
The dataset shown on Resource Watch was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “Carbon Monoxide (CO) Total Column”.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [absorbing aerosol index (AAI)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-AER-AI).

Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Station Forecasts
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Station Forecasts dataset provides air quality forecasts for a group of cities taking part in the [CityAQ project](https://airquality.gsfc.nasa.gov/cityaq-pilot-combine-local-monitoring-data-geos-cf-model-outputs-develop-city-scale-operational). Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations are forecasted at the station level, and are shown in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). The dataset is updated daily and shows the forecasted concentration of NO₂ for the following five days. The forecast is generated by the source at an hourly time step, and Resource Watch aggregates to the maximum 1-hour concentation.
  
  
NO₂ emissions contribute to the formation of smog and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. The CityAQ project aims to help cities around the world to know more about the levels, sources, and impacts of air pollution. Many of the places with the highest level of pollution have the least information to work with to know their air quality and manage it accordingly. Free and publicly-available air quality data from satellites, along with low-cost sensor systems and output from air quality models, have the potential to augment high-quality, regulatory-grade data in countries with in situ monitoring networks and provide much needed air quality information in countries without them. By combining the strengths of these multiple monitoring technologies, an integrated air pollution network has the potential to provide free/low cost and publicly-accessible air quality information to health and air quality managers in cities around the world.

  
  
These forecasts were modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) by combining local air quality monitoring information, made available with support from the World Resources Institute (WRI), with the outputs of NASA’s global Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). The CityAQ project objective is to provide participating cities with useful forecasts that they can use to anticipate air quality events, communicate with stakeholders, and manage local interventions more effectively. It looks to test and refine a methodology for combining locally held information with globally consistent analysis to offer new local tools and, in the future, potentially improve global analysis by aggregating fragmented local data into programmatically useful datasets and make the GEOS-CF forecasts usable by all world cities. The organizations involved in the CityAQ project aim to refine a scalable approach for engaging with users to co-create air quality tools that leverage and extend existing scientific analysis.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Validated or raw station level measurement data is collected from either government sites or [OpenAQ](https://openaq.org/#/).
Validated air quality observations of government sites were obtained from the air quality data portals of [Bogotá](http://rmcab.ambientebogota.gov.co/home/map) and [Sao Paulo](https://servicos.cetesb.sp.gov.br/qa/), or in the case of the Mexican cities of Monterrey, Guadalajara, Salamanca and León were shared directly by state governments. Near-real time, raw observations for the cities of Addis, Jakarta, as well as the following cities in the mexican state of Guanajuato: Guanajuato city, Irapuato, San Miguel de Allende, Silao, Celaya, San Luis de la Paz and Abasolo were retrieved from OpenAQ. For station-level data to be included in OpenAQ’s catalogue, it must meet the minimum data requirements as described by [OpenAQ](https://github.com/openaq/openaq-fetch/blob/master/README.md).  
 
   
  
Meteorological and atmospheric chemistry information at each of the CityAQ stations is obtained from NASA’s GEOS-CF model. GEOS-CF provides global hourly analyses and forecasts of atmospheric composition at 25-kilometer spatial resolution. To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. Any correlation between cloud cover and surface PM2.5 should be captured similarly by GCC and GOCART. The PM2.5 dataset shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GCC module. A detailed description of GEOS-CF can be found in [Keller et al. (2021)](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1029/2020MS002413). 
 
  
  
Since the model output is too coarse to resolve fine-scale air quality features characteristic of urban environments, a bias-correction algorithm is applied to account for the spatial representation error, as well as other potential model biases such as errors in the model representation of transport or chemistry.  The bias-correction methodology uses the [XGBoost machine learning algorithm](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/en/latest/#) to develop a machine learning model that predicts the model bias at each of the observation stations as a function of the current meteorological and chemical environment and time. Once trained, the machine learning model is used on a daily basis to calculate the expected model bias at a given site and this value is added to the ‘raw’ (i.e., uncorrected) GEOS-CF predictions.
 
  
  
The machine learning training is based on the 2018–2019 observation–model differences and designed to predict the systematic model bias between hourly PM2.5 observations and the model predictions at that location. These biases can be due to errors in the model, such as emission estimates, sub-grid-scale local influences or meteorology and chemistry. Since model biases are often site-specific, a separate machine learning model is used for each site. The input features to the machine learning algorithm encompass 9 meteorological parameters (as simulated by the GEOS-CF model: surface northward and eastward wind components, surface temperature and skin temperature, surface relative humidity, total cloud coverage, total precipitation, surface pressure, and planetary boundary layer height) and the modeled surface concentrations of 51 chemical species (O3, NOx, carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and aerosols). In addition, it provides as input features the hour-of-day, day of week, and month of the year; these allow the machine learning model to identify systematic observation-model mismatches related to the diurnal, weekly and seasonal cycle of the pollutants. This bias correction methodology is based on [Keller et al. (2021)](https://acp.copernicus.org/articles/21/3555/2021/).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CityAQ datasets for [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/403726e5-6852-49f4-9dce-b82b599b09fc) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/f5599d62-7f3d-41c7-b3fd-9f8e08ee7b2a) 

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Forecasted data at an hourly time step is available from the source. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_004_city_aq).
