title: Fishing Activity
description:
### Overview  
  
The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS).

  
  
Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. 

  
  
Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. 

  
  
GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646).

  
  
After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. 

  
  
 To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by all vessels other than trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW data for [Trawling Activity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6ccfb266-20cd-4838-82b0-5309987a62f0). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. 

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global
scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030a_rw1_fishing_activity)  
  
### Disclaimer  
  
Excerpts of this description page were taken from the source metadata. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Mexico City Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Forecast dataset provides weather and air quality forecasts for Mexico City. This dataset represents the forecasted density for Nitrogen Dioxide in parts per billion (ppb). The forecast offers an hourly estimate on Nitrogen Dioxide density with a spatial resolution of 1 kilometer (km), encompassing Mexico CIty and its Metropolitan Area (MCMA).

  
  
A number of hazards related to pollutants is known, which depends on the physical characteristics of the individual exposed to pollution, the time of exposure and the type of pollutant. Effects can range from respiratory discomfort to the worsening of pre-existing conditions like asthma, particularly in children and the elderly. 
NO₂ is a highly reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] (https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂. In the MCMA the main source of NO₂ comes from vehicles that burn fossil fuels. In addition,the pollutant has a strong seasonal behavior with higher concentrations during the cold-dry months of the year. According to the [Mexico City Ministry of the Environment (SEDEMA)](http://www.aire.cdmx.gob.mx/descargas/publicaciones/flippingbook/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017/mobile/informe_anual_calidad_aire_2017v3.pdf), NO₂ concentrations in the MCMA have remained below the limit levels indicated in Mexican regulations, as well as those recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) and EPA, though higher concentrations have occasionally been recorded in the areas of the city with greater mobility. Showcasing the spatial distribution of NO₂ in the MCMA will help provide insights about the way a city can produce information according to its needs while complementing global air quality models. The forecast helps the Mexico CIty government to issue health warnings based on the expected air quality for a given day, like recommending citizens to avoid open-air exercise or to limit their use of fossil fuel vehicles.

  
  
The forecast was generated by SEDEMA with help from the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). SEDEMA provides a tool for the inhabitants of MCMA to make well-informed decisions about dangerous air pollution activity on a given day. SEDEMA works on five environmental issues: air quality and climate change, land conservation and biodiversity, sustainable urban infrastructure, water supply and quality, and environmental communication and education.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The dataset is comprised of the following models:
  
  
Weather: Estimates the weather conditions of the MCMA using data from global systems. It harnesses the [Weather Research and Forecasting Model-Advanced Research (WRF-ARW)](https://www.mmm.ucar.edu/weather-research-and-forecasting-model), which is a mesoscale numerical weather prediction system designed for both atmospheric research and operational forecasting applications. The model generates  temperature, wind, rainfall and solar radiation, among other weather related indicators.among others.
  
  
Emissions: This model makes use of emission inventories for the MCMA to estimate NO₂ levels on an hourly basis, as well as its geospatial distribution.
  
  
Chemical Transport: This model harnesses the outputs from the weather and emissions models as well as other chemical and physical mechanisms to simulate transformations in the atmosphere and the influence of weather dynamics in these processes. For this purpose, the [Community Multiscale Air Quality Modeling System (CMAQ)] (https://www.cmascenter.org/cmaq/) is employed to forecast the behavior of the pollutants in the MCMA.

   
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows forecasts for [Air Quality: Mexico City Carbon Monoxide (CO) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e39f5910-a9b8-4ef1-b4b4-f6b141b15541), [Air Quality: Mexico City Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/59790e64-d95d-43fa-a124-5c7eb1cb4456), [Air Quality: Mexico City Ozone (O₃) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/00d6bae1-e105-4165-8230-ee73a8128538) and [Air Quality: Mexico City Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Forecast](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7a34b770-83f9-4c6a-acb8-31edcff7241e)

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The source also includes the outputs for their weather model as well as the measurements of the Mexico City Weather Monitoring System (SIMAT) using their air quality index. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/loc_mcaqf_mexico_city_aq_forecast).

title: Coral Reef Connectivity
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset estimates the level of connectivity between each area containing coral reefs and other such areas. Connectivity refers to the extent to which populations are linked by the exchange of eggs, larval recruits, juveniles, or adults—an exchange which is primarily conducted via ocean currents. A coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by Wood et al. was applied by the 50 Reefs Project to simulate coral exchange between 2003 and 2011, ultimately yielding connectivity estimates globally at 0.05° resolution. These estimates were based on potential dispersal only; settlement and post-settlement survival were not modelled.

  
  
Connectivity within and between protected areas is important for maintaining diversity, fish stocks, and especially important for maintaining ecological resilience. While poorly understood, it is a key factor to consider in marine reserve design as it may enhance resilience to disturbance and be important for the persistence of populations. Both of these are important processes in the context of conservation planning under climate change, the dominant threat to coral reefs in the coming decades. Even if the goals of the Paris Climate Agreement are achieved, 70-90% of coral reef areas are likely to cease to be suitable for coral growth by mid-century. Coral communities that survive will play a key role in the regeneration of reefs by mid-to-late century. 

  
  
The purpose of the 50 Reefs Project was to develop a long-term strategic plan for the conservation of coral reefs by identifying 50 large (500 km²) regions that are the least vulnerable to climate change and which are positioned to facilitate natural coral reef regeneration. These locations constitute important opportunities for novel conservation investments to secure less vulnerable yet well-connected coral reefs that may help to repopulate degraded areas after the climate has stabilized. The strategy and actions proposed by the project should strengthen and expand existing conservation efforts for coral reefs as the world faces the long-term consequences of intensifying climate change.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The authors used a coral larvae dispersal probability model developed by [Wood et al.](https://doi.org/10.1111/geb.12101), basing their findings on simulations of larvae dispersal over a 93 month period. Within this modeling, 115 million particles (representing larvae from a generic broadcast spawning coral) were released from each of 12,397 habitat cells on a monthly basis between 2003-2011. Again following Wood et al., the authors used two measures of connectivity: (i) outgoing settlement, which is the proportion of particles that reached any habitat cell, including the source cell, and (ii) export, which is the proportion of particles reaching any cell other than the source cell, hence omitting self-seeding. These were combined into an overall "connectivity" score.

  
  
The dataset contains entries for each of the approximately 54,586 0.05° degree (approximately 25 km² but [changes with distance from the equator](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616)) raster cells identified as containing coral habitat by a dataset from [Coral Reef Watch](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/). The values were standardized to mean 0 unit variance for subsequent analysis by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. The resulting scores reflect how far the values were below or above the population mean. The data table also contains: (1) an ID field that assigns a unique numeric identification number to each cell; (2) two fields representing the latitude and longitude of the center of the cell; (3) scores corresponding to other essential components of the 50 Reefs assessment; and (4) one final variable representing the aggregate score of the 50 Reefs analysis.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://conbio.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/conl.12587).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. The 50 Reefs initiative generated scores for several other factors crucial to their assessment: thermal history and recent thermal conditions, predicted future thermal conditions, and cyclone and storm risk. In total, the component scores were derived from 174 separate variables relevant to these topics; these components were also combined into one final assessment score using a custom weighting.

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/ocn_017_coral_reef_connectivity).  
  
### Disclaimer

title: Global Temperature
description:
NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) team assembles its temperature analysis from publicly available data acquired by roughly 6,300 meteorological stations around the world; by ship- and buoy-based instruments measuring sea surface temperature; and by Antarctic research stations. These raw data are analyzed using methods that account for the varied spacing of temperature stations around the globe and for urban heating effects that could skew the calculations. There are sufficient observations from 1880 (particularly in the Southern Hemisphere) to produce a reasonably precise global temperature record. Prior to that, uncertainties (due to gaps in spatial coverage) increase substantially. This graph illustrates the change in global surface temperature relative to 1951-1980 average temperatures. Sixteen of the 17 warmest years in the 136-year record all have occurred since 2001, with the exception of 1998. The year 2016 ranks as the warmest on record. This research is broadly consistent with similar constructions prepared by the Climatic Research Unit and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. title: Agricultural Exposure to Water Stress
description:
This map of baseline water stress in major crop producing areas was created by WRI's Aqueduct program as part of the Water Risk Atlas, an online mapping tool that displays various aspects of water-related risks. The map displays the major crop producing areas for 13 major commodity crops (cocoa, coffee, cotton, maize, oats, oil palm, oranges, canola, rice, rubber, soybeans, sugarcane, and wheat) and 9 crop groups (cereals, fiber crops, fodder crops, fruits, oil crops, legumes, roots and tubers, sugar crops, and tree nuts), and the levels of water stress (low, low to medium, medium to high, high, and extremely high) experienced in these major crop-producing areas. Baseline water stress refers to the annual water withdrawals (municipal, industrial, and agricultural) expressed as a percentage of the total annual available flow. Higher values indicate more competition among users. Arid areas with low water use are shown in gray but scored as high stress when calculating aggregated scores. Baseline water stress is calculated by dividing water withdrawals (2010) by mean available blue water (1950-2008). Areas with available blue water and water withdrawal less than 0.03 and 0.012/m2 respectively are coded as “arid and low water use." Crop production in each category is computed by overlaying gridded crop production data, which was pulled from 2 articles in Global Biogeochemical Cycle (2008), "Farming the Planet: 1. Geographic Distribution of Global Agricultural Lands in the Year 2000" and "Farming the Planet: 2. Geographic Distribution of Crop Areas, Yields, Physiological Types, and Net Primary Production in the Year 2000." The authors of these studies identified croplands and crop production using a high-resolution satellite-derived land cover data set and agricultural inventory data to derive a global map of croplands. title: Effect of Agricultural Policies on Commodity Prices
description:
The Nominal Rate of Protection (NRP), released by the AgIncentives partnership led by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), measures the extent to which a set of agricultural policies affects the market price of a commodity. It is computed as the price difference, expressed as a percentage, between the farm gate price received by producers and an undistorted reference price at the farm gate level, or the price a farmer receives versus the price a farmer would receive without these policies in place. The reference price is calculated for more than 50 countries using exchange rate, quality and quantity adjustments, transportation and processing costs, and so on. The purpose of this indicator is not to provide a holistic measurement of various agricultural policies, in contrast with the Producer Support Estimate or the Nominal Rate of Assistance. It focuses only on the price implications of policies and will be larger for countries using price interventions compared to countries using farm subsidies. title: Soil Moisture
description:
The NASA-USDA Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) Global Soil Moisture data set is produced by the NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Hydrologic Science Laboratory in collaboration with the USDA Foreign Agricultural Services and the USDA Hydrology and Remote Sensing Lab.  
  
This data set provides 3-day composites of global soil moisture estimates from April 1, 2015 to present. This data set includes both surface and subsurface soil moisture estimates (mm), as well as percent soil moisture (%).  
  
SMAP Level 3 soil moisture observations are collected with a satellite-based, L-band radar and radiometer instrument. This satellite covers the globe every three days, providing high-resolution data with an accuracy of 0.04 m³/m³. SMAP data are assimilated into the modified Palmer two-layer soil moisture model with a 1-D Ensemble Kalman filter approach. The assimilation of this SMAP data is done to correct model-based soil moisture predictions that can be prone to errors in regions with limited rain gauge data.

title: [Archived] Global Hunger Index
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2018, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality.  
  
The 2018 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. In the GHI by Severity layers, countries are classified as having low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger.   
  
### Methodology  
  
GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger.  
  
First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators:  
  
1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient);  
  
2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition);  
  
3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and  
  
4. Child Mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments).  
  

Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades.  
  
Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight.  
  
This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores.

title: [Archived] Effect of Agricultural Policies on Commodity Prices
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](641c0a35-f2e5-4198-8ed9-576ea7e9685a) as a replacement.**_
  
The Nominal Rate of Protection (NRP), released by the AgIncentives partnership led by the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), measures the extent to which a set of agricultural policies affects the market price of a commodity. It is computed as the price difference, expressed as a percentage, between the farm gate price received by producers and an undistorted reference price at the farm gate level, or the price a farmer receives versus the price a farmer would receive without these policies in place. The reference price is calculated for more than 50 countries using exchange rate, quality and quantity adjustments, transportation and processing costs, and so on. The purpose of this indicator is not to provide a holistic measurement of various agricultural policies, in contrast with the Producer Support Estimate or the Nominal Rate of Assistance. It focuses only on the price implications of policies and will be larger for countries using price interventions compared to countries using farm subsidies. description:

The SIGI covers 5 dimensions of discriminatory social institutions, spanning major socioeconomic areas that affect women’s lives: discriminatory family code, restricted physical integrity, son bias, restricted resources and assets, and restricted civil liberties. The SIGI’s variables quantify discriminatory social institutions such as unequal inheritance rights, early marriage, violence against women, and unequal land and property rights. It provides a strong evidence base to more effectively address the discriminatory social institutions that hold back progress on gender equality and women’s empowerment. title: Global Land Cover
description:
### Overview  
  
The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) delivers a global Land Cover product at 100-meter spatial resolution (CGLS-LC100) on an annual basis from 2015-2019. Each pixel value corresponds to a different type (class) of physical coverage of the Earth's surface, e.g. forests, grasslands, croplands, lakes, wetlands. The classifications follow the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (UN-FAO) Land Cover Classification System (LCCS) scheme. Resource watch displays 11 discrete LCCS classifications, with all forests grouped into open or closed classes.

  
  
Land cover plays a major role in the climate and biogeochemistry of the Earth system. Understanding patterns in land use and transitions of land cover classes over time is crucial to understand, monitor, and manage a number of processes at global level. Therefore, accurate and spatially detailed maps on land cover and land use are relevant to a broad range of issues including deforestation, desertification, urbanization, land degradation, loss of biodiversity and ecosystem functions, water resource management, agriculture and food security, urban and regional development, and climate change and are critical to make informed policy development, planning, and resource management decisions. 

  
  
The Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) is a component of the Land Monitoring Core Service (LMCS) of Copernicus, the European flagship programme on Earth Observation. The Global Land Service systematically produces a series of qualified bio-geophysical products on the status and evolution of the land surface, at global scale and at mid to low spatial resolution, complemented by the constitution of long term time series. The products are used to monitor the vegetation, the water cycle, the energy budget and the terrestrial cryosphere.  
  
### Methodology  
  
For the global land cover 100-meter resolution data, the main inputs are PROBA-V satellite observations, organized into millions of Sentinel-2 equivalent tiles of 110x110-kilometers.

  
  
These satellite observations are put through an algorithm, that includes:
  
  
- pre-processing, sensor specific data cleaning, and outlier screening 
  
  
- data fusion between the 5-day 100-meter resolution and daily 300-meter resolution data;
  
  
- extraction of 183 metrics, including the base reflectances, vegetation indicators, time series harmonics and descriptive statistics;
  
  
- the use of 168K training points, collected at 10-meter resolution, from GeoWIKI’s crowd-sourcing, for year 2015
  
  
- the use of well-established, external datasets for the shoreline masking, ecological regionalisation, built-up (urban) cover, permanent and seasonal water cover, arctic vegetation, weather and topography; supervised classification and regression.

  
  
The classified metrics are calculated over a three year period (epoch), in three processing modes:
  
  
- base maps for epoch 2015, that serves as reference for the classifier and regression models,
  
  
- consolidated maps (epochs 2016, 2017 and 2018) with full years of prior and pastor data and 
  
  
- the near-real time (nrt, 2019) maps with one year prior and only three months pastor data.

  
  
The final maps are validated using an independent set of 21,700 validation points, also sourced from Geo-WIKI.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [user manual](https://land.copernicus.eu/global/sites/cgls.vito.be/files/products/CGLOPS1_PUM_LC100m-V3_I3.4.pdf).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows 11 of the 23 discrete LCCS classifications from the CGLS Land Cover Product. The 12 original forest classes are shown as two classes, open and closed. The ocean and unknown classes are not displayed. 

  
  
Historical data on global land cover from 1992 to 2019 can be found on Resource Watch [here](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/soc068brw2-Global-Land-Cover-IPCC-Classification).

  
  
The products are provided as single-layer, internally compressed GeoTIFF files, per 20x20 degree on the [Land Cover viewer](https://lcviewer.vito.be/), as global files on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/copernicus-land-cover?page=1&size=20), and analyzed on [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_Landcover_100m_Proba-V-C3_Global).

  
  
The annual LC product also includes data for cover fractions (%) for the 10 base classes, an indicator to distinguish forest types, an indicator for the input Data Density, and a change confidence layer (after 2015) are available in the data from the provider. The Land Cover viewer also shows annual maps of change occurrence and of change processes.

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.


  
  
The products are provided as single-layer, internally compressed GeoTIFF files, per 20x20 degree on the [Land Cover viewer](https://lcviewer.vito.be/), as global files on [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/communities/copernicus-land-cover?page=1&size=20), and analyzed on [Google Earth Engine](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/COPERNICUS_Landcover_100m_Proba-V-C3_Global).

[Archived] Maritime Boundaries
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6af67024-b917-4944-851a-152b566ff1a8) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2018 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries.

  
  
The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference).  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php).

title: Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Aerosol Index Satellite Measurements dataset provides global monthly averages of an index that measures the presence of aerosols that absorb ultraviolet (UV) radiation in the atmosphere, such as dust and smoke. This index may be referred to as the absorbing aerosol index (AAI) or the UV Aerosol Index (UVAI).

  
  
Absorbing Aerosols are solid and liquid particles suspended in the atmosphere. They are made up of primary aerosols and secondary aerosols. Primary aerosols are emitted directly, whereas secondary aerosols are formed by gases reacting in the atmosphere. Absorbing aerosols are mostly made of dust and smoke. The main sources of aerosols are combustion, like burning biomass, and natural sources, like volcanoes. The AAI can show dust and smoke particles coming from events like dust storms, volcanic eruptions, fires, and biomass burning around the world.

  
  
The dataset is made up of data collected from the Sentinel-5 Precursor (S5p) mission, a low Earth orbit polar satellite system.The S5p mission is part of the Global Monitoring of the Environment and Security (GMES/COPERNICUS) space component program headed by the European Commission (EC) in partnership with the European Space Agency (ESA). Its goal is to  provide information and services on air quality, climate, and the ozone layer. The S5p mission includes the TROPOspheric Monitoring Instrument (TROPOMI), which takes daily global observations of key atmospheric components, such as absorbing aerosols, at a 5.5 x 3.5 kilometer (km) resolution.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The TROPOMI AAI dataset was created with data collected by the S5P satellite mission. UV-absorbing aerosol data was collected by determining the amount of Rayleigh scattering that occured in the UV spectral range for a pair of wavelengths. A spectral range is the range of light wavelengths that a specific spectrometer can measure, and in this case it refers to the wavelength of light that UV-absorbing aerosol molecules emit in the atmosphere. Rayleigh scattering is the scattering of light particles without causing a change in their wavelength. The UV-absorbing aerosol data collected was then compared with a calculated theoretical Rayleigh scattering value based on no UV-absorbing aerosols being present in the troposphere. The difference in scattering between the two data points represents the amount of UV-absorbing aerosols present and is the absorbing aerosol index. A positive AAI value indicates that UV-absorbing aerosols are present. 

  
  
The dataset was mapped by the Google Earth Engine team using the [harpconvert] (https://cdn.rawgit.com/stcorp/harp/master/doc/html/harpconvert.html) tool. For more information on this conversion please see the Google Earth Engine documentation. The offline version of this data is displayed on Resource Watch, which is more complete than its near real-time counterpart, but is released on a greater delay due to the additional processing time needed. For the full documentation, please see the [source methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-5p/products-algorithms) associated with the “UV-Aerosol Index”.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows TROPOMI data for [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-NO),  [ozone (O₃)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-O), and [carbon monoxide (CO)] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/Air-Quality-Measurements-TROPOMI-CO).
  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset.Additional data for formaldehyde (CH₂O), sulphur dioxide (SO₂), methane (CH₄) and clouds are available from the data provider. Both a near real-time and an offline version of each of these compounds are available. Please see the [Google Earth Engine data catalog](https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/tags/tropomi) to access this data. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data

title: Marine Protected Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Marine Protected Area (MPA) dataset contains officially designated parks, reserves, and other formal conservation areas around the world that have a substantial maritime component. Protected area data are provided via [Protected Planet](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/thematic-areas/marine-protected-areas), the online interface for the World Database for Protected Areas (WDPA). The WDPA is a joint initiative of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) and the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) to compile spatially referenced information about protected areas. The data is provided as shapefiles and updates monthly. Each record is either represented as a polygon boundary, or if unavailable, a point location, along with descriptive information, such as the name, legal designation, and mode of administration. As of May 2019, the WDPA included data on 242,784 protected areas, of which 91% were polygons and 9% were points.

  
  
Over 70% of the surface of Earth is ocean, comprised of highly diverse ecosystems, and providing a wide range of marine ecosystem services that support human society, health and the economy. Much of the recent growth in MPA coverage has been driven by the establishment of very large MPAs over 100,000 (square kilometers) km². These vast MPAs each contribute a significant part of the total global ocean coverage, with the 20 largest making up the majority of the world’s MPA coverage. While these represent huge commitments to conservation, there is a need for international collaboration to ensure that MPAs achieve their desired conservation value. The information contained in the MPA dataset contributes to the UNEP-WCMC's mission to place biodiversity at the heart of environment and development decision-making to enable enlightened choices for people and the planet.

  
  
The mandate of the database dates back to 1959 when the UN Economic and Social Council called for a list of national parks and equivalent reserves in recognition that they "are valuable for economic and scientific reasons and also as areas for the future preservation of fauna and flora and geologic structures in their natural state." The first UN List of Protected Areas was published in 1962, and subsequently evolved into the WDPA. The database is also used to generate indicators to track progress towards the Convention on Biological Diversity Aichi Biodiversity Target 11 and UN Sustainable Development Goals 14 and 15.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data for protected area records in the WDPA have been obtained from nearly 500 sources. Along with information on the data verifier, these sources are listed in the source table that is included with each monthly release. Data for protected areas designated under international agreements and conventions are often sourced from the relevant convention secretariats. Data for national-level protected areas have been sourced from national authorities wherever possible. Information may also be supplemented by data from other agencies, organizations or individuals. All data in the WDPA have been verified either by the national authorities or by non-government expert partners, with the exception of some data included before the verification process was established.

  
  
Data in the WDPA must meet the Protected Planet data standards. These were developed in 2010, regularly updated and subsequently revised in 2015 to ensure consistency in the way the WDPA is compiled, checked, managed, and presented. Standards are important to ensure all information is supplied in a common format that is interoperable and useful for a wide variety of reporting and analytical purposes. There are four key requirements:

  
  
 1. All sites must meet the IUCN definition of a protected area
  
  
 2. Spatial data from Geographic Information Systems (GIS) and an associated list of attributes must be provided
  
  
 3. Source of information must be provided
  
  
 4. The WDPA Data Contributor Agreement must be signed
 
  
  
The Protected Planet data standards also encompass standards specific to other databases, such as the Global Database on Protected Area Management Effectiveness.

  
  
The MPA dataset comprises protected areas in the WDPA that intersect with the marine part of an internal base layer—generally, the ocean or seas, but not lakes.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.protectedplanet.net/en/resources/wdpa-manual).  
  
### Additional Information

### Visualizing the Data

title: Hourly Precipitation
description:
This data set published by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives hourly precipitation estimates in mm/hr from latitudes 60N - 60S at a 0.1° resolution. The Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation (GSMaP) is a product of the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission.   
  
 Values are estimated using multi-band passive microwave and infrared radiometers from the GPM Core Observatory satellite and with the assistance of a constellation of other satellites. GPM's precipitation rate retrieval algorithm is based on a radiative transfer model. The gauge-adjusted rate is calculated based on the optimization of the 24h accumulation of GSMaP hourly rain rate to daily precipitation by NOAA/CPC gauge measurement.   
  
  Data is available from 2014 through present day and is made available with a four hour latency as JAXA processes the satellite data.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Land Deals
description:
The Land Matrix Online Database on Land Deals tracks large-scale land deals that are made for agricultural production, timber extraction, carbon trading, industry, renewable energy production, conservation, and tourism in low- and middle-income countries. A deal is referred to as an intended, concluded, or failed attempt to acquire land through purchase, lease, or concession that must (1) entail a transfer of rights to use, control, or ownership of land through sale, lease, or concession; (2) have been initiated since the year 2000; (3) cover an area of 200 ha or more; and (4) imply the potential conversion of land from smallholder production, local community use, or important ecosystem service provision to commercial use. Resource Watch shows the number of concluded deals that cover an area of 200 ha or more per year since 2000. Because of the nature of land acquisitions, it is difficult to obtain this information from official sources, therefore data are attained from (1) research papers and policy reports by international and local organizations and NGOs; (2) personal information contributed through the Global Observatory website; (3) field-based research projects; (4) official government records; (5) company websites; and (6) media reports. title: Water Temperature and Salinity
description:
Water Temperature and Salinity are two products from the Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM), created by the HYCOM Consortium, the National Ocean Partnership Program (NOPP), and the United States Global Ocean Data Assimilation Experiment (GODEA). HYCOM is a fully three dimensional, multivariate, variational ocean data assimilation system that produces simultaneous analyses of temperature, salinity, geopotential and vector velocity.   
  
The analysis is run in real-time and updates daily. The data have been interpolated to a uniform 0.08 degree lat/long grid between 80.48°S and 80.48°N. The salinity, temperature, and velocity variables have been interpolated to 40 standard z-levels (vertical depth).   
  
The high resolution makes HYCOM eddy resolving. Eddy-resolving models can more accurately simulate western boundary currents and the associated mesoscale variability and they better maintain more accurate and sharper ocean fronts. In particular, an eddy resolving ocean model allows upper ocean topographic coupling via flow instabilities. The coupling occurs when flow instabilities drive abyssal currents that in turn steer the pathways of upper ocean currents. In ocean prediction this coupling is important for ocean model dynamical interpolation skill in data assimilation/nowcasting and in ocean forecasting, which is feasible on time scales up to about a month.   
  
Sea surface temperature (SST) retrievals are empiracally derived using stored regressions between cloud cleared satellite SST radiances and drifting buoy SSTs. The regressions are global, calculated once, and held constant.

title: Near-Term climate hazard indicators across India – Early Century Projection - SSP 585
description:
### Overview
 
 
 This dataset provides insights into India’s climate projections for the period 2021–2040, focusing on extreme weather events such as heat waves, droughts, and intense rainfall. The data is essential for understanding the regional risks posed by climate change and for supporting targeted strategies to safeguard lives and livelihoods across the country. The data is provided at district level. 
 
 
 ### Methodology
 
 
 **Layers of interest**: Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃), Average Annual Precipitation Change (%), Average Annual Relative Humidity (%), Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days), Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days). 
 
 
**Data sources**: The dataset integrates outputs from 34 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (CMIP6) models. The daily precipitation dataset (grid resolution: 0.25° × 0.25°), maximum, minimum and mean temperature datasets (grid resolution: 1°×1°) developed by the India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used as observed data. 
 
 
### Estimation Methods
 
 
 The India Meteorological Department (IMD) have been used for statistical downscaling of the coarser resolution CMIP6 model simulations to 25 km. The study employed bias-correction procedure for daily datasets for precipitation, maximum temperature, and minimum temperature, as developed by Mishra et al. (2020). Climate projections are analysed for various temperature and precipitation changes under both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. 
 
 
 The projections include two key scenarios: 
 
 
 SSP2-4.5 (Middle of the Road): Moderate emissions and adaptation. 
 
 
 SSP5-8.5 (Fossil-Fueled Development): High emissions and heavy reliance on fossil fuels. 
 
 
 The historical simulation period 1951 – 1970 was selected as the ‘baseline period’ and for future climate projections, the time period 2021–2040 was used. In the present format, all the model simulations and observations have been maintained to a uniform grid resolution of 0.25°×0.25° for making them consistent for computing the Multi-Model Mean (MMM). For precise diagnosis of precipitation and temperature changes on a space and time scale in the present and future climate, the final parameters are presented at district level through district level mean aggregates. 
 
 
 For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at Mishra V, Bhatia U, Tiwari AD (2020) Bias corrected climate projections from CMIP6 models for Indian sub-continental river basins. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.3874046 and https://azimpremjiuniversity.edu.in/data-and-methods. 
 
 
### Description of the Layers
 
 
**Average Annual Maximum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily maximum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average maximum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Minimum Temperature Change (℃):** The daily minimum temperature data for each year is extracted and averaged to calculate the yearly average minimum temperature. The average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in temperature was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for each year is extracted and averaged across years to calculate the yearly average precipitation. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Annual Relative Humidity (%):** The annual average relative humidity for each year is calculated considering all the parallel to the temperatures available and presented for the period 2021–2040. 
 
 
 **Average Southwest Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Northeast Monsoon Precipitation Change (%):** The annual precipitation total for the northeast monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in precipitation for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Southwest Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering June-July-August-September of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. 
 
 
 **Average Change in Number of Heavy Precipitation Days during Northeast Monsoon (number of days):** A heavy rainfall day as per IMD is whenever daily rainfall exceeds 64.5 mm. The number of heavy precipitation days for the southwest monsoon season covering October-November-December of every year is extracted. The yearly average from climate projections for the period 2021–2040 was compared against the historical simulation period 1951–1970 and the change in number of heavy rainy days for the season was calculated. 
 
 
### Visualizing the Data
 
 
The data is presented district wise with a time slider with a dropdown selector for changing between the layers. The values are visualized using a gradient based on the selected year in the slider, ranging from lighter shades of yellow (indicating low values) to darker shades of green (representing higher values).
 
 
### Disclaimer

description:
The Global Roads Inventory Project (GRIP) dataset was developed to provide a more recent and consistent global roads dataset for use in global environmental and biodiversity assessment models. 
 The GRIP dataset is mainly aimed at providing a roads dataset that is easily usable for scientific global environmental and biodiversity modelling projects. The dataset is not suitable for navigation. GRIP4 is based on many different sources (including OpenStreetMap) and to the best of our ability we have verified their public availability, as a criteria in our research. The UNSDI-Transportation datamodel was applied for harmonization of the individual source datasets. 
 We have only included included highways, primary and secondary roads as part of this dataset. The original GRIP dataset consists of tertiary and local roads as well.

title: Out-Of-School Rate
description:
The rate of out-of-school children, generated by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), is the percentage of children not in school by year per country. The data extend back to 2014. The UIS gathers these statistics using questionnaires, which are sent to UNESCO Member States annually. The questionnaires are based on international standards, classifications, and measures that are regularly reviewed and modified by the UIS in order to address emerging statistical issues and improve the quality of data. The UIS collaborates with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Eurostat to collect data with surveys (collectively UOE). The UOE questionnaire compiles data from high- and middle-income countries that are members or partner countries of the OECD or Eurostat. The UOE survey gathers more detailed education statistics. Midyear population estimates for countries with at least 90,000 inhabitants are provided by the UN Population Division to calculate the percentages. title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for black carbon (BC). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Black carbon is the sooty black material emitted from gas and diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, and other sources that burn fossil fuel. It is made up of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter. PM2.5 can have significant health risks for people with compromised respiratory systems, the young, and the old. Black carbon is a global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate. Inhalation of black carbon is associated with health problems including respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and even birth defects. Black carbon also contributes to climate change causing changes in patterns of rain and clouds.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The black carbon station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.

title: Mangrove Extent Change
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the change in the global extent of mangroves between 1996 and 2016. Comparable maps of mangrove gain and loss (corresponding to smaller timesteps) were part of the creation of the first global map of mangrove extent produced via an automated, reproducible, and globally consistent methodology, which used a combination of optical and radar satellite data. The data have an effective resolution of approximately 25 meters at the equator.

  
  
Mangroves are forested intertidal ecosystems that perform critical landscape-level functions related to the regulation of freshwater, nutrients, and sediment inputs into marine areas. They play a key role in helping to control the quality of marine coastal waters. Mangroves are of critical importance as breeding and nursery sites for birds, fish, and crustaceans. Additionally, they constitute important sinks for carbon storage. Once abundant along the world’s tropical and subtropical coastlines, mangroves are in global decline. Significant drivers of change include removal for aquaculture, agriculture, energy exploitation and other industrial development, with an unknown proportion of the remaining mangroves fragmented and degraded. Mangroves are also sensitive to climate change effects such as sea level rise, temperature extremes, and changes in hydrology.

  
  
The underlying mangrove extent dataset has been generated by the [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) – a collaboration between Aberystwyth University (U.K.), solo Earth Observation (soloEO), Wetlands International, the World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). DOB Ecology supported the mapping in Africa through the Mangrove Capital Africa project. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The net extent change in global mangrove area from 1996 to 2016 was calculated by comparing the [global mangrove extent maps](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/45) provided by [Global Mangrove Watch (GMW)](https://www.globalmangrovewatch.org) for the corresponding years.

  
  
**1996 and 2016 extent maps:**

  
  
To develop the 1996 and 2016 mangrove extent maps, GMW first created a baseline map of mangroves for 2010 at a global level through a random forests classification of both Landsat sensor spectral composite data (all spectral wavebands) and Advanced Land Observing Satellite (ALOS) Phased Arrayed L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data.The classification was confined using a mangrove habitat mask, which defined regions where mangrove ecosystems can be expected to exist. The mangrove habitat definition was generated based on geographical parameters such as latitude, elevation, and distance from ocean water. Training for the habitat mask and classification of the 2010 mangrove mask was based on randomly sampling 38 million points using historical mangrove maps (for the year 2000) of Giri et al. (2011) and Spalding et al. (2010) and the water occurrence layer defined by Pekel et al. (2017).

  
  
The maps for 1996 and 2016 were derived by detection and classification of losses (defined as a decrease in radar backscatter) and gains (defined as a backscatter increase) between the 2010 ALOS PALSAR data and JERS-1 SAR (1996) and ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 (2016) data. The change pixels for each year in question were then added or removed from the 2010 baseline raster mask (buffered to allow detection of mangrove gains also immediately outside of the mask) to produce the new extent maps. Classification accuracies of the changes were assessed with over 45,000 points, with an overall accuracy of 75.0%. 

  
  
**1996–2016 mangrove extent change map:**

  
  
WRI derived the 1996 to 2016 extent change map by directly comparing the corresponding extent layers provided by GMW (rather than combining the change layers calculated by the authors). This comparison was performed by calculating the geometric intersection of the 1996 and 2016 extent layers. The intersection was erased from the 1996 extent to obtain loss polygons and erased from the 2016 extent to obtain gain polygons.

  
  
For the full documentation for the 1996 and 2016 extent maps, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/10/10/1669).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [mangrove extent time series](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/386314c4-ab42-47a7-b2cd-596b788e114d), which shows total mangrove forest cover, rather than change.   
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [GitHub](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_005a_mangrove).

The Fragile States Index (FSI), produced by the Fund for Peace (FFP), measures the vulnerability of states to collapse. It not only highlights the normal pressures that all states experience but also identifies when pressures exceed a state’s capacity to manage them. The FFP collects millions of reports and information from around the world, detailing existing social, economic, and political pressures. Based on the comprehensive social science approach of their Conflict Assessment System Tool (CAST), data from 3 main streams--preexisting quantitative data sets, content analysis, and qualitative expert analysis—are triangulated and subjected to critical review to obtain final scores for the index. The higher the index score the closer a state is to failure. The index is produced annually and covers 178 countries. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually.
  
  
The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. 
  
  
The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. 
  
  
Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types:
Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted
Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment
Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel
Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance)
  
  
Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. 

  
  
The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Hydropolitical Tension and Institutional Vulnerability
description:
### Overview  
  
The Transboundary Freshwater Dispute Database (TFDD) catalogs the number and delineation of the world's international river basins and also contains physical, socioeconomic, and political data relating to each of them. In the context of these datasets, an international river basin is defined by its ultimate outlet to an ocean, sea, or inland water body and has year-round flow crossing or drawing a political border. This database includes data at the scale of basins as well as basin country units, which is an area of an international river basin that falls within a particular country. 

The Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension estimates the relative level of risk a basin or basin country unit has for political tension over its transboundary rivers. This risk is based on:
  
  
 1. **water infrastructure development**: the ability to deal with disputes arising from the development of new water infrastructure
  
  
 2. **institutional vulnerability**: the capacity of a basin country unit to absorb tension, which is expressed by the presence or absence of treaties, treaty provisions, and river basin organizations

This data was calculated by TFDD-affiliated researchers as a part of the Governance thematic group within the Transboundary Water Assessment Programme's River Basin Component.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The delineation and count of international river basins and basin country units were determined using the [Register of International River Basins](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/content/register-international-river-basins) and watershed boundaries from the [HydroBASINs](https://www.hydrosheds.org/page/hydrobasins) dataset. HydroBASINS provides global coverage of watershed boundaries with several levels of sub-basin delineations, including watersheds that range in scale from tens to millions of square kilometers (see [Lehner & Gill, 2013](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/hyp.9740)).  For full documentation on the spatial boundary data, please see the [methodology](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/07900627.2019.1572497).

Institutional Vulnerability is measured by five components of formal transboundary cooperation. The five components are:
  
  
 1. at least one water treaty
  
  
 2. at least one treaty with an allocation mechanism
  
  
 3. at least one treaty with a flow variability management mechanism
  
  
 4. at least one treaty with a conflict resolution mechanism
  
  
 5. at least one river basin organization
  
  
The presence of a component is summed to give the institutional vulnerability score from 0 to 5, with 0 being the most vulnerable and 5 being the least vulnerable. 

Relative Risk Category for Hydropolitical Tension is calculated based on the basin country unit's institutional vulnerability score and the presence of a large dam or water diversion project in the basin country unit or upstream of it. If a basin country unit has a lower score for its institutional vulnerability and has infrastructure development in the basin country unit or upstream, it is in a higher risk category for Hydropolitical tension. Relative Risk ranges from 1 (very low risk) to 5 (very high risk). 

For full documentation on the metrics shown in this dataset, please see the [Transboundary River Basins report](https://transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/sites/transboundarywaters.science.oregonstate.edu/files/Database/ResearchProjects/TWAP/GEF_TWAPRB_FullTechnicalReport_compressed.pdf).   
  
### Additional Information
