title: Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for fine particulate matter (PM2.5). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
PM2.5 are fine inhalable particles, with diameters that are generally 2.5 micrometers and smaller. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particle pollution exposure.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time. 

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).

  
  
### Methodology  
  
The fine particulate matter (PM2.5) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.

title: Tree Cover
description:
### Overview  
  
The Tree Cover dataset measures areas of tree cover in 2000. Tree cover is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters (m) in height and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 1 arc second which is approximately 30 m × 30 m at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Forests provide a wide range of ecosystem services that are [critical to biodiversity richness, climate regulation, carbon storage, and water supplies](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/309/5734/570?ijkey=493d3bb49264119aa5ed9175119f7e221b2093d6&keytype2=tf_ipsecsha). They provide shelter to a variety of wildlife species and supply humans with [essential products including lumber, paper, and firewood]( https://www.fs.fed.us/forestmanagement/products/#:~:text=Forest%20products%20include%20materials%20derived,nuts%2C%20and%20other%20natural%20products). In the global fight against climate change, the forest ecosystem is playing an incredibly important role since it [absorbs and stores large amounts of carbon](https://www.undp.org/content/undp/en/home/blog/2018/Forests-A-natural-solution-to-climate-change-crucial-for-a-sustainable-future.html). Through measuring the tree cover density of global forests, this dataset provides decision makers with a consistent basis on which to understand the [causes of tree cover loss](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/342/6160/850). It also helps to quantify other critical environmental issues, such as the economic drivers of [natural forest conversion to more intensive land uses](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1549-0831.1998.tb00691.x) and the effectiveness of [protected areas around the globe](https://doi.org/10.1038/nature02422) to represent species diversity.

  
  
The dataset was created through a collaboration among the Global Land Analysis & Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland (UMD), Google, United States Geological Survey (USGS), and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) with the aim to provide a spatially and temporally detailed quantification of global forest change. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The data was generated using multispectral satellite imagery from three sources: the Landsat 5 thematic mapper, the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager sensors. [Images captured during growing seasons](https://doi.org/10.14358/PERS.70.3.313) were used since they are more appropriate for mapping land cover. More than 1 million satellite images were processed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval and 400,000 Landsat 5, 7 and 8 images for the 2011-2019 interval. 

  
  
The following steps were taken to pre-process the images:
  
  
1. Pixel values were recalculated if image resolutions were changed.
  
  
2. Images were screened for clouds, shadows and water.
  
  
3. Images were [calibrated and normalized](http://gsp.humboldt.edu/OLM/Courses/GSP_216_Online/lesson4-1/radiometric.html) to make them comparable with one another.

  
  
Land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled with a supervised learning algorithm, which involved [using labeled data to develop a machine learning model](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/problem-framing/cases#what-is-supervised-learning) to identify per pixel tree cover. To facilitate processing, each continent was characterized individually: North America, South America, Eurasia, Africa, and Australia using [Google Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/), a cloud platform for earth observation data analysis that combines a public data catalog with a large-scale computational facility capable of handling large volumes of geospatial data. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows [Tree Cover Loss](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) and [Tree Cover Gain](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/426fe3f0-12de-4adb-b3aa-850eb04f75b4) from the same dataset. 

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the reference multispectral imagery from 2000 and 2019 is available from the data provider. 
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button. 
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/for_001_rw2_tree_cover).

Tropical Cyclones
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the paths cyclones have followed and their intensities, from 1980 to the present. The data includes information on tropical cyclones by location, ocean basin, scale, name, wind speed, and other intensity parameters. The International Best Track Archive for Climate Stewardship (IBTrACS) is run by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

  
  
According to NOAA, a tropical cyclone is a weather event that produces rotating clouds, high winds, and thunderstorms. These cyclones are called hurricanes in the North Atlantic, central North Pacific, and eastern North Pacific. Elsewhere they are called typhoons or tropical typhoons. The disruptions from tropical cyclones have significant impacts on human life, property, and ecology. By compiling data in one place, this dataset can support scientific research efforts in understanding the distribution, frequency, and intensity of tropical cyclones, and assist emergency managers with disaster mitigation efforts. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Researchers obtained this data from various agencies either directly through agency websites or via personal communication. The data originated from satellite observations. The data files were then converted into a common format with two general steps. To solve the double-reporting issue with various data sources, step 1 identified each unique storm with an algorithm based on the storm’s position. Step 2 harmonized intensity estimates across data sources so that the intensity parameters are comparable. In cases of different sources having different positions and intensities, researchers calculated the average values from all available reports. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.ametsoc.org/doi/pdf/10.1175/2009BAMS2755.1).

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Fragile States Index
description:
The Fragile States Index (FSI), produced by the Fund for Peace (FFP), measures the vulnerability of states to collapse. It not only highlights the normal pressures that all states experience but also identifies when pressures exceed a state’s capacity to manage them. The FFP collects millions of reports and information from around the world, detailing existing social, economic, and political pressures. Based on the comprehensive social science approach of their Conflict Assessment System Tool (CAST), data from 3 main streams--preexisting quantitative data sets, content analysis, and qualitative expert analysis—are triangulated and subjected to critical review to obtain final scores for the index. The higher the index score the closer a state is to failure. The index is produced annually and covers 178 countries. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Non-CO₂ Agricultural Emissions
description:
The non-CO₂ agricultural emissions data set, published the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in its FAOSTAT database, contains all the non-CO₂ emissions produced in the different agricultural emissions subdomains (enteric fermentation, manure management, rice cultivation, synthetic fertilizers, manure applied to soils, manure left on pastures, crop residues, cultivation of organic soils, burning of crop residues, burning of savanna, energy use) and provides a picture of their contribution to the total amount of GHG emissions from agriculture. GHG emissions from agriculture tabulated here consist of non-CO₂ gases—namely, methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O)—produced by crop and livestock production and management activities. The FAOSTAT emissions database is computed following Tier 1 IPCC 2006 Guidelines for National GHG Inventories. GHG emissions data are provided by countries, regions, and special groups, with global coverage, relative to the period 1961-present (with annual updates) and with projections for 2030 and 2050. GHG emissions are expressed as Gg CO₂ and CO₂e (from CH₄ and N₂O), by underlying agricultural emission subdomain and by aggregate (agriculture total, agriculture total plus energy, agricultural soils). title: [Archived] Out-Of-School Rate
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](b2483333-693a-44e2-ae00-47f21c6a00bd) as a replacement.**_
  
The rate of out-of-school children, generated by the UNESCO Institute for Statistics (UIS), is the percentage of children not in school by year per country. The data extend back to 1999. The UIS gathers these statistics using questionnaires, which are sent to UNESCO Member States annually. The questionnaires are based on international standards, classifications, and measures that are regularly reviewed and modified by the UIS in order to address emerging statistical issues and improve the quality of data. The UIS collaborates with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) and Eurostat to collect data with surveys (collectively UOE). The UOE questionnaire compiles data from high- and middle-income countries that are members or partner countries of the OECD or Eurostat. The UOE survey gathers more detailed education statistics. Midyear population estimates for countries with at least 90,000 inhabitants are provided by the UN Population Division to calculate the percentages. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

title: Projected Dry Spells (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Change in dry spells is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average dry spells during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). title: Wood Fiber Concessions
description:
### Overview  
  
The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for the establishment of fast-growing tree plantations to produce timber for paper and paper products. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from the Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Concession name, group and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset. Wood Fiber Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. 

  
  
Wood fiber is a cellulose material extracted from trees and converted to wood pulp to make paper products. These products include paper, paperboard, cardboard and tissue. The year-round growing season and low cost of business has made tropical regions a popular wood fiber growing location. In these areas, it is common practice to clear land and plant fast-growing trees like the acacia. [Studies have shown](https://www.wri.org/blog/2017/07/drivers-deforestation-indonesia-inside-and-outside-concessions-areas) that these practices contribute to deforestation and [destruction of carbon-rich peat soils](https://www.wri.org/blog/2018/01/save-indonesias-carbon-rich-peatlands-start-mapping-them). Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of wood fiber plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. 

  
  
The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute (WRI)](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near-real-time. Understanding when and where deforestation is occurring is critical for ending illegal deforestation, fires, and unsustainable practices. Farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources. Additionally, this data can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The term “wood fiber concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale fast-growing timber plantations. GFW generated the Wood Fiber Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Republic of the Congo, Indonesia and Malaysia. Most locations in the dataset include the concession name, group and area (ha). 

  
  
Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies, environmental impact assessments and non-profits. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information, such as concession name and area, was added to the polygons as attributes. The Wood Fiber Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=wood%20fiber). 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data

title: Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Ozone (O₃) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for ground level ozone (O₃) . It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Unlike stratospheric ozone, which forms naturally in the upper atmosphere and protects us from the sun's harmful ultraviolet rays, ground-level (or tropospheric) ozone is created through the interactions of man-made (and natural) emissions of volatile organic compounds and nitrogen oxides in the presence of heat and sunlight. Cars and gasoline-burning engines are large sources of volatile organic compounds (VOCs). VOCs also come from consumer products such as paints, insecticides, and cleaners as well as industrial solvents and chemical manufacturing. High concentrations of ozone near ground level can be harmful to people, animals, crops, and other materials. Ozone can irritate the respiratory system, causing coughing and irritation. Ozone can aggravate pre existing respiratory problems like asthma, emphysema, and bronchitis and reduce the immune system's ability to fight off infections. Additionally, it can inflame and damage cells that line the lungs. It is possible for ozone to cause irreparable lung damage. These effects can be worse in children and exercising adults.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The ground level ozone station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.

title: Projected Cumulative Precipitation (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Projected Change in Dry Spells (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A dry spell is a five day period with less than 1 millimeter (mm) of precipitation. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Change in dry spells is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average dry spells during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The dataset is shown at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The average annual number of dry spells for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting precipitation data for a given year and summing the number of 5-day periods with less than 1 mm of precipitation. If a dry period lasted longer than 5 days, each additional day without precipitation was counted as a fractional (1/5) dry period. For example, a dry period of 8 days would count as 8/5 of a dry period (1 + 3/5). The average annual number of dry spells were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in dry spells. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of dry spells in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of dry spells between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Air Quality: Particulate Matter (PM10) Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Particulate Matter (PM10) Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for inhalable particulates (PM10) . It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
PM10 are inhalable particles, with a diameter of 2.6 to 10 micrometers. These particles come in many sizes and shapes and can be made up of hundreds of different chemicals. Some are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks, while others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. The size of these particles allows them to get deep into the lungs, and some may even get into the bloodstream. Numerous scientific studies have linked particle pollution exposure to a variety of health problems, including: premature death in people with heart or lung disease, nonfatal heart attacks, irregular heartbeat, aggravated asthma, decreased lung function, and increased respiratory symptoms. They are not as harmful as fine inhalable particles (PM2.5), but still present a health risk particularly for people with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The inhalable particulates (PM10) station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [black carbon (BC)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003gnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-BC_1).
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/cit_003_air_quality). Coordinates provided in the source data were used to map these data for display on Resource Watch.  
  
### Disclaimer

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Crops
description: "All crops" represent all of the crops that are included in the tool as displayed in the menu. Pixels are shaded if they contain at least 10 hectares of crop area within the 10x10 km pixel. If there are multiple crops meeting this criteria per pixel, the predominant crop (based on production) is displayed. If a single crop is selected, and the pixel colors are shaded by level of production. The crop layers displayed on the map reflect 2005 data regardless of the timeframe selected.

title: Water Risk Baseline
description: Water stress measures the ratio of total water withdrawals to available renewable surface and groundwater supplies. Water withdrawals include domestic, industrial, irrigation, and livestock consumptive and nonconsumptive uses. Available renewable water supplies include the impact of upstream consumptive water users and large dams on downstream water availability. Higher values indicate more competition among users.

title: Kcal per capita
description: Kilocalories per person represents the average availability of calories per person, by country. Note that it is not crop specific.

title: Food production
description: Total crop production represents crop area harvested * yield, by country. Note that production represents total production of a crop, not just for human consumption but also for livestock feed, biofuels, etc.

title: Food Demand
description: Food demand for crop represents aggregate household food demand for the selected crop(s), by country.

title: Net trade
description: Crop net trade represents the amount of the selected crop(s) that is traded by country, where positive values indicate greater exports than imports.

title: Projected Annual Average Temperature U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Projected Heating Degree Day U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual heating degree days (HDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. HDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is below 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 50°F, the HDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual HDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. HDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, HDD are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for heating buildings.

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Heating Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual HDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily HDDs were calculated by subtracting daily average temperature values from the baseline temperature of 65°F. If the daily average temperature was above 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual HDD was calculated by summing all daily HDD values over a given year. Annual HDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the HDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual HDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Projected Cumulative Precipitation U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:

Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. title: [Archived] Energy Facility Emissions (U.S.)
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](f61e9516-ae23-4870-b26b-4d1b57ac3225) as a replacement.**_
  
The Energy Facility Emissions data set, published by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), provides greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions data for large facilities and industrial sources that emit over 25,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e) per year in the United States. The EPA collects annual reporting of GHG data from these large facilities and publishes the data through the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program (GHGRP). The data set includes facility names, locations, fuel types, industry sectors and subsectors, annual facility emission thresholds, and greenhouse gas types. Users can search for national, state, local, sector, and facility-specific data. All reports submitted to EPA are evaluated by electronic validation and verification checks. This data set reflects 85-90% of total U.S. emissions and spans 2010-2016. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Projected Dry Spells U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Dry Spells dataset in the United States (U.S.) shows change in average annual dry spells at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. Average annual dry spells are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that the number of dry spells is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. title: Electricity Installed Capacity
description:
### Overview  
  
Electricity installed capacity measures the [maximum electric output](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3) an electricity generator can produce under specific conditions. This dataset reveals the amount of electricity all the power plants in a country can produce within a year and helps quantify the [growth of energy resources](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/what-generation-capacity). However, considering many generators do not operate at their full capacity all the time, a generator's actual electric output [varies based on conditions at the power plant, fuel costs, and/or as instructed by the electric power grid operator](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3). Therefore, this dataset represents the theoretical electricity output that is possible, rather than the actual electricity generation.
  
  

The Electricity Installed Capacity dataset was released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). This data was reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is available for the years 1980-2019, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
EIA compiled data from a list of external sources including  
- International Energy Agency (IEA)
- Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
- Platts World Power Plants Database
- International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)
- International Hydropower Association (IHA)
- United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database
- BP Statistical Review of World Energy
- Other government agencies, research institutes, and companies
  
  

Electricity data shows the capacity as of December 31 each year. Data from both utility and non-utility sources was used. EIA is in the process of creating specific country-level metadata for this dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. 
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Total Energy Consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/67cf410f-4cdf-4437-aa09-187e5fa590ae) dataset and [Electricity Consumption] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/eef10736-8d8b-4ac9-a715-ef0653a83196) dataset by EIA.
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the electricity installed capacity of different energy resources from 1980 through 2018 is available from the data provider. 

For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/upload_eia_data). This data has been mapped on Resource Watch by joining it with Natural Earth boundaries.

title: Plastic density in the oceans
description:
### Overview  
  
The dataset represents the count (pieces per square kilometer) and weight (grams per square kilometer) densities of plastic particles floating in the ocean. The data was created from an oceanographic model of floating debris dispersal and calibrated using data from surveys done during 24 expeditions conducted from 2007-2013. The results have been adjusted for a variety of factors like particle fragmentation and wind driven mixing of water. The data is presented in four particle size categories ranging from 0.33 millimeters to >200 millimeters. The final results are shown in raster format at a spatial resolution of 20 kilometers. 
  
  

Plastic pollution is globally distributed across all oceans and is regarded as a major health issue for marine and human life. As plastic degrades it forms microplastics that are often consumed by marine fauna, slowly working up the food chain. In addition, floating plastics can move across oceans and transport species to non-native regions. 
  
  

This study was conducted to help countries understand their impacts on the ocean and to be used in implementing plastic waste reduction policies. It was authored by researchers from a variety of organizations and funded by an array of environmental and educational groups. The data has global coverage and is available at a spatial resolution of 0.2° or about 20 kilometers.  
  
### Methodology  
  
To gather the mass and count of the ocean’s plastics, the researchers conducted 24 expeditions (2007–2013) across all five subtropical gyres, coastal Australia, Bay of Bengal, and the Mediterranean Sea. During these expeditions 680 surface net tows and 891 visual survey transects of large plastic debris were conducted. Surface net tows were done using a mesh size of 0.33 millimeters towed at 0.5 to 2 meters below the ocean surface for 15 to 60 minutes. Visual surveys were carried out using dedicated observers viewing 20 meter sections next to the boat noting large floating debris. Debris observations were broken into nine categories, four categories for fishing-related debris: buoy, line, net, and other fishing gear, and five categories for other plastics: bucket, bottle, foamed polystyrene, bag/film, or miscellaneous plastics. All 1,571 mesh and visual surveys included data on plastic counts and 1,333 of them also included data on debris weight.
  
  

The data was used to create debris estimates and calibrate an oceanographic model based on water movement to show the dispersal of floating debris. The model used to describe oceanic currents was the US Navy’s Hybrid Coordinate Ocean Model (HYCOM). This was combined with a Lagrangian particle-tracking model Pol3DD to mimic how plastic particles move through the ocean. The model assumes that amounts of plastic entering the ocean depends on three principal variables: watershed outfalls, population density, and maritime activity. The results were adjusted to compensate for wind driven mixing of the surface layer that forces plastic particles below the surface. Additionally, conservative estimates for particle fragmentation rates were used when determining particle count. Through this methodology, estimated values were generated for the count and weight of ocean plastic in four size classes: 0.33-1.0 millimeters, 1.01-4.75 millimeters, 4.76-200 millimeters, and >200 millimeters.
  
  

For full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0111913).

title: Local Threats to Coral Reefs
description:
### Overview  
  
The health of coral reefs is threatened from many nearby human activities. This dataset describes, individually and in aggregate, the threat posed by the following nearby activities: coastal development, marine-based pollution, watershed-based pollution, and overfishing and other destructive fishing practices. This dataset expresses these threats via an index of low, medium, or high threat severity at a 1 km resolution (the integrated threat index also includes a "very high" category).   
  
The dataset was created at the World Resources Institute (WRI) as part of the Reefs at Risk Revisited study and represents threats for the year 2011. The coral reef location dataset used was based on 500 meter resolution gridded data reflecting shallow, tropical coral reefs of the world. Organizations contributing to the data and development of the map include the Institute for Marine Remote Sensing at the University of South Florida (IMaRS USF), Institut de Recherche pour le Développement (IRD), United Nations Environment World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), WorldFish Center, and WRI.  
  
### Methodology  
  
Local threats to coral reefs include: coastal development; marine-based pollution and damage; watershed-based pollution; and overfishing and destructive fishing practices. To combine these into one index, the authors defined the factors that contribute to each threat in the following way:  
  
The coastal development threat includes the number, size, population density, and population growth rates of human settlements on the coast; locations of seaports, airports and hotels; and traffic from tourism.  
  
The marine-based pollution and damage threat includes datasets on distance from commercial and cruise ports, shipping intensity as measured by a voluntary reporting scheme, and presence of oil infrastructure.   
  
The watershed-based pollution threat to coral reefs includes sediment deposits accumulated throughout watersheds and released at river mouths. The Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) is used to calculate the relative erosion potential (REP) for all land areas. The REP levels in a watershed are used to determine how much sediment gets loaded into the water courses of the watershed. Factors such as mangroves and dams reduce the total sediment delivery at the river mouth. A model is used to disperse the accumulated sediment amount in the surrounding ocean area. Thresholds are established to differentiate between ocean grid cells at low, medium, or high threat from sediment deposits.  
  
Severity of overfishing was estimated based on proxies for demand for fish products---coastal population density, extent of official fishing areas, and reef and shallow shelf areas---with special adjustments made to account for increased demand when in proximity to large populations and market centers. Areas where destructive fishing practices occur, such as using explosives or poisons, were included based on observations from monitoring and mapping exercises undertaken by field experts.   
  
The overfishing and destructive fishing threat level may be reduced by one level if a grid cell was inside a marine protected area that had been rated as having “effective” or “partially effective” management. These ratings were sourced from regional experts, who were asked to rate marine protected areas on a three-point scale for management effectiveness.   
  
Depending on the size of these threat factors, distance thresholds are established for whether that threat factor puts a nearby ocean grid cell at low, medium, or high risk of damage to coral reefs. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://wriorg.s3.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/pdf/reefs_at_risk_revisited.pdf?_ga=2.65485742.1818236267.1556558259-801875434.1487936749).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for global threats to coral are available from the data provider.  For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Annual Surface Water Coverage
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the locations of seasonal water and permanent water for each year between 1984 and 2020. A permanent water surface is an area that is underwater for all 12 months of the year, while a seasonal water surface is underwater for less than 12 months of the year. This dataset has a 30 meter resolution. 
  
  

Water is essential for Earth’s plant and animal life, as well as for many human activities. Surface water also affects the exchange of heat, gas, and water vapor between Earth’s surface and atmosphere. The dataset can be used to support sectors such as water resource management, climate modeling, biodiversity conservation, and food security. 
  
  

This data is a part of the Global Surface Water dataset, created by the European Commission’s Joint Research Center.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Water coverage was detected using satellite imagery from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 that was collected between 1984 and  2020. To detect water, researchers used big data exploration and information extraction techniques such as expert systems, visual analytics, and evidential reasoning. An expert system is a classification process that can account for data uncertainty and incorporate image interpretation expertise. 
  
  

In some places, observations for all 12 months of the year were not available. For example, some parts of the world experience a polar night during parts of the year, in which the night lasts for more than 24 hours. These areas do not have adequate imagery to detect surface water coverage for all 12 months. In cases where 12 months of data was not available, water is considered to be permanent if the number of months where water is present is equal to the number of months where valid observations were acquired. Likewise, if the number of months where water is present is less than the number of months of valid observations, water is considered to be seasonal.
  
  

Ice is treated as a nonvalid observation. If water is present throughout the unfrozen period, the lake is considered to be a permanent water surface. 
  
  

If the area of the lake contracts during the unfrozen period, then the pixels along the borders of the lake will be considered as seasonal water. 
  
  

For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20584).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for monthly recurrence and monthly water history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
