title: Frost Free Season
description:
Frost free season represents the annual average longest streak of days above freezing, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Antarctic Sea Ice Extent
description:
### Overview  
  
The Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset shows the extent of sea ice in the Antarctic for the latest month. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). Data was collected daily and averaged at the end of each month to produce monthly ice extents. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice is currently present in the Antarctic region. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand the current Antarctic sea ice extent. Typically, Antarctic sea ice extent reaches its maximum in September and minimum in February. Although Antarctic sea ice extent varies significantly from year to year, the average ice extent has not changed over the past 40 years. According to the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/understanding-climate/understanding-climate-antarctic-sea-ice-extent), natural variability in the Southern Ocean and in atmospheric circulation patterns have a greater impact on Antarctic sea ice extent than climate change. However, climate change is disrupting wind patterns, currents and ocean temperatures across the globe. These changes may eventually impact Antarctic sea ice extent.

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Data was collected daily at a spatial resolution of 25 km. The Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) instrument aboard the [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP) satellites](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) measured the data. NSIDC used this satellite data to create the [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081) dataset. The Monthly Antarctic Sea Ice Extent dataset was generated from the NRTSI dataset. 

  
  
The SSMIS instrument senses microwave radiation emitted from the Earth's surface. The amount of microwave radiation emitted from an object depends on its physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water, allowing SSMIS to easily distinguish sea ice from ocean water. SSMIS data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), which is a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1). Gridded ice concentrations are the percentage of ice in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. If a cell contained more than 15% ice concentration, it was classified as ice. Otherwise, it was classified as water. 

  
  
Sea ice extent was delineated by the location where ice ends and the open ocean begins. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Maximum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/15a0b176-8313-4859-af90-5c198e50a605), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f) and [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1).

title: Cooling Degree Days
description:
A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This data set shows CDDs under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: U.S. Wildfire Hazard Potential
description:
Federal wildfire managers often want to know, over large landscapes, where wildfires are likely to occur and how intense they may be. To meet this need we developed a map that we call wildfire hazard potential (WHP) – a raster geospatial product that can help to inform evaluations of wildfire risk or prioritization of fuels management needs across very large spatial scales (millions of acres). Our specific objective with the WHP map was to depict the relative potential for wildfire that would be difficult for suppression resources to contain. To create the 2014 version, we built upon spatial estimates of wildfire likelihood and intensity generated in 2014 with the Large Fire Simulation system (FSim) for the national interagency Fire Program Analysis system (FPA), as well as spatial fuels and vegetation data from LANDFIRE 2010 and point locations of fire occurrence from FPA (ca. 1992 – 2012). With these data sets as inputs, we produced an index of WHP for all of the conterminous United States at 270 m resolution. We present the final WHP map in two forms: 1) continuous integer values, and 2) five WHP classes of very low, low, moderate, high, and very high. On its own, WHP is not an explicit map of wildfire threat or risk, but when paired with spatial data depicting highly valued resources and assets such as structures or powerlines, it can approximate relative wildfire risk to those specific resources and assets. WHP is also not a forecast or wildfire outlook for any particular season, as it does not include any information on current or forecasted weather or fuel moisture conditions. It is instead intended for long-term strategic fuels management.

title: U.S. Flood Hazards
description:
The National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL) is a digital database that contains flood hazard mapping data from FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). This map data is derived from Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMRs).The NFHL is for community officials and members looking to view effective regulatory flood hazard information in a Geographic Information Systems (GIS) application.

The NFHL provides users with the ability to determine the flood zone, base flood elevation and floodway status for a particular geographic location. It also has National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) community information, map panel information, cross section and hydraulic structure information, Coastal Barrier Resource System information (if applicable) and base map information, such as road, stream and public land survey data.  A full list of the layers available in the NFHL may be found in the NFHL GIS Services User Guide.

The NFHL data set represents the current effective flood risk data for those parts of the country where maps have been modernized. It is a compilation of effective Flood Insurance Rate Map (FIRM) databases and Letters of Map Revision (LOMR). The NFHL is updated as new data reaches its designated effective date and becomes valid for regulatory use under the NFIP.

title: U.S. Billion-Dollar Disasters
description: The National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) is the Nation's Scorekeeper in terms of addressing severe weather and climate events in their historical perspective. As part of its responsibility of monitoring and assessing the climate, NCEI tracks and evaluates climate events in the U.S. and globally that have great economic and societal impacts. NCEI is frequently called upon to provide summaries of global and U.S. temperature and precipitation trends, extremes, and comparisons in their historical perspective. Found here are Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters: the weather and climate events that have had the greatest economic impact from 1980 to 2018. The U.S. has sustained 233 weather and climate disasters since 1980 where overall damages/costs reached or exceeded $1 billion (including Consumer Price Index adjustment to 2018). The total cost of these 233 events exceeds $1.5 trillion. Please note that the map reflects a summation of billion-dollar events for each state affected (i.e., it does not mean that each state shown suffered at least $1 billion in losses for each event).

title: Projected Change in Frost Free Season (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset shows the change in annual average frost free season at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. A frost free season is the largest number of consecutive days in a year where the minimum daily temperatures are above 32 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. Frost free season projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in frost free season is shown as the number of days difference between the frost free season during the projected decade and the baseline time period. The dataset is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. In particular, it can be used to understand and adapt to changing agricultural growing seasons and productivity in individual regions. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Frost Free Season dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average frost free season for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting daily minimum temperature values for a given year and finding the largest number of consecutive days where the minimum temperature exceeded 32°F. The average annual frost free seasons were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then the baseline average was subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in dry spells

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the frost free season in 2000 is actually an average of the annual frost free seasons between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Air Quality: Nitrogen Dioxide (NO₂) Modeled 5-day Forecast
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows forecasted nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) concentrations at Earth’s surface, modeled by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Goddard Earth Observing System Composition Forecast (GEOS-CF). NO₂ is a highly reactive air pollutant, produced by fossil fuel combustion from power plants and gasoline-burning vehicles. NO₂ is used as the indicator for the larger group of nitrogen oxides (NOx), which includes nitrous acid and nitric acid.  
  
NO₂ emissions contribute to the [formation of smog](https://www.environment.gov.au/protection/publications/factsheet-nitrogen-dioxide-no2) and can significantly harm human health. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/no2-pollution/basic-information-about-no2), breathing air with a high concentration of NO₂ can irritate airways in the respiratory system and long-term exposures can contribute to asthma development. Even exposure to elevated NO₂ concentrations over short periods can aggravate respiratory diseases, particularly asthma, leading to respiratory symptoms (such as coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing), hospital admissions, and visits to emergency rooms. People with asthma as well as children and the elderly are generally at greater risk for the health effects of NO₂.  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b). The GEOS-CF system runs once a day and produces a global, near-real-time forecast up to five days into the future at 15-minute and one-hour time intervals. The data has a global coverage at a resolution of 25 kilometers x 25 kilometers. GEOS-CF also creates global forecasts for a variety of other air quality indicators.  
  
GEOS-CF was developed by NASA's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO). You can find forecasted concentrations for each compound on the GMAO website.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The GEOS-CF model provides analysis on the composition of a range of air pollutants including PM2.5, O₃, and NO₂. This model is driven by the GEOS weather forecasting system and the GEOS-Chem atmospheric chemistry model.  
  
To produce estimates of aerosol concentrations, the GEOS-CF model runs two aerosol schemes: the GEOS-Chem aerosol mechanism (GCC) and the Goddard Chemistry, Aerosol, Radiation, and Transport (GOCART) module to simulate the effects of aerosols in the atmosphere. The GOCART aerosols are constrained by satellite observed aerosol optical depth, while the GCC aerosols are purely model derived. The PM2.5 data shown on Resource Watch is produced by the GOCART module.  
  
All emissions modeling for GEOS-Chem is handled by the [NASA-Harvard emissions component (HEMCO)](https://www.geosci-model-dev.net/7/1409/2014/gmd-7-1409-2014.html), a stand-alone software component for calculating emissions in global atmospheric models. Anthropogenic emissions are acquired as monthly averages from the [HTAPv2.2](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/15/11411/2015/) and [RETRO](https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1029/2007GB003031) emissions inventories. The monthly averages are broken down into hourly values by sector-specific factors. Emissions of CO ([Oda et al., 2017](https://www.earth-syst-sci-data.net/10/87/2018/)) and SO₂ ([Liu et al., 2018](https://www.atmos-chem-phys.net/18/16571/2018/)) are scaled using a factor based on satellite data. Emissions from biomass burning are taken from [Quick Fire Emissions Database (QFEDv2.5)](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Darmenov796.pdf), volcanic emissions of SO₂ are from [CARN (2019)](https://disc.gsfc.nasa.gov/datasets/MSVOLSO2L4_3/summary), and other natural emissions are taken from various sources. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://gmao.gsfc.nasa.gov/pubs/docs/Knowland1159.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows GEOS-CF forecasts for [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ebc079a1-51d8-4622-ba25-d8f3b4fcf8b3) and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/645fe192-28db-4949-95b9-79d898f4226b).

  
  


Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional forecasted data for other compounds, times, and levels of the atmosphere is also produced by GEOS-CF. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average minimum temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the minimum temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average minimum temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in annual average minimum temperature is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average minimum temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting and averaging all daily minimum temperature data over a given year. The average annual minimum temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average minimum temperature.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average minimum temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual minimum temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The change in extreme precipitation is shown as the multiplicative difference between annual average days of extreme precipitation during the projected decade and the baseline time period. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days dataset was created with precipitation data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India
description:
Crop Land Area, Yield and Production - India

SOURCE: Directorate of Economics and Statistics, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India

LINK: https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web; https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf

Overview

The dataset comprises five-year averages of production (in tonnes), productivity/yield (in tonnes per hectare), and area (in hectares) for 55 major crops across India from 1997–98 to 2022–23. The information is provided at the district level, covering major seasonal time periods of each crop within each year. The yearly datasets were derived from crop-wise APY dataset (https://data.desagri.gov.in/website/crops-apy-report-web).

Methodology

Pre-Processing: The dataset available as excel report was processed and joined with district shapefile (recent by mid of year 2022, containing 755 districts) obtained from Survey of India website. To simplify the presentation, the raw yearly data was averaged into five-year intervals to highlight trends in crop production and acreage across each district. The periods were labelled as follows: 1995-2000 as 2000, 2001-2005 as 2005, 2006-2010 as 2010, 2011-2015 as 2015, 2016-2020 as 2020, and 2021-2023 as 2023. This approach was adopted based on feedback from stakeholder engagements.

Layers of interest: Rice Area (in Hectares), Rice Production (in Tonnes), Rice Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare), Cotton Area (in Hectares), Cotton Production (in Tonnes), Cotton Yield (in Tonnes/Hectare)

Seasons considered for Rice crop: Kharif, Rabi, Autumn, Summer
Seasons considered for Cotton crop: Kharif, Rabi

The agricultural crop year in India runs from July to June. The cropping season is divided into two main seasons: (i) Kharif and (ii) Rabi, based on the monsoon. The Kharif season occurs from June/July to September/October during the southwest monsoon. It aligns with the Asian summer monsoon and is mostly rainfed, with limited irrigation arrangements. The Rabi season lasts from October to March and is grown under irrigated conditions. The Summer and Autumn seasons are shorter and found only in a few states. The Summer season runs from February/March to April/May and is mostly grown under irrigated conditions. The Autumn season, from May/June to October, is mainly for long-duration crops like sugarcane and some vegetable crops. For rice crop, the season is followed in particular states of India that do not receive considerable rains from the Asian summer monsoon.

Area, Yield, and Production Estimation Methods

The methods for estimating area, yield, and production of crops follow standardized processes under India's agricultural statistical framework.

1. Area Estimation Methods

1.1. Temporarily Settled States (Land Record States)
Crop area is estimated through field-to-field enumeration by a village accountant (Patwari/Karnam). The data is recorded in the Khasra register (a field-wise crop record). The area statistics are aggregated at village, tehsil, district, and state levels.

1.2. Permanently Settled States (Non-Land Record States)
Establishment of Agency for Reporting Agricultural Statistics (EARAS) is used:
- A random sample of at least 20% of villages is surveyed annually.
- Complete enumeration is conducted within selected villages.
- The process ensures coverage of all villages over five years.

1.3. Non-Reporting Areas
Area estimates are derived using remote sensing technology and aerial photography. Ground truthing and validation methods are used to improve accuracy.

2. Yield Estimation Methods

General Crop Estimation Surveys (GCES)
The yield is estimated through scientifically designed crop-cutting experiments (CCE). The methodology is as follows:

2.1. Sampling Design
Stratified Multistage Random Sampling:
- Strata: Administrative divisions (tehsil/block).
- Primary Sampling Units: Villages (selected randomly).
- Second-Stage Sampling Units: Fields within selected villages.
- Ultimate Sampling Units: Experimental plots of standard size (e.g., 5m x 5m).

2.2. Plot Selection
Two fields are randomly selected per village. A random plot (e.g., 5m x 5m) is located within each field using random numbers. For row-planted crops (like cotton), longer plots (e.g., 10m x 5m) are used.

2.3. Harvesting and Recording
The experimental plot is harvested before the rest of the field. The produce is:
- Weighed immediately for gross yield.
- Adjusted if required (e.g., driage experiments for rice).

2.4. Driage Adjustments
- Rice: Driage experiments are conducted to adjust for moisture content, ensuring yields are reported as dried grain weight.
- Cotton: In the case of cotton, the final produce is expressed in terms of lint after adopting ginning percentage (kapas to lint) as obtained from the ginning factories.

3. Production Estimation Methods
Area and yield are multiplied to estimate production at village, district, state, and national levels.

4. Validation of the Area, Production and Yield estimates
Final aggregation and validation occur at the national level by the Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES). Production estimates are validated using:
- Remote sensing data,
- Historical trends,
- Market and trade data,
- Reports from local agricultural officers.

For the full documentation, please see the source methodology at https://www.mospi.gov.in/sites/default/files/publication_reports/manual_area_crop_production_23july08_1.pdf.

Visualizing the Data
The data is available as district-level aggregates. By selecting a specific crop, area, production, yield statistic, and preferred season, the relevant layer is displayed with a gradient based on the 2023 crop year, ranging from yellow (for low values) to green (with darker shades representing higher values). The cursor can be dragged over districts and clicked to view the 5-yearly averaged values from 1995 to 2023. The 'No Data' value, represented by black, indicates either that the season was not practiced in the district during that year or that data is unavailable from the source.

Disclaimer

title: Extreme Precipitation Days
description:
Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Fires (VIIRS)
description:
The Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite (VIIRS) active fires data (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT) constitute the latest fire monitoring product to be added to FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System), which identifies global fire locations in near-real time. Information is collected from the VIIRS sensor and processed with a fire detection algorithm to flag active fires. Each dot on the map represents the center of a 375 m pixel that has been flagged by the algorithm. The VIIRS data provides a higher resolution data set than the active fires data from MODIS.  The VIIRS data have higher spatial resolution (375 m pixels vs. 1 km pixels), which improves detection of smaller fires and provides a more reliable estimate of fire perimeters. The VIIRS data are also better calibrated to detect fires at night. The active fires data are available to view and download for the past 24 hours, 48 hours, or 7 days. Older fire data will be available for download from the NASA FIRMS website beginning in mid-2016. Each fire alert has a confidence value of low, nominal, or high to help users gauge the quality of individual hotspot / fire pixels. 

PREPdata shows only a subset of this data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link.

title: Saltmarshes
description:
### Overview  
  
The Saltmarshes dataset displays the distribution of saltmarshes globally, drawing from occurrence data (surveyed and/or remotely sensed). The dataset captures location data for saltmarsh in 99 countries worldwide. The data were collected from 1973 to 2015, with most occurring after 2005.

  
  
Saltmarshes are highly productive ecosystems that are rich in biodiversity and underpin the estuarine food web. In particular, saltmarshes serve as nesting, nursery and feeding grounds for numerous species of birds, fish, molluscs and crustaceans. Saltmarshes are extremely valuable but often overlooked ecosystems, contributing to livelihoods locally and globally through the associated ecosystem services they provide, including fish production, carbon storage, and coastal protection. Despite their importance, saltmarsh areas are declining around the world, having lost between 25% and 50% of their global historical coverage ([Crooks et al. 2011](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/18318/605780REPLACEM10of0Coastal0Wetlands.pdf), [Duarte et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12237-008-9038-7)). Vast areas have been lost through conversion to agriculture, urban and industrial land, while remaining saltmarshes face many other current and potential threats ([Gedan et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163930)).

  
  
In light of increasing anthropogenic and environmental pressures on coastal ecosystems, global data on the occurrence and extent of saltmarshes are needed to draw attention to these critical ecosystems and the benefits they generate for people. The dataset was developed to establish a mapped baseline inventory of the extent of the global distribution of saltmarshes. The data aim to support resource management, strengthen decision-making, and facilitate tracking of progress towards global conservation targets set by multilateral environmental agreements. The UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) collated and integrated the dataset with support from Conservation International and The Nature Conservancy.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Saltmarshes dataset consists of data derived from peer-reviewed articles and [grey literature](https://www.greylit.org/about), including reports and databases created by governmental and non-governmental organisations, universities, institutes and researchers globally. Data in the original source materials were collected using remote sensing and field-based survey methods. Data quality ranges from high-resolution maps to low-resolution representations, with the scale varying from 1:10,000 to 1:4,000,000, with most falling within the 1:10,000 to 1:100,000 range. Data contributors were asked to submit metadata with each dataset to provide the contextual information important for informing analyses. Saltmarshes were identified in accordance with definitions provided by data sources, where available, or were determined using expert opinion (available in the supplementary material).The precautionary principle was applied to ensure consistency across designations: if the authors were uncertain about the classification of the habitat, it was not included. Please refer to the supplementary material and associated [metadata](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/pdfs/43/WCMC_027_Global_Distribution_of_Saltmarsh.pdf?1617122640) from the authors for more information regarding each data source presented.

  
  
 For the full documentation, please see the source [publication](https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.5.e11764).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional point data is available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/wat_069_rw0_saltmarshes).

title: Global Soil Properties
description:
### Overview

This dataset describes select global soil parameters regridded and upscaled from the Harmonized World Soil Database v1.2. The HWSD provides information for addressing land competition for food production, bio-energy demand, and biodiversity threats. It is also used as an input to model global carbon cycles. The data are presented as a series of five critical layers at 0.05-degree (~5 km) spatial resolution.

### Methodology

**Data Sources:** The Harmonized World Soil Database integrates over 15,000 different soil mapping units, combining global, regional, and national updates (SOTER, ESD, Soil Map of China, WISE) with the FAO-UNESCO Soil Map of the World (FAO, 1971-1981).

**Estimation Methods:** HWSD v1.2 (FAO 2012) provides the most comprehensive database of soil characteristics available for global analysis. Soil characteristics are derived from real soil profiles considering pedogenic development, land use, land use history, and disturbances. Properties in HWSD are available for both surface soil horizons (0-30 cm) and deeper soil profiles (30-100 cm).

### Description of the Layers

**Topsoil Clay Fraction (% weight):** Percentage clay in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Clay consists of fine-grained particles (<0.002mm) that exhibit plasticity when wet and harden when dried or fired.

**Topsoil Silt Fraction (% weight):** Percentage silt in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Silt results from mechanical weathering of rocks through glacial grinding, wind abrasion, or river erosion. It is primarily composed of quartz and feldspar.

**Topsoil Sand Fraction (% weight):** Percentage sand in the topsoil (0-30 cm). Sand particles range from 0.0625 mm to 2 mm and feel gritty when touched. Classified into very fine, fine, medium, coarse, and very coarse based on size.

**Topsoil pH (-log(H+)):** The acidity or alkalinity of topsoil (0-30 cm) measured in a soil-water solution. Categories include:
- Extremely Acidic (pH < 4.5): Found in Acid Sulfate Soils (e.g., mangrove soils, cat clays).
- Very Acidic (pH 4.5–5.5): Often influenced by aluminum toxicity.
- Acidic to Neutral (pH 5.5–7.2): Optimal for nutrient availability and most crops.
- Carbonate-Rich (pH 7.2–8.5): May reduce nutrient availability like phosphorus and iron.
- Highly Alkaline (pH > 8.5): Typically sodic with high sodium, affecting soil structure.

**Topsoil Organic Carbon Content (% weight):** Indicator of soil fertility and health. Classified as:
- Very Low (<0.2%): Requires significant soil amendments.
- Low (0.2%–0.6%): Poor in organic matter.
- Moderate (0.6%–1.2%): Better fertility and structure.
- High (1.2%–2.0%): Favorable conditions for crop growth.
- Very High (>2.0%): Highly fertile and well-structured. 

### Visualizing the Data

The dataset is available at ~5 km resolution. Lighter shades indicate lower values, while brighter shades (orange-red) indicate higher values.

title: Madhya Pradesh Change in Rainfall
description:
The data represents projected change in the annual rainfall from baseline (1981-2010) towards mid-century (2021-2050) in percentage. This data is an output from a hydrologic model, SWAT (Soil and Water Assessment Tool) which has been use to assess the impact of projected climate change on water resources. The SWAT model (Arnold et al., 1981, Neitsch et al., 2022) is a distributed parameter and continuous time simulation model. The SWAT model has been developed to predict the hydrological response of un-gauged catchments to natural inputs as well as the manmade interventions. The model (a) is physically based; (b) uses readily available inputs; (c) is computationally efficient to operate and (d) is continuous time and capable of simulating long periods for computing the effects of management changes. The major advantage of the SWAT model is that unlike the other conventional conceptual simulation models it does not require much calibration and therefore can be used on un-gauged watersheds (in fact the usual situation). 

The SWAT model is a long-term, continuous model for watershed simulation. It operates on a daily time step and is designed to predict the impact of land management practices on water, sediment, and agricultural chemical yields. The model is physically based, computationally efficient, and capable of simulating a high level of spatial details by allowing the watershed to be divided into a large number of sub-watersheds. Major model components include weather, hydrology, soil temperature, plant growth, nutrients, pesticides, and land management. The model has been validated for several watersheds.

Input data used are terrain, landuse, soil, daily weather data (rainfall, maximum and minimum temperature, wind speed,, relative humidity and wind speed), cropping pattern, reservoirs and any man made structure with their characteristics.
The outputs provided by the model are very exhaustive covering all the components of water balance spatially and temporally. The sub components of the water balance that are more significant and were used for analyses include:

• Precipitation.

• Total flow (Water yield) consisting of surface runoff, lateral and base flow.

• Actual evapotranspiration (Actual ET).

• Base flow.

• Ground water recharge.

title: Average High Temperature
description:
Annual average high temperature, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Projected Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

title: Soil Carbon Stocks
description:
The International Soil Reference and Information Centre - World Soil Information (ISRIC-WIS) uses machine learning techniques to develop global maps of soil properties at various soil depths, as well as characterizing bedrock depth. Soil organic carbon stocks are reported in decigrams per kilogram for six standard depth intervals: depths of 0-5 cm, 5-15 cm, 15-30 cm, 30-60 cm, 60-100 cm, and 100-200 cm. Soil organic carbon stocks are important because they are correlated with the productive capacity of land to generate food and other plant life. Soil property estimates are generated using machine learning techniques that combine soil samples, expert opinion, and remote-sensing data. It takes as inputs soil observations from about 240,000 locations worldwide and over 400 global environmental covariates describing vegetation, terrain morphology, climate, geology and hydrology. The quantification of spatial uncertainty for this dataset showed metrics in line with previous studies at global, continental, or large region scale. The qualitative evaluation showed that coarse scale patterns are well reproduced.

title: [Archived] Global Land Cover (IPCC Classification)
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](b2f00f99-46ed-43e6-a7a1-a5809d9369d4) as a replacement.**_
  
The Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Land Cover (LC) project of the European Space Agency (ESA) delivers consistent global LC maps at 300 m spatial resolution on an annual basis from 1992 to 2019. Each pixel value corresponds to the label of a land cover class defined based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) categories. This unique data set was produced thanks to the reprocessing and the interpretation of 5 different satellite missions.   
  
Baseline LC maps are generated thanks to the entire MERIS FR and RR archive from 2003 through 2012. Independently from this baseline, LC changes are detected at 1 km based on the AVHRR time series between 1992 to 1999, SPOT-VGT time series between 1999 and 2013, and PROBA-V data from 2013. When MERIS FR or PROBA-V time series are available, changes detected at 1 km are remapped at 300 m. The last step consists in back- and updating the 10-year baseline LC map to produce the 28 annual LC maps from 1992 to 2019. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard
description:
### Overview  
  
The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset shows the projected inundation depth for river basins around the world, in a business as usual climate scenario. In this dataset, the inundation depth represents the depth of water over normally dry ground that would occur during 100-year floods. Inundation depths are calculated for the baseline year 2010 and predicted for future years 2030, 2050, and 2080. The dataset has a spatial resolution of 30 arc seconds, which is approximately 1 km x 1 km at the equator but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator.

  
  
Flooding is likely to intensify in the coming decades due to climate change. It is among the most serious of all global risks, causing loss of life and damage to property, livelihoods, and economies. As urbanization and economic growth put more people and assets into flood-prone areas, it is important to calculate flood risks and hazards around the world. However, these hazards are usually underestimated due to lack of data and information. This dataset helps change that by providing high resolution inundation depth data.

  
  
The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created by the World Resource Institute (WRI) to assist in creating water use policies and assessing flood risks. This dataset is part of WRI’s Aqueduct datasets. Aqueduct helps to identify and evaluate water risks around the world.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Aqueduct Riverine Flood Hazard dataset was created using a Global Flood Risk with
IMAGE Scenarios (GLOFRIS) framework. GLOFRIS combines a global hydrological model called PCRaster Global Water Balance (PCR-GLOBWB) with river and floodplain routing scheme to make long-term simulations of river discharges and flood levels for a variety of climate conditions. In addition, meteorological datasets from European Water and Global Change (EUWATCH) were used to force PCR-GLOBWB over various time periods. Floodplain water volumes were then calculated using the PCR-GLOBWB outputs for a 2010 baseline, along with future climate scenarios in 2030, 2050, and 2080. The output flood volumes were converted to high resolution inundation maps using a volume spreading flood model.

  
  
The “Riverine” hazard represents flooding from river overflow and occurs in river basins with an area of at least 10,000 kilometers squared. However, smaller floods do occur more regularly than larger floods. The data on Resource Watch shows what a 100-year flood (1% probability of occurrence per year) will look like for the selected years (2030, 2050, and 2080).

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Aqueduct also provides datasets on coastal hazards and other water risks. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/wat_067_rw0_aqueduct_riverine_flood_hazard).

title: Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature
description:
### Overview  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset shows the change in annual average temperature at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the temperature between the years 1985 and 2015. Average temperature projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.
  
  
The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Average Annual Temperature dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 
  
  
This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Projected Change in Annual Average Temperature dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

  
  
CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

  
  
The annual average temperature for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis using the following steps:

All daily low temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average low temperature value.
All daily high temperature data over a given year was extracted and averaged to produce a yearly average high temperature value.
Average annual temperature was calculated by taking the mean of the average daily temperature over a given year. Average daily temperature was calculated by dividing the sum of daily low temperature and daily high temperature by 2.

  
  
The average annual temperatures were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in annual average temperature.

  
  
The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the average temperature in 2000 is actually an average of the annual average temperatures between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows projected change NEX-GDDP RCP 8.5 data for [Projected Change in Annual Average Minimum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3d8e2e82-b33a-4898-90e5-6e4a1d007b82), [Projected Change in Annual Average Maximum Temperature](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/c4b12251-2d61-458f-a2c0-096c37901ade), [Projected Change in Heating Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/1d2f4eae-10e1-4ea6-980c-501b34106de2), [Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc), [Projected Change in Frost Free Season](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d3f512c0-fbb0-47d5-9ac9-a452574c8e58), [Projected Change in Extreme Heat Days](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/3941bbba-181b-434a-84c3-fcdfa5234735), [Projected Change in Annual Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/faf79d2c-5e54-4591-9d70-4bd1029c18e6), [Projected Change in Dry Spells](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/d0f46576-411d-48aa-8df8-d89a3792cdce), [Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/66d28bbc-1e6e-4156-9ba2-875ecab665af).

  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data. Additional data is available for emissions scenario RCP 4.5. For access to the original NEX-GDDP dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/cli_050-059_066-075_nexgddp_and_loca).

title: Maritime Boundaries
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2019 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries.

  
  
The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference).  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php).
